Your experience at Hamdeok (⑤) will vary wildly. It's a beach where things happen. Even swimming. Pros: Hamdeok is surrounded by some fairly muscular resort action for a beach of this size, and it gets more than its fair share of activities. Volleyball tournaments, beach parties, and above all the music festivals. If you happen to be around for the Stepping Stone Festival in July, go. The best concerts I have seen in Korea have been at Hamdeok. The audiences are happy, diverse, family friendly, and enthusiastic, and for the most part enjoy very moderate amounts of both testosterone and alcohol poisoning - emphasis on   for the most part  . Hamdeok is fairly central. It's close to Jeju City and many of the activities and sites that make Jeju a growing tourist destination, but far enough away from the airport that you are not always drowning in swarms of airplanes and their contents. You can find a variety of decent places to eat in the vicinity. The sand and surf is a very pleasant combination of white, blue and green. If you've been to Australia or Hawaii, you probably won't be impressed. However, for Korea it's superb, and for Jeju it's a solid place to go if you want to do some casual swimming. But take note: this is not where you go for snorkeling or quiet sunbathing. Hamdeok does boast some strong outdoor lighting for evening swims, which is nice, as well as some convenient and beautiful coastal walks/hikes, often punctuated with spectacular sunsets. Cons: This is a small beach which can very easily become overcrowded, or even insanely overcrowded. It can also be noisy enough during the weekend to drive away even the most dedicated of extroverts. The first time I went to Hamdeok I became convinced that the loud speakers - all blaring entirely different music and/or announcements at the same time - were actually designed to create overlapping kill zones. There are tables with umbrellas for rent on the beach, as well as stands with various floating devices, but they are all of average quality at best, and I found the entire set up disruptive of the beach experience. The swimming is fair, but don't expect to do much more than just swimming. I've seen waves at Hamdeok, but not often, and certainly not much in the way of water sports like surfing. And keep in mind that Korean lifeguards are assiduous in their monitoring of swimmers - i.e. you won't be able to go out too far before the whistles blow. The bathroom facilities are weak, with austere changing areas, and ice cold showers that you have to pay for. Bring your own shampoo, etc. Hamdeok is also growing in popularity, so the current balance of tourists-to-beach may soon tip into an unacceptable range. There are already times when driving along the beachfront road becomes an exercise in patience and defensive driving, often due to gallivanting hordes of people under the influence of tourism, which is far worse than alcohol when it comes to lowering inhibitions and promoting idiocy. There has also been a troubling increase in the kind of businesses that want to capitalize on the   tourist beach experience  , selling tawdry souvenirs, poorly handled food, and watered down drinks made with the worst commercially available ingredients they can find. You will know them by their flashing lights and loud, thumpingly generic club music being boom-boxed into your face. However, considered these places a   pro   if you enjoy the spring break mentality and mild diarrhea. Lastly, the weather of Jeju is capricious, so just accept the fact that it will probably rain at least once as you storm the beach. But that's just Jeju.

You can get here from Seogwipo on the 701 bus - costs 3,300 KRW each way and takes about 80 minutes.  After the bus drops you off, turn off one of the streets to the right and keep walking until you find the parking lot and entrance way.  There's a small exhibition before the ticket office, but there's not much in there, lots of photos and a little signage.  There's also a water drinking fountain just outside if you need to fill up.Note there are no garbage bins, so you will need to take all rubbish away with you.  Entrance fee is 2000 KRW.  All well signposted and lots of steps.  It will take about about 20 minutes to walk to the top.  There are lots of places to stop and sit and take photos and there are lookouts at the top for photos in all directions.  When you get to the top, all you can do it look around and come back down again.  You're not able to walk around inside the cone or around the edges.  (so yes we took our picnic back down again).When you walk back down, be sure to go to the small cove on the right hand side where you will see a (FREE) exhibition of women divers.    This happens at 130pm and 3pm.  Five older women divers took to the water, with their full old wetsuits on and 10 minutes later started coming back in with the octupus that they had caught. Only two caught some while we were there and came back out of the water clutching it, straight to the area where they sell the seafood that you can buy and take into the restaurant area to get it cooked for you.It's a pleasant way to spend an hour or so, but its a pain to make a specific trip here from Seogwipo (and longer from Jeju City), so plan something else around it.

Whilst I'm giving the Teddy Bear Museum just 2 stars for quality, value for money, class of exhibits, and any actual worth as a proper   museum  , I have to admit that my visit made me laugh. I'm not sure though that derisive snorting sarcasm was what they were looking for.This museum is a pile of pants, masquerading as teddy bears.. The   attractions   are about 15 to 20 poor quality adult-human-sized bears, dressed in various outfits of clothing, with a challenge to guess   who   they are dressed as. Military uniform and two medals apparently is enough for a bear to resemble Prince William, for example - and a grey wig and   E=mc2   to represent Einstein.Then there are the bear portraits. Frames containing bears dressed to vaguely resemble famous portraits. Mona Lisa teddy bear, anyone?There's no   history   of the teddy bear, no collection of historical bears, no pictures / video clips of teddy bears being made, no maps showing where different types of teddy bears originated from - nothing educational whatsoever. There are no audio tours, no leaflets or signs to show the visitor around, and certainly no staff available to talk to about any   exhibits  , whether you are Korean, English, American or anything else.The gift shop on the lowest floor contained the largest number of bears - none of them particularly special, all just your usual cheap mass-produced bears, but at slightly hiked up prices.By far the worst part of the visit was the funniest. Your ticket includes entry to the   Elvis Stage Show  . Oh dear Lord, where on earth do I start? The show is on every 15 minutes. In a room with about 12 benches in it. There is a curtain at the far end, hiding the   stage  . On the quarter hour, the announcement is made -   The King of Rock and Roll, Elvis, is in the house!   The curtains open, and there it is. The Elvis Presley Show. Six, sad, lonely looking teddy bears, dressed in stage show outfits, rocking gently on their animatronic sticks. The three backing singers sway gently on the right, the drummer's arms flail up and down towards the drums, the guitarist's arm moves.Elvis meanwhile gyrate and swivels his hips, the crowd goes wild. Oh, no, sorry, that last sentence was a lie. Elvis sways and looks like he almost falls several times.Worst animatronic puppetry in the world. Hilarious. Hilariously BAD. Less than two minutes later, the curtains shut, and   Elvis has left the building   - until the next showing in approximately 12 or 13 minutes' time....Don't go to the Teddy Bear Museum thinking you'll have an interesting visit. Go to see the absolutely bizarre vision that South Koreans have of   entertainment  .

While we were excited to visit the longest lava cave in Asia, we were very disappointed. There is no path to walk on in the cave except for very limited areas, so this makes for a difficult walk on slipperly and very uneven surfaces with deep puddles everywhere, making it essential to watch your every step rather than enjoying the cave. The lighting in the cave is ridiculous and poorly done, with sparingly placed bright lights aimed at the path rather than on the sides of the cave, so that your eyes are hit with bright lights such that you can't see the actual cave well. The few parts they lit, they added changing colours so you can't actually see the natural colours of the cave. Walking through the 1 km available does not provide much change in the scenery, so it was more an exercise than an interesting exploration.I'd recommend that you visit the caves within Hallim Park, which are much better presented with a safe path to walk on. Although the path throught the three sections of the cave are shorter, you can see much more. Go to Halim Park and skip Manjang Cave.

When we arrived at Jeju, we took a taxi to Jejueco and left our luggage with time since check-in time was in the afternoon. All in all, there are 6 themed model parks with over 250 models exhibited: they include the world?s largest glass ball and largest glass diamond, a glass stonewall, a mirror lake, and a glass bridge etc...The exhibition was definitely a breathtaking sight to behold: glass displays made of all kinds of shapes and sizes! We couldn't help but be amazed and ended up taking - pictures of all the art pieces. For more on the experience and photos, please check out my blog: http://www.travelbytez.com/2015/02/glass-castle-jeju.html

When visiting other countries I realize the treatment of animal standards may differ, but I at least look for animals to be happy. This falconry “center”was bittersweet. Some of the animals had wonderful enclosures, but the birds of prey were treated very inhumanly. The same birds of prey/owls were tied to stands for the whole 3 hours we were there, with no food or water, in the blaring sun, with no supervision as people crowded and tried to touch them to the point they would flinch or try to fly away, only to be yanked by their chains. Their inhumane treatment brought tears to our eyes. At the far part of the center, we came upon their enclosures, cages about 5 x 5 x5 feet wide, where other birds of prey were chained, with little place to move and absolutely no enrichment toys.? This is unacceptable. There was a raccoon in a small enclosure with no enrichment toys, solely used for tourists to take selfies with. Last but not least, a pair of Coaty were also in a small enclosure. Their baby was on display in a small cage by the gift shop with no water. This “Center” does have some acceptable enclosures for fowl, rabbits, budgies, and the alpaca interaction was amazing, but surely they can treat all their animals with dignity. While we were there, a macaw flew away into the surrounding trees. Clearly the parrot did not have an attached handler nor proper training for flighted birds.

What a great place to visit especially on a rainy dayIt traces the history of computing from the 50s to the present day in a very informative wayHowever of somewhat more interest to particularly children is the very interactive history of computer gaming. This includes the ability to play the old games like tv tennis and space invaders to more modern gamesA great way to spend a couple of hours , it certainly kept me and the grandchildren entertained
Went with my kids and parents. We explore every part of the park. From Caves, cactus to folk villages. We enjoy the plantation at the park and flowers definitely. Must visit

Went up and down seongpanak. Went with my parents who are in their early 50s. The way up gets a little tough after the 12:30 point. We started at 6:30 and got to that area by 11:00. On the way down gets very boring. Bring lots of water and wear shoes. You'll see old Korean people wearing stuff you'd wear to summit some crazy mountain but just good shoes with good grip (not converse) will be good for the hike. Of course hiking boots would help. Things to bring: hand sanitizer, water, sunscreen, gatorade/pocari sweat if it's very hot. Bring some food and bags for trash as you have to take it all with you. Overall probably 4/5 experience but nice to experience with family. Probably not good for young kids - people with health problems die each year per locals.

Went there with my friend, we took bus from Jungmun (at the bus stop nearby tourist information center, at the right hand side). We took bus no. 781 and alighted at Teddy valley golf and resort, from there turn left (after you alighted) and walk straight for 1 min, you will see the museum at your left hand side. The entrance ticket cost 12000 won per adult. There are gift shop, Kitty History Hall, Music Education Hall, Art Gallery, Hello Kitty Caf챕, 3D Theater and more.. The Hello Kitty Cafe is very big and is beautifully designed and decorated.. There are a lot of cute hello kitty inside the museum and there are also some outside the museum. If you are a hello kitty fan, this is a must visit place when you come to Jeju.The museum closes at 6pm, so you might want to go there earlier.

Went there twiceFirst time we went there was already late, around 10pmOur hotel concierge recommended one particularly bbq restaurantBut, the restaurant that we want to eat was already closedSo we ate restaurant next to itIt was good and cost us around 30.000 won for 2 personThe next day,We ate the restaurant that we wantIt was amazingBetter than beforeI definetely come here again

Went there by bus using the 201 bus line, it will stop you to the 'entrance' (basically the highway) which is a long far walk into the actual entrance. There's a small bus stop where you can take another bus in (slow) but taxis will frequent the highway entrance looking for customers. The cave itself its a magnificent sight to behold..it's huge! Not sure about all the negative reviews about it poorly lit and all, because the place is actually adequately lit (to fit the ambiance of a cave, no artificial colored disco lights) and concrete steps are placed everywhere in the tunnel to prevent accidental missteps. The ground is naturally uneven, you can't expect marbled tiles here. It can get quite cold and wet at 10-13deg, so bring a light jacket and proper walking shoes. Overall it's quite an experience, you can tell your friends that you've been in the underbelly of a volcano!

Went there as part of tour. Find it really fascinating n entertaining. Worth it to go there one afternoon. Takes only 15 mins... Bus turn off engine, pour warmer on the road, letting water bottle roll, n closing your eyes n walk!

went there after breakfast and was a good time to start if you didn't care too much of sunrise view. Even though it was windy and chilly, got up to the top sweaty and hot. you see see pretty ckear view from the top; Udo island, the wind turbines in the east, Seopjikoji in the south.
went part of Yeha east tour. Spent 1 hour hiking deep inside the caves. Beautiful, damp and enjoyable.

Went on a day hike up and down the Seongpanak trail! It was a gorgeous day, about 18C and I couldn't have asked for better weather. It took about 10 hours round trip. Started around 8:30am and made it down by 6:30pm. Luckily the sun didn't go down until 7:15ish so I had plenty of light to guide me.Now, I am not a hiker by any means and this was one of the toughest hikes I've been on. To be honest, it wasn't because the trails were all that difficult - it was actually quite pleasant through the woods and there were 2 rest stops along the way. The first stop is basically a bathroom break and the 2nd had some food available before heading up the last (somewhat steeper) trail to the lake up top. Oh, by   food   I mean some cup ramen and snacks. They also sold water and sports drinks. It would be helpful for you to bring food of your own. They also have no garbage cans so you need to carry and dispose of your own trash once you get back down.The reason why this trail was difficult for me was because I simply wasn't ready for a 20km hike! By the last 5km of the descent, I felt my feet and legs were going to fall off or give in to becoming jelly due to all the stairs and rocks. Make sure you have proper shoes! All in all, I'm glad I did this hike - it was worth it when I got to the top and was able to experience amazing views and clean air. And the flowers!! It was simply beautiful. Just expect to have sore calves for a few days following :)

Went in the morning. The view is breathtaking. Must visit. Korean artists love this place for a good reason. Featured in some korean shows as well. It's very pretty. Packed some sandwiches, lay a mat, have a breakfast and feel the breeze.

Went for a stroll after visiting Hanna Mountain. The cactus conservatory was impressive and we rounded up that part of Hallim Park with a thirst quenching cactus drink.  Similarly the cool walk into the lava cave, and the connecting limestone cave was particularly enjoyable, taking shelter from the melting sun. Highlight of this trip was feeding of birds inside a bird house.   We purchased their food at the vending machine.  Having them eating out of one's palm brought back fond memories of childhood.

Well, its certainly not the Giant's Causeway, but still quite an impressive natural rock formation.  We were at the convention centre and found ourselves with a few hours spare one afternoon so it was a no-brainer to stroll down to the coast and view this rare feature.  Fairly busy, then then so is the GC.   Comfortable walkways and great views.  Certainly something to fill your trip to that part of the world with.

Well, if you like teddy bears, drop by this place to see their collection.  Honestly, I get more excited browsing teddy bears at a departmental store.  This place is probably losing its charm as it is mainly visited by tourists sent here by tour buses and very little koreans or free-n-easy tourists.

Well, at the shore, practically still in the city, you can find this rock which probably originates from a lava eruptions, as everything on this island. With some imagination, I could identify a dragon's head. Nothing particular. It's like one tour guide said: everything on Jeju island is small and cute.

Well worth the trip! The museum is very well presented and organized. So cute! So pink! Lots of kids and laughter about. You can opt to pay for extras, like buttons, passport stamp collecting and heart shaped tag to write on and lock onto the balcony. Some furniture is a bit run down but overall it is really well cared for. The staff is very friendly and helpful. You can also get small food and drink from the cafe and there is a jungle gym are for children to play. They have a short movie and photo station on the roof at the end. The gift shop had lots to choose from and prices were pretty good compared to official merchandise sold elsewhere online. Spent almost the whole day there and I loved every second of it. The museum is incredibly interactive, it would be hard not to have fun. Brought my boyfriend and even he couldn't believe how fun it was :)

We were very excited that our trip coincided with the market. The market was packed with people and it seemed like all the locals were there and had been looking forward to it all week.We bought fruits and snacks there. Prices are definitely cheaper than at the marts. Although the aunts and uncles manning the stalls didn't speak much English, they were all very helpful and we communicated mainly with gestures and our limited vocabulary. Do try all the snacks and eat at the food stalls there!

We were there on a tour bus, the trick to this road is actually from the surrounding which trick your eyes into believing that you are going up hill when in fact the slope is going downhill. Only go to this place if you are part of the tour otherwise waste of time.

We were on a mountain holiday.  OUr goal was to walk up the highest mountain in each country.  Korea's Hallam Mountain was our first country and our first mountain. Be prepared if you have not hiked in Korea before to be the dowdiest dresser on the mountain!  Our Korean friends are the snappiest dressed walkers on earth.  Oh, and don't think you will ever be alone.  On the day of our walk it was slow raining,misty and miserable.  Early in the morning, getting off the bus and thinking no-one else would be silly enough to walk on such a miserable day, we were so surprised to see great crowds of Korean tourists all decked out to walk up Halla.  We  packed lunch before we left but there is a good restaurant to the right of the car/bus park where you can get a good breakfast for a fixed price and also order lunch to take with you up the mountain.  Halla proved to be a challenge even though it is the lowest altitude moiuntain  of the countries we will visit.  The access track is very long and because traffic is regulated in both directions you must keep up a steady pace to get to the check points on time.  This is the most critical advice we can provide.  Check locally  and carefully what times you can climb up, and what times you need to come down the mountain.  Finally enjoy.  We were constantly overtaken by our Korean climbers who relished the speed of their ascent and descent, but in the end we both arrived together since they always found time to have a snack and a drink along the way.  Great fun, go slow, enjoy!  Oh, and avoid the snow and ice patches that were still plenty in late April - take/rent walking poles.

We were lucky to start the hike with a beautiful warm Autumn day and clear skies. We started around 7 in the morning at the Gwamneumba campsite, getting a taxi ride from Jeju city was easy and cheap - about 10500 won gets you right in front of the gate. We chose to go Gwamneumsa - Seongpanak, as research suggests that most people who did it preferred to avoid masses of people.. Gwamneumsa also boasts the best views, and it sure lived up to it.The Gwamneumsa trail was lovely at first, most tranquil. But then shortly afterwards, it started getting quite difficult having to balance hopping between and stepping up uneven surfaces of lava rocks..Great views came 2/3's in and at the very last part of the trail.. There's also drinking water available at a small fountain in front of a bridge 2/3 way in. The bathrooms on this trail were pretty gross, one of those toilets that pile waste at the bottom - only that the bottom wasn't very far down.. I would say the bottom was less than a metre, many outdoor bathrooms have their toilets down 20m!.. But consider oneself to be lucky to have bathrooms!We reached the summit around 1pm, having taken countless 2 minute breaks along the way. We were quite slow and took it easy. The lake at the top looked much like a drying pond, I think views would probably have looked better in the Spring. There's nothing much else there, a resting area, a helipad and a wifi tower.Next - Climbing down Seongpanak trail.. The first check point on the Seongpanak trail sells FOOD! We didn't know that, as many sources state there are no food stalls on the mountain.. There's 2 minute noodles, chocolate, bottled water, pocari sweat, tissues, etc. Then on the checkpoint after that you have a small fountain of drinking water.The rest of the trail was a nightmare. We didn't have the correct hiking gear and very underprepared trekking in sneakers and boots. Many say that Seongpanak is easier because its a slope, but having to balance each step as we walked on lava rocks was most tiresome. 99% of the time you're just looking down at your feet making sure it lands on a rock, and you're doing it in a hurry because you're trying to reach the end before the sun sets! And you'd probably be doing that for about 6km.It would have been much easier to go up Seongpanak and down Gwamneumsa, as it is much easier to go down by steps rather than on a slope with uneven rocky terrain.Make sure you have the correct hiking gear - sticks and shoes. Our legs ached! Mostly caused by keeping our balance on the uneven, rocky terrain. My partner ended up with a crook knee, micro ligament tear. We reached the exit gate at 5:30pm! Taxi ride back to Jeju city was about 15000 won.I give this 3 stars because a lot of effort is involved for minimal reward. Yes it is a mountain, and I have hiked other incredible mountains with magnificent views like huangshan and wulingyuan. My expectations were very high as well, the most you get are views of the city, mountain fauna ( though very beautiful), and the drying lake. Do it for the enjoyment of experience and go the other direction, climbing down Gwamneumsa would be so much easier as there are better stairs, not just kilometres of rocks on a slope! And with the right gear! ;)Enjoy!

We were fortunate to catch a not-as-crowded ferry at around 2plus and stayed till 530pm and got back around 6pm. Ferry ride takes around 15mins but get up early and start walking towards the exit if u don't want to be Squashed w the main crowd! Upon arrival on the island, we decided to take the bus tour (costs 5000KRW/pax) which stops at 2 locations- the lighthouse peak as well as the beach.I must say Udo is very very windy so make sure u gear up and tie your hair if necessary!Hiking up to the lighthouse took us around 15mins up(lots of stairs, but after that it's v scenic). We had a good view of the whole island, despite being drizzly throughout the day. Dennis Cafe is really nice, cozy and affordable peanut ice cream as compared to the crowded 'Running man' ice cream shop which wasn't actually good. If I could go back, I would definitely bring my international driving license and rent an E bike!

We were dropped by a taxi at the beginning of the Seongpanak trail (a little way up the volcano), but you can catch the bus there if you prefer and there is a bus stop right near the entrance. The track is 9.6km (19.2km return), and took us about 6 hours return walking at a medium pace, including breaks at Sokbat shelter (4.1kms up - toilet facilities only) and at Jindallaebat shelter (7.3kms up - toilet and small kiosk). We had initially wanted to walk up the Gwaneumsa trail and then down the Seongpanak one, but were too tired to get up before 6am to achieve it in one day. Walking the Seongpanak trail up and down was a great experience in itself, even though it is apparently not as scenic as others. But, because it's one of the easier ones, it is packed with tourists, most of whom are not seasoned walkers, so be prepared for being held up a fair bit (and witnessing some pretty avoidable but hilarious injuries!).The trail is quite an easy one in comparison to other hikes we have done - no really steep bits or actual climbing - more of a gentle incline, with boardwalks in parts, dirt paths and as you get higher, rough rocky paths. The only strenuous thing about the trail is that it is long? It will take you all day, and you have to start early so you reach the Jindallaebat shelter before a certain hour (changes depending on the season, but in September it was 12:30pm) or the ranger won't let you continue - for obvious reasons, there's no lighting at night to climb back down, so he doesn't want to come and find stupidly lost tourists! You can check the times on the official Hallasan website. You don't really need proper hiking boots/other equipment for this hike (we did it in light walking shoes), but if you have weak ankles I would probably recommend wearing hiking boots with ankle support, especially for the walk back down the rocky paths. Take plenty of water and snacks - don't rely on the shelters like the Koreans do, they may sell out/be extremely busy, and you have to get to Jindallaebat by 12:30! We just bought some muesli bars, fruit, WATER and energy drinks like gatorade/powerade at a 7/11 before we left Jeju city in the morning, and were almost the only ones who had thought ahead! On the way back down, the Jindallaebat shelter will be quieter, so it's the perfect opportunity to then buy some of their hot ramen noodles or a chocolate bar. I would also recommend bringing a light rain jacket, and a waterproof backpack/cover for your backpack - it showers sporadically within the fog. I also took a plastic bag to put my camera in to keep it dry.When we began our walk, it was quite chilly at the entrance and the local walkers laughed at us wearing shorts - but by the time you get a few kilometres in, you'll be stripping off layers of clothing, so totally wear shorts if you want to - it's quite warm in the sun on the summit, so everyone will be peeling off their layers anyway! There was a thick fog hanging low over the volcano for about 2/3 of the walk, so it's a bit muggy, but the side of the mountain is lush and green, an eerily quiet forest. As you get higher, suddenly you notice you're climbing above the fog - feels like you've popped out above the clouds, on top of the world! The last part of the track is quite windy, and you can see how the wind has beaten its wooden steps, which are strewn everywhere. Be careful in the last part and beware pushy tourists! But, once you get to the summit, at Dongneung Peak (no facilities on the summit, by the way), the view is breathtakingly beautiful - like nothing I've ever seen before! The crater when we were there was overgrown with vegetation, with a small crater lake. Such a wonderful experience, and most definitely a highlight of our trip to South Korea! You must hike Hallasan during your stay at Jeju-do!

we were definitely not prepared for this - in terms of experience and equipment!started off at about 9am on the Eorimok route. the entrance was a 10 min walk from the bus stop. then, it was off on the hike!initially the trail was straightforward. then it gradually went into a steep ascent. the path was quite rocky and unstable. but there were sufficient rest stops along the way. also people going in the same and opposite direction to you so you will not be alone (unless you hike in the middle of the night)there were also multiple signboards along the route providing interesting facts about Hallasan and also maps showing your current location and remaining distances to go to the next point.there was almost a natural portable water point where you can refill your bottles. remember to stay hydrated throughout and take breaks when needed.needless to say, the views along the route were truly breathtaking but the higher elevation you reach, the colder it becomes. also, the winds were very strong!we reached the Witseoreum shelter at about 12pm and had lunch there. The locals actually brought hot water in their thermos flasks and had cup ramen there!after lunch, we started our descent on the Yeongsil trail and reached the entrance of Yeongsil at about 2pm and there was a 2km walk out of the entrance to the bus stop.by then our legs were aching and heavy, but we pushed on. overall the hike took about 5 hrs.in summary, we should have worn more proper hiking footwear, wear thicker clothing (as higher you go, the colder it gets) and more food and snacks!we decided we will come back to attempt the summit next time.

We were brought to this house with an old man waiting for us. He gave us a tour around his house and then started selling us omjia tea, honey, horse bones pill, horse oil products. And they range from 45,000KRW to 140,000KRW. I'm not sure if there was any way you could avoid this.

We were a little disappointed after walking all the way down the hill at Sunrise Peak to see the women divers, only to find out that because of the holiday, they wouldn't be diving today.So as a consolation, our tour guide took us to the Haenyeo Museum.  This museum was dedicated to the Haenyeo women divers of Jeju and Japan.  It's a very nice museum with excellent displays, and you will learn a lot about the divers.I recommend seeing the video show before you start wandering around.

We went with high expectation, thinking that we could go into the larva tube. To our utmost disappointment, besides a 4-D movie, It was just a museum with some picture exhibits, and glassed up exhibits of a very small part of the larva tube. Admission was W3,000. It took us a long time to get there, as the bus was a 50 minute wait and it was extremely cold that day.

we went up by erimok, was the slightly shorter course but scenery was still fantastic towards the top. took us 3.3hours to reach the 1700m resting point which sells korean cup noodles at only 1500+won (ard there). this is not the peak, if you like to challenge yourself further, will have to walk for another 3-4 hours to the peak. So if you really decide to go to the peak, then just use the Seongpanak or Gwaneumsa course, its shorter.We were lucky to meet some locals who advise us to walk down by yeongsil. And apparently yeongsil has the most scenic view out of all the courses. Only thing is that its full of stairs... so dont advice ascending by yeongsil. We could see ppl giving up halfway on our way down yeongsil. One more problem abt yeongsil for those who dont drive is that the bus stops 2km away from the main entrance (20mins BRISK walk) and its quite steep on most parts. Or else you can actually catch a taxi from the bus stop, should be a 5mins journey.

We went to this folks village on our own but not with tour, therefore when we reached there, there is only 5 of us, the staff approached us and starts telling us Jeju Folks Cultural stories, the entrance is free and the guide is free, but at the end of the guide, you'll be brought to a room where they'll start selling you the local specialties, we got some discount since we're not with tour (as usually places like this required to pay tour agent some fees), but if you don't want to buy anything, just say thank you & leave, that's all 븝

We went to the Jungmun Golf Club to have a Moonlight Walking Tour as part of the preparation for the 2020 Jeju Olle Walking Festival. The tour took us only 30 minutes, and later on, we enjoyed performances by local artists under the bright moon. You can witness the mesmerizing scenery of the sunset and the sea from the golf course.

We went to the Glass Castle in spite of the 9000 Won entry fee simply because of all the hassle we had gone through to get there. Inside, it was really nothing more than a glass art museum, and a relatively small one at that. Admittedly, there were some very creative works of art, but there was a lot that wasn't that impressive as well. Over half of it is outside so, if you are there on a rainy day like we were, that will kill the experience even more. If you have young children forget it, there is almost nothing for them to do without spending additional money for them to make a glass craft. The crafts are neat but spendy. At the end of the museum, there is a gift store that, in my opinion, was really the only good reason to come here. Lots of cool trinkets to get for gifts and souvenirs - of special note are the hand painted, hollow, personalizeable, crystal balls. If you are up to the trip and willing to pay the cash to look at glass art go for it. Otherwise, there are other more interesting things around to do.

We went to see waterfall at 12PM, there were loads of people, nevertheless view was stunning, waterfall is huge. I'd say better go in day time as when sun is starting to set you'd get weird shadows on your pics and it just won't be the same. Bear in mind you'll have to walk on huge rocks so it's not very safe for toddlers and those carrying their babies, not suitable for those with walking difficulties. Better wear sports clothes which would cover legs in case you fall, to prevent scratches or whatever other injuries. It says no swimming but we took off our shoes and walked in shallow water. It was cold but fun. We also sat on rocks in close proximity to waterfall and splashes from it made us quite wet. But it was spectacular. Such a unique place! Tickets are 1,000 for 16-24 year olds, they require ID. For adults it's 2,000.

We went to Ilchul Land primarily for Micheon cave. For families and those with small children this cave is great. We even saw some strollers making there way in the dark. We went in July and while it was hot and humid outside  inside the cave we needed light jackets - the difference in temperature was that drastic. The kids walked down and immediately asked for their sweaters. That said  the temperature change was welcome on such a hot summer day. The cave is not very long which is great for kids  it's fairly well lit while maintaining the dark atmosphere of an underground cave. It's wet inside  like most caves are so be sure to have some good shoes on and the part open to the public is quite large with some parts requiring you to duck (clearance for a short section is 1.5 meters).Apart from the cave the other attractions are good if you're looking for a leisurely stroll with things to see. The park is set up so that you follow a blue line on the ground that takes you through all the different parts of Ilchul Land. There were a number of sculptures  some gardens  Jeju stone men  and artwork. The cactus garden was hot and interesting. Not many   activities   on the walk but a good stroll. I forget the exact admission price but I believe it was about ??0000 per adult and ??000 per child.

We went to eorimok trail to enjoy the winter festival. Great outdoor fun for children. Best part its free (except for 1,000krw parking fees). My kid loves d slide!! There?s even a museum to learn how hallasan mountain was formed. In my opinion this is the best place to visit in jeju.

We went there with both of our children (at the time, 4 and 2 years old). There was plenty for them both to see and neither of them got bored. My 4 year old particularly liked the lava tubes and both my wife and I found them very interesting too!

We went there for sunrise. We just took 20 minutes to reach the look out points and waited for the sun rise, but since the route is steep and made up of only stairs, a more relaxed walk should be planned.Turn right to the farthest end after descending from the look out where the outer landscape of this tuff cone can be seen clearly.Mind there are two flights of stairs. One for uphill  and one for downhill.There are   diving women   shows at 1330 and 1500 if the weather is good.2000 won for adult admission.

We went on a cloudy day and the driver drove us all the way to the entrance at Yeongsil.  Having a hot afternoon the day before, we thought it would be warmer thN the day before as we Han to walk uphill. The driver saw us in our thin layer, offered me a rain and wind breaker and a pair of gloves. I reluctantly accepted them out of courtesy but later genuinely thanked him after four hours.On a windy and cloudy October morning, the temperature actually dropped as we ascended. Two hours later it got even much colder with strong gusts, as we approached near to split of the main road to either continue uphil to the top, or to go downhill to the other parking lot. I had to use my gloves and another layer there. My husband regretted not bring his hat on a cloudy day to protect his cold ears (anyway later I found his nose sunburnt even on a cloudy day)We used our walking sticks and wore our hiking shoes, which I found very helpful. We saw some people who really had difficulty completing the loop.  I suggest tourists first decide whether you physically can complete the four hour trip (adults) to the other parking lot. If not, better discuss with your driver (if using one) to meet in the starting point, or decide where to park your car, if not taking the bus.Pack your bag reasonably and don't take any unnecessary items. Some snacks are helpful though as there are no snack bar at all. I suggest also try to bring your garbage downhill as I don't think there will be regular cleaner everyday up/downhill for hours'hike.
We went in a downpour and did not expect much.  However, the artists who designed the tableaux are very creative.  You can't help smiling.

We went here on our way to south jeju.It was a nice place where we can see the various art forms possible with glass.A sculpture of a horse made with glass was displayed, which was really looking cool...

We wanted to hike to the summit of the Hallasan mountain, and decided to use the Seongpanak trail.It's roughly 9 kms from the parking lot to the summit, and it took us around 2h50m at a constant pace with few stops. This is a very scenic hike starting in the middle of the forest, and close to the top through prairies. The hike is properly maintained with stairs and paths, but some parts have many rocks, and thus proper hiking shoes are highly recommended.The views from the summit are spectacular!

We want to cover a few attractions in one day, thus, we chosen the shorter route up a part of Mount Hallasan (can't recall the name if the trail). Glad, we made the right choice, 1.3km up to 1,163m in about 45min, not really scenic until you reach the top. The trail is very well laid, easy to walk, good for beginners and not so fit. Up, enjoy the view, photo taking and down, all done in <2.5 hours.

We walked up Yeongsil and down Eriomok. Would definitely recommend getting a taxi right up to the start of the trail if you want to start walking straight away. As other mentioned, it is a long, winding up hill 2.5 km walk from the bus stop. It cost us 30,000 won in a taxi from the other side of Seogwipo. The walk up was beautiful and the rest area with bathrooms at the top was  a surprise. We brought all our own food and drinks and didn?t see anywhere selling, which we enjoyed at the top. The walk down was equally lovely although the hard bit lasted longer so we were glad we did it on the way down. A short 10 minute walk from the base of Erimok are the bus stop going to Jeju City or Seogwipo. All in all it was a lovely hike and we thoroughly enjoyed it. Took us about 6 hours including numerous stops here and there and a 30 minute lunch break.

We walked up the Gwanmeusan Trail, only 20 minutes from downtown Jeju-si. It took us, going slowly with lots of rests about 9.5 hours. Good hiking shoes required. We witnessed multiple shoe failures. You have to hike back down shoeless if your shoes rip apart and they will due to the volcanic rocks used on the rrail. The rocks are cute until they aren't. They are murder on the feet, ankles, knees, and legs on the way down.We went in April 20 and it was warm... only one water stop about 3/4 way up.18+ miles round trip. Please ask questions if you have concerns. It is quite breathtaking but a strenuous hike. Many turn back early. Must make it to the Samgakbong shelter by 12:30. No support on the trail.... 2 bathrooms though about 1/4 and 3/4 way up. Must start return hike by 2PM... still took us 4 hours to down due to strenuous terrain and infinite number of stairs.

We visited Woljeongri Beach as a rest stop while driving just to have some ice cream.  Even though the weather wasn?t particularly good in the midst of the monsoon season, the beach still looked amazing with turquoise water.  You can go pretty far out and the water remains shallow although we didn?t go in as the water was a bit cold.  There isn?t a lot of parking available nearby but plenty of decent restaurants and cafes nearby.

We visited Udo with my brother as part of our trip on Jeju. It is easily accessible via ferry (don't forget to bring your passport to buy a ticket!). We did the recommended tour (4h, with lunch time) and it was beautiful: campaign, port, cliffs, lighthouse... We definitely recommend it. We rate it 4 stars and not 5 because of the garbages on the island, it wastes the beautiful landscapes!

We visited Udo Island in October 2016 and took the hop on hop off bus and got off at the first stop to climb up to the peak where the lighthouse was.  The climb took about an hour and though there were steps and a well travelled path, it still required some physical effort. There were hardly any trees and you would be well advised to wear a hat and sun block. Wear comfortable walking/hiking shoes and bring plenty of drinking water.  We climbed to the peak on a hot sunny day and had to stop a few times before we reached the lighthouse. The view was worth our effort.  Then we climbed down to the surrounding park, which was basically grassland with minimal trees and hardly any shelter. There were lots of other tourists.  We saw some horses grazing here and could see across to the mainland and sunrise peak as well as parts of Udo below.  This is the most enjoyable part of UDO for us and highly recommended.

We visited this site with a group of friends.Everybody had their own take on the mysterious road and all had their theories. A quick visit to the internet would provide the answer. However, this all detracts from the pure fun of the site itself. However, part of the fun is discussing the   mystery   of the road.The site is a simple narrow two-lane road. It is not huge. There is plenty of parking for visitors to stop and examine the surroundings.  There are snack stalls along the road where refreshments and some simple snacks can be bought. I noticed some posts on TA that say this is a   tourist trap  . I do not see how this would be the case as nobody is forced to buy or pay for anything.  Anything we bought was food, which, to me, does not seem to be predatory on tourists. In fact, I was hungry and thirsty and was happy to purchase some cooked local yams and cool refreshment. There are tourist traps on the island, but this is not one of them.Having said the above, the attraction is not a major development and is not meant to be a huge event to take up one's itinerary. It is a fun and simple site to visit which can be added to the list of places to visit when in Jeju.

We visited this road on the way back to the airport (stayed on South side of the island).  I would recommend this attraction if you happened to be on road-1139 or in the vicinity (e.g., visiting Loveland, or hiking trails nearby.  There are plenty of nicer things to see and do on the island but it?s worth a look/see, if you?re in the ?neighborhood.?  My wife got a kick out of it, using the water bottle, as previously advised by another post.  I was less than thrilled and found the art along the road and cafes to be more interesting around the mid-way point of the attraction.

We visited this area on our volcanic forces lava tour through Expedia in November 2016.  It was a cool, windy day so we didn't spend even an hour here.  Maybe 45 minutes.  You have to take stairways down to the cliff area.  Then we were freezing even with our layers and coats due to the wind blowing right through us.  It reminded us of the lava cliffs along the coast of Volcanoes National Park on the Hilo-side of the Big Island.  There are even palm trees in the garden area before you start descending towards the Oceanside cliffs.

We visited these as part of our guided tour and were impressed by the surrounding scenery and location. It's a wonderful way to see Jeju at its best, and the rocks are quite impressive. It doesn't take as long to see as you would think, but still worth an hour or so.

We visited the National Park as well as Mt. Hallasan during our trip to Jeju-do. It is a beautiful park with average to good hiking trails. We took the long trail (Seongpanak, 9,6km) up to the summit, which took us 2,5 hours (i will take you much longer if you hike slowly and take breaks!). The view from the Summit was just stunning! Definately worth it! I'd advise anybody hiking this trail to wear boots or other firm shoes since the trail is very steep and rock at some parts. You also have to start early in the morning (~8am) since you have to reachthe second station until 1pm to be allowed to go to the summit. Geaneumsa trail is currently closed!

We visited the museum a bit reluctantly and only because we had dragged our two children (10 and 15) round two scenic waterfalls and an archery practice place in the hours before. Our youngest daughter was definitely keen to do something that she chose. When we got there our suspicions seemed to be confirmed with a relatively high entrance fee (I think it was 6,000 won per adult) for what seemed to be a small place.However, once we got into the diorama room, both kids couldn't stop themselves from oohing and aahing the whole time. You really felt that somebody had fun putting it all together. It was in all the little touches (like adding little German flags to the 'storming of the Berlin wall' display) and the set ups such as the 'Bearacotta Army). As previous reviewers have mentioned, all of these are in glass cases so my husband (who is a very keen photographer with decent equipment) didn't deign to take any photos - our teenage daughter took over instead. Having just completed our photobook, I can only say that we had plenty of good shots, I could easily have filled 20 rather than 4 pages with good shots.We didn't miss any English explanations - the teddies really spoke for themselves. We also didn't approach it as a museum but rather as a fun place to look around. The re-enactments of historical events from the 20th century were also fairly self-explanatory.The shop was probably the only really boring bit since the selection was not particularly big and the prices, given the location, quite high.Overall, don't go if you want to learn anything about teddy bears but do go in with kids (or adults who appreciate the cuteness).

We visited the Jungmun Golf Club for doing the Moon Light Walking Tour. We went there to warm up for the Jeju Olle Walking Festival. The view was awesome and it was a nice experience to walk there during sunset. At the end, they prepare a concert for all the participants there.

We visited Seongsan Ilchulbong on two separate days - the first was in the afternoon to see the women free-divers' performance (1pm/3pm) and the second was in the wee hours of the morning (5+am) to see the sunrise. The free-divers were all middle-aged women who looked old enough to be our mothers. Despite their age, it was amazing how they managed to hold their breath so long underwater to harvest the seafood which you could buy from them and eat on the spot (they'll prepare/cook it in whichever way you want). The way they sang prior to the dive and the way they chatted and swam out to sea together reminded us of the friendly grannies in our neighborhood enjoying a nice chit-chat over tea. To see the sunrise at the peak, we started our climb at 4+am (it helps to stay in a hotel within walking distance to Ilchulbong). It was pitch-dark and torchlight was a must. The climb was shorter than expected and we reached the top before 5am. Thankfully the sky was clear that morning and we managed to catch a beautiful sunrise (around 5:30am) that was nothing short of amazing.

We visited on a particularly windy day which made it unfit for swimming. However, the landscape itself was great to look at, especially the black volcanic rock contrasting with the white sand and turquoise waters. I'm sure this beach would be stunning in better weather.

We visited on a dull wet day but even then there was plenty of sparking glass to see.  Everything you can imagine made of glass.  I loved the mushrooms and pumpkins and some of the weirder sculptures.  On a sunny day it must be even better.  Great place to take kids and, except for woodland walk it is all accessible for people with walking problems.There are examples from different parts of the world and you can watch craftsmen making things - and even book an experience to try it yourself.

We visited Mount Halla National Park yesterday, Aug 25th, and it was an excellent experience and great views!It is very easy to get there by the 740 bus from Jeju Bus terminal, now here is the tricky part.. there are several entrances and trails. All of them are intense hiking. Use comfortable shoes, take lots of water and snacks.. there is nothing to buy up until the very top, which is noodle soup, water and chocolates......We took the Eorimok trail to go up to Witsae Shelter and took the Yeongsil trail to return down and my recommendation is:Take Yeongsil train, the view is by far much better than the one from Eorimok trail.In order to get there:Take 740 bus and get down on Yeongsil ticket office (@45m) and from there take a taxi to the main entrance (there is a taxi that goes up and down all the time and charges 5000). Please take the taxi, otherwise you will end up walking uphill for @2km. Once at the entrance... just follow the signs to Witse Shelter. Take lots of pictures along the way!Again ... it is uphill .. from @900m to @1750m, with lots of stairs and rock trails on both trails. Up and down in @5 hours is an ok time.Enjoy !!

We visited May 2016, rainy weather but still open. The staff or local tour guide are very helpful that they provide umbrella that we can use around the folk village. Take note, the staff tour guide we met don't speak much of English, good thing we have our own private tour guide that help on translation. Appreciate the staff for her patience because even though all of her explanations need to be translated, I felt like she didn't skip any detail that we need to know. My favorite part when she showed us those black pig that is famous for their BBQ. Also, the drink that they offer is good that we end up buying one.

We visited here as part of of our cruise ship day tour of the island. This is a very pretty place with amazing photo opportunities throughout. We purchased one of our favorite souvenirs from a kiosk selling genuine Jeju produced hats. We enjoyed the gardens and the walk over the bridge with the amazing views of the gorge and waterfalls. Be aware that the VERY long walk down to the   close-up   of the waterfalls is rather taxing and may not be worth the effort. Overall, a great experience!

We visited Hallim Park as part of our Western Jeju Discovery Tour so we just had a limited time to go around the park. The park has a lot of attractions but our helpful tour guide told us to focus on just a handful to maximize our time spent in Hallim Park.Our first stop would be the Hyeopjae Cave and Ssangyong Cave, located at the far end of the park. This would require some walking uphill and downhill, but the entire pathway is well-paved so you won't have to worry about losing your balance. The caves are relatively small, but still interesting to look at.After that we made our way down, passing by the beautiful and serene Jeju Stone and Bonsai Garden. It would be impossible not to be relaxed by this astonishingly peaceful sanctuary.On our way to the Cherry Blossom Garden, we passed by the Jae-Am Folk Village; which featured interesting stone sculptures and traditional Jeju village huts.Other attractions we decided to skip would be the Wild Grass and Flower Garden, the Bird Garden, the Water Garden and the Subtropical Botanic Garden.

We visited Hallasan National Park in mid December. We ascended via Gwaneumsa trail (8.7km) up to the peak and descended via the Seongpanak trail (9.6km). Gwaneumsa is shorter but more challenging on the way up, it is easier on the knees. We started at 07:30hr, which is the sunrise time. The initial hike was relatively flat, walking on uneven big rocks. There were signs throughout the trail, indicating where you are, distance and estimated time to the peak. Snow started to appear midway and we had to put on crampons on our boots. We took about 3 hours to reach the shelter and another 1 hour 45 minutes to reach the peak. Unfortunately, the weather was cloudy at the peak with low visibility. It was very windy and cold. We joined the queue to have photos taken at the iconic landmark.We started our descent at 12:45hr, arrived at the shelter at 15:15hr, had a short break before descending the remaining 4.1km. We took about 4 hours for the entire descent, exhausted by then.This is the first time my friend and I hiked in snow during winter. We took longer than expected as we were extra careful and also took many photos. Overall, it was a great first time experience hiking on snow.Tips for winter hiking:1. Start as early as possible so that you are not pressured to reach the shelter before 1200hr.2. Wear comfortable shoes, preferably water resistant or waterproof.3. Be extra careful when stepping on the big rocks during the initial trail. They are uneven and may twist your ankles. 4. Crampons are necessary, while trekking poles are optional.5. Wear layers of clothing so that you can add/remove when necessary.6. Wear beanie hat and neck covering to protect your ears/neck from the cold, especially at the peak.7. Bring your own food, snacks and water/energy drink. There are no food stalls nor toilet at the peak.8.Toilet facilities are only available at the shelters, hence relief yourself before proceeding.Hope you enjoyed the hike.

We visited as part of a group/tour and arrived late in the day (about 5pm). Huge carpark just outside.Not at all busy. Our guide walked us around the village and gave informative information (in English) about the history of the island and the life styles of the people that would have/do live here.The few residents that we saw didn?t want photos taken, I thought a little strange since they live in a ?theme park? and must see tourists every day of the year.We were allowed to poke our heads into specified rooms/houses.There was a shop for gifts etc and a WC block for the use of behind the guest villa at the backWe spent about 40 mins here

We visited a part of this forest during a day tour. The air was refreshingly clean. The paths leading through the forest are nicely done. There is also a fountain of mountain water, which is apparently very clean and healthy. Small but cute.

We travelled on a rare rainy day in Jeju, but June, our tour guide, made our trip happy and smooth with her professional arrangement, detailed introduction of the scenic spots, fluent English, sharing on Korean culture and her personal experience on how she feels about Jeju. I am particularly impressed by the guided tour she gave us in the Manjanggul Lava Tube, her intriguing story of haenyeo and their livelihood and our hiking experience at Seongsanilchul Pong. In as short as a day we have seen most of what lies in the northern and eastern coasts of Jeju Island, felt for ourselves the beauty of the natural landscapes and understood how inhabitants of this island have lived since the last century. It was an amazing travel experience and we give credits to June for the nice private tour.

We travelled from Seogwipo by bus to Jungmun Elementary school.  Thereafter, we were supposed to hop on another bus to the stop nearest to the entrance of Yeongsil Trail.  However, we did not read the bus schedule careful enough to notice the change in the schedule during winter.  The bus starts later and ends earlier during winter.  We ended sharing a cab with the other 2 tourists who happened to be there earlier than us and were heading to the same destination.  The guy who mended the convenient store near the bus stop was so nice that he helped us to call the taxi.   It was a blessing in disguise since the taxi actually sent us right to the door step of the Yeongsil Trail entrance in which otherwise, we would have to walk up for about 2 km to the starting point of the trail.  Should you travel with baggage, the park office (which I guess so) can keep them for you.  I?m not sure of the storage capacity or if lockers are available, or this is just an additional service provided for those who happen to travel there with their baggage.It took us slightly more than 3 hours to hike up to Witsoreum Shelter since we?re quite slow and took plenty of photos.  The Koreans took 2 hours only.  The wind was very strong, so do take care of your scarf or anything which is light.  Witsoreum Shelter is where you can opt to go back down with the same trail or by another trail, Eurimok Trail.  However, the other trail was closed on that day.There?s a canteen and restrooms at Witsoreum Shelter.  The canteen sells instant noodle and simple snacks.  After eating and disposing the residue of the noodle, you have to bring the trash back for disposal.  Plastic bag for keeping your trash is provided but I find it rather thin.  However, we brought some plastic bag along with us for this purpose as well since we had some snacks while hiking up.The fog was building up when we left at about 1:10 am.  It took us about an hour and 40 minutes to descend.  Overall, this was a good experience.  We were just on time to catch the last bus back to Jungmun Elementrary school (if I recall this destination correctly).

We took up this challenge in early April, just stepping into Spring. We took the bus from Jeju Express Bus Terminal, took about 40 minutes to reach the Eorimok bus stop. Before taking the bus though, we highly recommend to check with the Tourist Information Center just outside the bus terminal on the last returning bus. Thankfully we checked, the last bus in March period was 4.55pm at Eorimok. Summer periods probably have a later last bus back. This bus serves the Yeongsil trail entrance as well.There is still a ~20 mins walk along the road before reaching the entrance to the Eorimok trail. Impressive mountain views once you reach the park entrance.The Eorimok trail starts off deceptively tame for about 500m. Once you get the past the wooden bridge, the tough hike starts. For the next 2km, we experienced the toughest climb of the entire trail. Steep and large steps at times, with large, uneven rocks littering the way up. The view is mostly green at this point.Near the end of the first 2km, we started to see melting ice along the trail. Certain parts were still iced up; we had to climb on top of the ice to traverse. Due to the melt, it was quite slippery. A hiking stick or 2 is highly recommended, though we had not brought any for our trip.After 2km, the trail leveled off into a plateau, a welcome rest after a seemingly endless slog. Strong winds and rain pummeled us that day, but all the more made the challenging climb more exciting and enjoyable. The rest of the way to the Witse Oreum was of average difficulty, and the landscape was foggy and snowy/icy. We encountered many instances that we had to walk on the ice so be sure to be equipped with good shoes to reduce the chance of slipping on the ice.We finally reached the Witse Oreum after about 3 hours, and bought and slurped down the ramen and its soup, as well as a chocolate energy bar. They also carried stuff like crampons and plastic sheet raincoat (we bought it for the heat trapping characteristic rather than for shielding against rain, we foolishly did not expect snow and ice in April tbh :P).We originally wanted to go down via the Yeongsil trail which meets the Eorimok trail at the Witse Oreum, but a pair of local, seasoned hikers who turned back for Eorimok warned us that the Yeongsil trail is still mostly frozen over and is very difficult to traverse at this time. Due to the lack of proper equipment, we heeded their advice and went back down Eorimok instead.The trip down was much faster, but hurt our knees more due to the impact. Tread with care as the uneven terrain may cause slip and falls.The journey down took approximately an 1.5 hours.Overall it was really challenging but fun.Things to note:1. Take note of the last bus timing or you may have to hitch a ride back to town.2. And of course, cater buffer time to reach the bus stop, there is still a 20 min walk to it.3. Hiking gear, especially proper shoes and a hiking stick or 2 is highly recommended.4. Early April features unmelted snow in the terrain, wear proper clothing.5. The same bus goes to the Yeongsil trail, may want to try hiking that as well (on different days of course)6. The Eorimok is pretty challenging for a novice like myself, heard from locals that the Seongpanak trail on the Eastern side is more relaxing but longer.7. The Eorimok trail does not reach the summit, if you want to reach the summit, try the Seongpanak or Gwaneumsa trails instead.

We took the steeper but shorter gwanumsa trail up to the summit from where we got brilliant views of the crater lake, and the gentler but longer seongpanak trail down-I think this was a good choice because both my friend and I find going downhill more difficult than up. We took a taxi to the gwanumsa starting point. We comfortably reached the summit by 1 pm and ate our lunch of kimbap(bought from a store near our hostel,  there's no kimbap sold at the gwanumsa trailhead, so make sure you buy beforehand). Although the trail is relatively easy, there are only a few points where fresh water is available,  so bring enough drinking water.  If you want to climb to the summit, there's also a fixed time by which you have to reach a checkpoint,  which is closed after that time. I really liked the varying landscape and vegetation. The only bad part was the washrooms - extremely dirty.

We took the shortest trail, or the Eoseungsaengaok trail, which starts at the same place as the Eorimok trail. It is about 30-45 minutes walk to the top of a hill and from there you can see the scenery. No food or drink sold anywhere along the trail and there's no toilet.

We took the Seongpanak trail since we wanted to go to the top.  Believe me it's not easy! It is 9.6 km long (one way) and there are signs all along stating how far you have come. But the path, well its not a path, extremely rocky and uneven. It gets difficult as you climb higher. You need to reach the last shelter before 1 pm (in summers) if you want to go to the top. But nobody tells you, until you reach there, that you have to start climbing down by 2.30 because they close it and you cannot view the crater if you reach after that.  I took us little more than 2 hours to climb the last stretch and we reached just on time. On the way back, we just stopped for a few mins and then we were completely alone! It was scary because it was getting dark and there was nobody at all. I don;t know whether it is safe after dark or not but I am sure it would be almost impossible to climb down after that. So please start early. I think the maintenance should be improved even if that means charging an entrance fee. The guy at the last shelter was closing at 4 pm and we had to request him for water on our way back. It took us more than 9 hours to complete the trek. Take lots and lots of water and some food also. Not for people with knee problems or not so active lifestyle. The view at the top was no doubt beautiful and you can see the volcano crater but you can also see the crater at Ilchulbong which is much easier. So, if you are going be ready for a challenge and reconsider your decision if you are not used to walking and hiking!

We took the Hallasan Yeongsil trail up to Witseoreum Shelter and back in early January (winter). The views were fantastic and the hike was just the right distance for us (1.5 hours up, 1 down). It was challenging but didn't wipe us out. Make sure you stop and have some noodles at the shelter, as dumb as it may sound I found this part to be the highlight of my Jeju experience. It would pay to do a small amount of research if you are planning to go as there are multiple trails of different lengths and difficulty. The Yeongsil trail is fairly easy apart from one steep section with ropes which were tricky in the snow (mainly going down). Most of the trail features steps when required, is well signposted and has guide ropes along the ridges. Also, make sure you head out early: we did and shared the path with only a few hikers but on our way down came across masses of people trying to go up. Most of the late arrivals didn't have snow crampons and/or not enough fitness/experience for this hike and many seemed to be turning back once it got steeper. I don't think they would had a very good time. You can buy cheap crampons at the bottom at the trail entrance and apart from warm clothes the only equipment you would need in winter (maybe hiking poles if bad knees or unsteady). In warmer months, some good boots, snacks and water would be fine.

We took ride on bus no. 282 from Arang Joeul Street to visit Teddy Bear Museum jeju which is nearby to Jungmun  tourist resort. Bus fare cost us only KRW 1150 per pax. The visit to Teddy bear museum was fantastic especially for my sister, teddy bear lover. It was amazing to see many collection of teddy bears from all over the world with different themes and events globally.  There were three sections of the teddy bear museum; starting from the history, artwork and forest of teddy bear. There was a garden outside of the museum with the construction of enormous teddy bear. We can get a glimpse of the LV and Swarvosky teddy bear. The most nostalgic teddy bear was the Princess Hour theme teddy bear. The most great thing to watch was the Elvis Presley show. However, the teddy bear sold there was expensive. It was worth to visit this place.

We took bus 182 early morning reached there around 7.30am and started to hike about 8am. It's good to bring hiking stick as there are lots of steps up, with a hiking stick it's easier to move up the rocky paths. It was very cold at the mountain so it's good to wear in layers and can remove the jackets if it gets too warm during the hike. We managed to reach Saraoreum shelter before 12pm where we ate and took a break before moving on to the summit. After 12pm no one is allowed to move on up to the summit from the shelter as it gets dark very early during winter time. We reached the summit just before 1.30pm. The ranger already chasing people to get down. It was very cold and windy at the top and it started to drizzle. So it's important to bring a raincoat too. I could'nt get a good view as it was very foggy and windy. We did'nt get some rest and started to descend. It took a long while to descend too as the path is very rocky and slippery. Lucky i have my hiking stick with me. Half way down it started to get dark we needed to use our handphones as touch light to guide us down the path. Very happy we are all able to reach the summit. It's a nice experience.

We took airport limousine bus 600 and got off at Paradise Hotel, the second last stop, and the journey took us 90 minutes. At the bus stop, we saw the sign pointing to Sojeongbang Falls and started walking there. Reaching the place, you need to go down the staircase to see the waterfall, the little brother of Jeongbang falls, as it is not as high. Feeling satisfied, we followed the pathway and continued walking to Jeongbang falls. Paying an entrance fee of 2000 won, going down the stairs, stepping on rocks of all sizes and shapes, we reach the waterfall that had been discovered in 219 B.C. Seobok was ordered by Emperor Qinshihuang to find an elixir of life with a big fleet of over 3000 people by sailing to the east. He chanced upon this waterfall and he had inscribed on the rock near the fall stating that he had passed here. The waterfall is 23m high and very close to the ocean. This is one of the waterfalls to visit in Jeju.

We took a walk up seongsan ilchulbong, to get a glimpse of the early morning sunrise.It didn?t disappoint.The walk was very easy to complete (we had a 7 & 4 year old with us).And not to be a cheapskate, but it?s totally free if you start your climb before 7am......after that time you have to purchase tickets.

We took a cab from Jejusi Shinjeju to Yongsil trail. Cost us around 23000krw for a 30mins ride. We started hiking at 1.30pm (trail closes at 2pm) and hiked for close to 2 hours up to 1650m. Total height was around 1900++ m. Didnt reach all the way to the top. However, the view was spectacular. Defintely believe it is one of the must visit places in Jeju.

We thought the kids might be excited by the maze but they were quickly bored by the turning and it started to drizzle.  Hide in the main building and left before an hour.  I think its 30,000W for 2 adults and 2 kids, not that cheap.  Not a cup of tea for everyone I guess.

We take this trail to climb Hallasan. This trail is very popular but the longest trail. It could take approximately 4 hours to climb to the top and 5 hours to climb down. if you are visiting in winter time, please prepare your crampon/ice cleat, since the trail road is slippery and covered by snow or ice. You could buy cheap crampon at E mart or Lotte Mart with the price less than USD 10, but it is very use full.

We stayed at Seowipo, near to the seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal as we knew that we needed to take an early bus to Hallasan. We noted that we needed to reach a certain point on Hallasan by 12.30pm as they would not allow people to continue to hike up after 12.30pm due to foreseen danger. We took bus 782 at 6.00am sharp from seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal and alight at Seongpanak bus stop to start our hike at Hallasan. There was a TV screen at the front of the bus that will flash and announce the current and coming stop in english clearly.  The ride took about 30 minutes. The cost of the ride was less than 2000won and the bus driver could provide change if needed. We alighted at Seongpanak bus stop on the side with a hiking track. That track was not the track up to Hallasan. We needed to cross to the opposite side and pass the souvenir and rest stop place to the correct Hallasan track (free entrance). In the beginning the track was gentle and doable. We managed to spot birds and deer grazing around. However, the rest of the track up was pretty boring as there was nothing much to see. After 1-2km, the hike started to be more steep (as in more elevated with steps) as there were many rocky steps to hike up. There were two rest stops before the summit that provided fairly clean and well-maintained toilet with toilet paper. However, there would not be any tap to wash hands. Therefore, remember to buy wet wipes to clean your hands. At the second rest stop, raman, drinks and crampons were sold. Get all the supplies you need before hiking up as there is no shops at the summit. It will be good to bring tomatoes or fruit for the hike as those provide fluid as well as sugar (instead of salty food item with msg ? this will make you feel sick). Anyway, you are not suppose to cook at the summit. Remember to bring trash bag to clear your trash too. From the second rest stop onwards, the steep rocky steps continued with harsher windy condition as you progress to the top. Therefore, remember to bring windbreaker and windproof pants as the wind was rather strong 1 to 2km before reaching the summit. We hike on 24 April with a summit temperature of 6 to 12 degree Celsius. We were blessed as there were no rain snow during the hike. The 1 to 2km up the summit consist of wooden steps that I found difficulty tracking up due to the wind and my lack of motivation (as I kept on looking at the summit and felt that it was so far away). Therefore, it would be better to just look at the steps in front of you and conquer those instead. When we finally reach the summit, we had a view of Baengnokdam crater and the surroundings. I was feeling nausea partly due to the fatigue as I did not exercise for 2 month prior to this hike. However, we managed to hike up to the summit in 3.5 hours. The wind continued to be harsh on us. Therefore we stayed for 15 minutes and decide to just hike down. Take pics even if you feel unwell. You will feel better as you ascend down. We hike down from the other hard track, the Gwaneumsa Trail although I was super tired. I did not regret that choice as it was much more scenic in comparison with the Seongpanak track. I thought that descending would not be a toll on me but I was wrong. As the track consist of many rocky steps, it was hard on my knees and I had to work on my balance too. The ajumma (they were over 50 years old) were able to hike way faster than me (in my early thirties). There was one rest stop only and we stop for the toilet. It was again clean with toilet paper provided. Generally, it was a descending hike with minimal ascending (with only a few flights of stairs up). We took 4.30 hours to hike down and I was totally shacked. The rest area at the bottom was also much more beautiful as compared to the Seongpanak rest stop. We wanted to take a bus back but we were told that there were no buses on Monday. There were buses back to Jeju city on other day from Gwaneumsa. (we noted that one of the bus come around 4pm towards Jeju city). We took a cab back to Jeju Dongmun Traditional Market for 20, 000 won. From the traditional market, we took a taxi for 3200 won to the bus terminal (bought bus ticket from the counter) to take bus 781 back to seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal (the journey was more than 1.5 hours).Personally, I find the hike difficult and I would suggest some stamina training to enjoy the hike better. I would suggest to hike when there is good weather as I find the hike difficult even in good weather (due to the rocky steps). Having said these, I would still recommend the hike as I love the challenge.

We stayed at Seowipo, near to the seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal and took bus 701 to Seongsan ilchulbong. The bus journey took more than 1.5hours and cost about 3300won one way and the bus driver could provide change if needed. There was a TV screen at the front of the bus that will flash and announce the current and coming stop in english clearly.  The TV screen will flash seongsan-ri entrance (I have attached the photo) and you can press the bell to alight. Just to note that the bus ride can be a nausea one as the driver usually travel at a high speed as there were many stops they need to embark on. We alighted and headed to the dark brown beach along Seongsan. Not sure why we need not need to pay for the entrance fee that day (25th April) but we were happy as the temperature was about 17 degree Celsius. We wore T-shirt with a windbreaker only as the sun kept us warm. A windbreaker will be good as it can be quite windy especially if you walk along the beach. There were 2 track at Seongsan. One track led to the peak of Seongsan which consist about 10 flights of stairs (Pretty doable even with poor fitness ? just take as many rest breaks as needed). At the peak, you will be able to have a panoramic view of the city and the surrounding water bodies. The other track is along the coast area with pretty wild purple (I think is Lunaria annua)  and yellow canola wild flower and volcanic stacked rocks.After Seongsan, you can continue to the Jeju Olle Route 1 to Al Oreum along the ocean area. The Jeju Olle Route 1 will pass by canola flower patches for photo taking, a nice ocean view with beaches for scenic viewing, a new hotel named as The Cloud, the ferry terminal, along many beautiful seashore where to can pick clams and walkway with dry cuttlefish along the coast. There were many restaurants along the way too. However, we started the walk at 1pm and took too many stops for picture taking. Therefore, we were unable to finish the walk to Al Oreum as we reached Jongdal Elementary school at 5.30 pm. Noted that there was no bus stop along the walk after the fish port/market to Jongdal Elementary school (there was a Ojo Haenyeo House bus stop). Therefore, make sure you start the Olle route earlier. We decide to go back as it was late by bus 701 back to the seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal from Jongdal Elementary school  as we noted that the bus will take about 2 hours to reach Seogwipo-si.

We stayed at Seowipo, near to the seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal and took bus 110 from Jungang Rotary bus stop to Jungmun Tourist Complex.
