Grounds are uneven and slippery due to water dripping from the ceiling, hence proper shoes are necessary. The lighting was quite dim and there were only a couple of descriptions along the way. I didn't come out with a full appreciation of the lava cave. The cave wasn't very spectacular but it's worth a visit if you are in the area.

Visited over Thanksgiving weekend and were surprised by all the snow! We had a rental car (with chains and GPS) ... 1139 was blocked off first attempt so we took 1131 and viewed the snow from Seongpanak Rest Area and we knew we wanted to hike the next day but didn't have enough time for the long trek so we approached from the other side on 1139. Arrived to Yeongsil Hiking Trail at 7:50 a.m. and had no problem parking at the entrance. Hiked/walked the 1 hour of 2 we had and reached the temple and entrance to the next 40 minute hike which would have taken us to Witse Oreum - fellow hikers informed us crampons were required from there and I don't doubt it, wish we had hiking sticks too, definitely not to be done in the snow with anything other than proper boots. It was a more difficult walk than we thought it would be, fairly steep toward the end and we were all down to long sleeved shirts even though the temp was freezing. Kids (9, 12 & 15) loved it, lots of stops to throw snowballs, etc. As we headed back down at 9:00 we started passing big crowds ... so glad we got out early and enjoyed the tranquil quiet of the snow covered forest! The road was just about cleared when we were leaving so it seems you can drive and/or take a taxi to the temple then do the 40 min hike to the final stop on a day when the roads are clear. Cars were parked for over 1 mile toward the access road so again, hit it early!  Mt. Halla was visible when we approached the top - the first we had seen of the crater in 3 days there, absolutely gorgeous.

Visited May 2016, season of summer but the day we visited it was a bit of rainy thus our tour guide told us to explore it before the rain totally pours as the place will be foggy means the view will be blocked. The view is nice, I traveled with my pregnant wife so we didn't went to the top as I assume you need to take that hundred or more steps to reach the top. Also, for the reason of not giving a perfect rating, the place is very crowded, though there is an entrance fee but no control of the number of tourist going inside. Its too many that we didn't enjoy much thinking that we visit it in off season, rainy weather, and even just wandering on the lower ground still crowded (refer to my picture that I took just in the entrance part only).

Visited Ma Park and we were pretty excited because we could feed the ponies! Then, we realised that there was a show and got ourselves a pair of tickets. Amazing stuffs! Stunts with horses and there was also a short drama. The only downside was my partner and I were just assuming of what they were talking about because there weren't any translations! We played the Gokart after that. The karts weren't really fast but that was alright. Had a few rounds and they took nice photos of you! Once is enough for this place!

Visited in October to see beautiful autumn colors revealing itself. I recommend to start early morning if you want to hike to the summit.  The cut off time for the summit can be anytime between 11am to 1pm depending on the season. There are 4 different trails around Hallasan Park - Gwaneumsa and Seongpanak takes you to the top. As Gwaneumsa is a bit boring I recommend to take it when you go up. Then go down Seongpanak, which is very pretty and one you do not need to rush when going down it will give you a chance to enjoy the views. The other trails are Eorimok, Yeongsil that are pretty but don't go all the way up (take them if you are going to be late and can't make the summit anyway). I wanted to try Donnaeko, but it was closed at the time of my visit. Overall great experience, not dofficult hike (unless it's winter) and beautiful views.

Visited here as part of my tour package. There is a ferry that can transport cars and people to the island. Upon reaching the island, we took a bus tour n brings us to a few locations. The most memorable one will be the hike up to the lighthouse. Tiring but fun and you can see the great ocean around. Took slightly more than a half day of tour in this island and it's fun :)
Virtual reality fun place where you can take snaps and poses with your favorite stars or participate in a surreal hologram concert! Great for kids, teenagers and fun-loving adults

Very talented artist and excellent works, a sad and interesting story. While the museum itself has only got a smallish collection, the park and the streets around the place is really worthwhile exploring, nice cafes and restaurants in the area too.

Very scenic throughout the trail with different surroundings - you would trek pass fruit farms, river streams, stone trails and lush trees (watch out for the spider webs!)We started at the finishing point of trail no. 7 and made our way back towards the starting point so that we would end up at the rock pools at Oedolgae for a dip. The markings were easy to follow (some had descriptions) and there were many resting pit stops along the way - toilets, pavilions, convenience stores etc. One of the pit stops we made was at Mango Holic - fresh cold mango desserts to cool us down on a hot day!Would recommend to wear sneakers and sun screen and allow 4-6 hours to trek comfortably and enjoy the whole trail.

Very interesting inside and out. The first floor is mostly modern about sexual preference health and rights but it is 95% in Korean. I would recommend to bring a Korean friend who doesn't mind translating if you are interested in that part. There was also a big wall of history at the very front which was all in Korean that would be worth translating. It wasn't very busy and some of the   hands on   things that would show examples were broken so I started with a mediocre impression. The bigger and more impressive part though is the number of historic sexual things they have on the second and third floor. Lots of artifacts about sex in Eastern cultures with some in Western cultures but a lot of things have their English translation. This part is much more impressive and interesting to look at. A lot of phallic objects and   traditional   pieces but it's historic and that is how people viewed sex in history. The more modern section is more modernly-styled and was a bit confusing (a lot of sex dolls...? kind of weird) and included more fetish stuff than I expected. Not much on queer and non-hetero there was a small section (in Korean) on the ground floor and then one very gray area display on the top floor but not a whole lot can be expected of Korea (where homosexuality is still viewed very negatively). Overall it was worth the price and was pretty interesting to look at. Having a translator or understanding Korean would make it more memorable.

Upon my arrival on the island, I bumped into Taiwanese travelers who recommended the Hallasan fried rice. The restaurant is within 15-20 walking distance to the port (where you got off the ferry).The fried rice was covered with vegetables and squid. The owner would go to each table to pour egg yolk and cheese and make the dish look like a volcano. While frying the rice, the owner would tell stories of the Jeju island and Udo island in fluent English. The fried rice then was turned into a heart shape. My family and I videotaped the process and had fun. Oh, the friend rice did taste yummy!

Up & down of the mountain took us 9.5 hours including some short rest time during the hike. We started the hike around 9am (recommend to start early, we were late), and came down around 6:30pm. Our legs were like jelly legs after the hike, but is worth the hike. You can see nice view along the journey. Please do not forget to greet everyone you met with   anyeonghaseyo  , they are all very friendly people. Wear a pair of good hiking shoes, bring some snacks with you and also water. The stalls along the mountain are closed during our hike, luckily we have prepared enough snacks and water. The view at the peak is breathless. A lots of old korean aunties and uncles also managed to reach the peak, so I guess we all younger than them have no excuses of not fit to hike, right? haha...Wear sport attire, although some said it will be freezing cold at the peak (about 1950 meters height), but believe me, you wont feel cold as you have already all sweat during the hike. We spent about 30mins to 1 hour at the peak taking photos, resting and having our snacks before going down again. A pair of good hiking shoes is important so that you won't get blister on your feet. We will go back again in different season if we have the chance. We were travelling there in Oct 2018.

Unlike Hello Kitty, I think most of us have cuddled or have in possession a toy teddy bear at a certain stage of our lives. So it is no wonder that the Teddy Bear Museum has such a wide appeal and which surely be included as a ?compulsory? destination on the itinerary of the independent travellers (especially those with children) and tour companies alike.Getting there and fees: We visited Teddy Bear Museum (GPS coordinate/code 7387600) on a rainy day, which was appropriate since the exhibits are predominantly indoor, except for the Teddy Bear Garden and Park where there?re a few teddy bear figurines outside and a park with great views of the sea.  The admission charges are 10,000 won for adults won, 9,000 won for teens and 8,000 won for children.The Museum/Attraction:  This Teddy Bear Museum is the first and largest teddy bear museum in South Korea. Once you enter, you are greeted by this huge teddy bear, who gives you a ?grand? welcome to further explore the five sections spread over 3 levels: The History Hall, The Art Hall and The Project Exhibition Hall, Gift Shop (all indoors) and an outdoor Teddy Bear Garden and Park. There?s also a caf챕/restaurant. Be prepared to spend at least 1 hour looking and taking photographs/selfies at all the interesting exhibits. The History Hall comprised of the history of bear manufacturing and some of the earliest toy bears, many of which are antique and rare. It also showcases milestones in human history, with the bears enacting several famous (human) historical scenes from different eras. This is indeed a refreshing concept for a museum! I particularly liked the teddy bears enacting the Titanic, landings on the moon and the iconic celebrities like the Beatles and Gandhi.In the Art Hall, you could see the world-famous artworks and designs in an art gallery form as well as animation characters beloved by children. I liked the Mona Lisa and two of the most expensive bears in the world - the Louis Vuitton teddy bear and the Diamond Bear. In the Project Exhibition Hall, you would meet teddy bears grouped to suit the theme of each exhibition. Not forgetting the large Gift Shop on the first level. While it offers plenty of gifts, these are nonetheless pricey. Nevertheless, you could take photos with Michael Jackson bear, Steve Jobs bear and a wedding couple bear amongst others. There?s also a mother panda with her baby pandas on display too.  We certainly enjoyed the wonderful experience of the Museum bringing out the child in each of us, and making us feel young again. Despite the pricey entrance fees, I still think the Teddy Bear Museum is worth visiting, and to me, once would be sufficient. But if you don?t like teddy bears at all, then it would be prudent to skip this attraction.

unless you have never had a view of any city from about 250 meters high, take the hike up.  otherwise the view is much much better from the bottomIt only costs about two bucks a person but there are throngs of people who visit this area.  Part of the reason is because it is one of the stops on the tour buses and there were flocks of visitors that day.  There is a wooden stairway all the way to the top and the view from atop is good.  But it is not spectacular by any stretch.  My suggestion is to pick a spot from one of the nearby restaurants for that photogenic moment.  We went to the Sunrise restaurant (대⑤ ) and the view from there was just as good

Unfortunately, many attractions in Jeju are man-made and not really worth your time.  However, I wish I had spent some more time at this location as it's one of the few natural, impressive landscapes that you will see in Jeju.  Sure, there's not much to see other than the cliffs and columns, but it is good to spend some time just taking it all in.  Another idea is listening to the sounds of the waves crashing the columns.  There is only a small area for you to take pictures, so I can imagine the place can get crowded during peak season and hours.  It also gets a little cold during the off-season in the fall, so beware.There is also a small park (if that's the best way of describing it) at the entrance of the cliffs that's worth a short look as well.  There are some vendors, small stone displays, and some assorted artistic pieces.

Udo was the best part of my Jeju visit. My sister and I rented scooters for two hours to get around the island, stopping wherever we wanted to take pictures or rehydrate (it was blazingly hot). We stopped at one of the beaches for a couple of hours, but it was just too hot to sit still on the sand. Rented scooters for the rest of the day and just zoomed around the island. True, there isn't too much to do on the island besides going to the beach or riding around the island. And the scooters/ATVs available for rent are a bit expensive (15,000won for 2 hours). But if you're looking for a relaxing day with beautiful sights, I highly recommend a visit.

Udo Island, a small volcanic island 10 minutes by ferry from Jeju Island. A day out on this island can be a bore to those who have no affinity to the outdoors, particularly that of the sea.But if you love the care-free life of roaming from one sandy beach to another rocky one. In between with lots of coastal features to be awed by, then this is the little paradise on earth.Udo is an island which allows you to go the entire distance around the coastal roads, in under 4 hours, including stops for pictures, strolls, ice-cream, desserts and of course a whole host of meals.  There are rugged, rocky coastlines and little stretches of sandy beaches with emerald waters.Getting from point to point on the island is very easy, either on bicycles, rental motorbikes and scooters. Mainlainders can ferry in their car for their own pleasure. We rented a motor-scooter for 25, 000 Won for just over 4 hours. The rental is for 2 hours (Won 25000)

Udo Island is what I imagined Jeju to be..beautiful coast line beside grassy fields. A relaxing day trip soaking up the amazing scenery. Well worth the (little) effort if you are in the area, and consider a day trip if you aren't!The port is about a 15 minute walk from Sunrise Peak. You buy ferry tickets in a white dome building; start by going to one of the desks with pens and boarding cards. Fill out 2 boarding slips EXACTLY the same (one collected on your trip to Udo and the other collected on your way back). For example, we were a party of two, and on BOTH slips we wrote BOTH our names and details. When you have completed the slips, go to one of the ticket windows and present the slips with your PASSPORT (for international travellers), and if like me, you don't know any Korean at all, just smile and say   Udo  . The lady will ask you if you are returning the same day and issue you return tickets costing 5500 won each. She will also tell you the last ferry time coming back from the island, in our case (November) it was 5pm.Off we went! The ride is about 15 minutes and you get lovely views of Sunrise Peak on the way. When we disembarked, we were immediately greeted (sold to) by various venders renting out pedal bikes or motorised vehicles. We chose the   old fashioned   bikes and had a wonderful time. It costs 10000 each bike, for the whole day. We took 2-3 hours biking around the coast (map provided) taking breaks to admire the scenery and have lunch. If you didn't make any breaks, our vendor thought it would take 1-1.5 hours around. My partner and I are healthy late-20-somethings that don't bike often, but we felt the trip was pretty easy and relaxing as its mostly flat. There are not many cars either, and other motorised rental vehicles zipping by, are small scooters/2-3 seaters, so biking around feels very safe. There are numerous eateries and toilet facilities all around the island. We stumbled upon a cart selling home made pies (Bulgogi, Spicy Chicken, Red Bean and Apple) and they were delicious! I wish I knew the name of it, but if you happen to see it and feel like pies..these are yum!Fit in a trip to Udo if you can..Its a beautiful place to spend some time..

Udo Island is one of the most beautiful places on earth. The island is surrounded by charming beaches and coastline. Just felt that a day trip here is not enough. Be sure to try its delicious peanut ice cream, peanut smoothie and peanut pizza! You can also rent a tuk tuk like tricycle around the island. A must visit indeed! :)

U-do is more of a small village, the citizens are so down to earth and friendly! Lots of fresh seafood be sure to try them out! Hop on a tour bus, driver will intro the island to you!Great for family vacations or exploring the island with friends and taking lots of amazing photos

Udo is a really small island, you can go around by bicycle in several hours. Udo is a volcanic island, so it has several nice beaches with white and black sand, impressing lava rock formations, caves etc. We went there several times, every time for 2-3 days, and every time it was just wonderful. You should go and spend a few days there if you want to relax in a quite and peaceful atmosphere with no nightlife, co crowds, no big attractions but with beautiful nature. Still, if you want to get in touch with the rest of the world - no problem here, our Korean mobiles were working fine, Internet was available right in the   arrival hall   of the port and in many   minbaks   (small Korean-style hotels).You can get there easily from Seongsan port  (＿?깆??고) of Jeju island by ferry in just 10-15 minutes. Ferries depart every hour from 08.00 till 17.30 or 18.00 depending on season. Most accommodations are found on on the White Coral Beach (Seo-bin-baek-sa, ＿?鍮諛깆?? or  Sanhosa, ??고몄?? ), 10 minutes walk from the port. They are all small 1-2 floor buildings located directly on the beach with seaview (Pensions, Minbaks). We never booked anything in advance, but found a room on site, but we went in May and October - not highest season. The rooms were always nice and big, also with kitchen and all the necessary kitchenware. Also there are small shops with snacks and some Korean restaurants.So, what to do in there?- swim in the pure emerald water of White coral beach, see the special kind of sand, it really feels like you are in tropics ^^- rent a bike and go around the islandThe road goes nicely along the shore, there were almost no cars except on the busier Jeju-facing side, and we enjoyed the scenery very much!  - Geommeolle Beach (寃?硫?)This is a black sand beach with very beautiful and unusual rock formations and caves, and we spent a very good time there. You can go in caves and see small rocks piled up on each other. And once a year they have a symphony concert in the caves!!Also, if you are a diver with a certificate, there is a diver center there. We tried to do it, but we did not have a PADI certificate so they refused, they do not do fun dives.And  we took a motor boat (10 000W/person) to see farther caves with a spectacular view of Udo cliffs (Hu-hae-seok-byeok, ＿?댁＿?踰). If you are lucky, you can also see a peculiar site called Ju-gan-myeong-weol - sun reflecting at the ceiling of a cave giving a   moon shape  . We also went up the hill, nice view of both Udo and Jeju!!What problems you can encounter in Udo?- languageLocal people are friendly and try to help, but they do not understand English!!So if you do not speak Korean, print out Korean names of what you want to visit and some basic Korean phrases (preferably in Korean, not transcriptions, because pronunciation may be tricky). BUT! the owner of the LOG-house speaks English very good!- foodThere is no Western restaurants on the island, only Korean!! The shops on the beach only sell snacks like Ramen, but there is a bigger mart inland called Hana-ro Mart with fruits, vegetables, milk, etc. (??濡 留, try to ask locals for directions and go there by bike, you will find it, there is no place to get lost ^^). And it could be a good idea to bring some food with you from Jeju, especially if you want something like cheese, wine etc.

Took the seongpanak trail up the mountain and must be at the last checkpoint before 1:00 pm or you'll not be allowed to the peak. from the information/parking space down to the station is about 5 km..? and from the station to the peak another 3-4 KM. approx 4-4.5 hrs (walking) from start to the peak. Trail is not very difficult, the first part is not so steep and you could run it if fit enough. but the last few Km is steep and knees gets tired climbing all that stairs. shelter at the last station do sell some drinks, chocolate bar, pie, hot coffee, ramen. Do not climb when it's raining as there's no view but you'll just get wet and cold, unless it's just the climb that's important, It's still relatively easy to go with proper weather suitable clothes.

Took bus 781 from City Hall in Jeju City about 30-40min bus ride for 1300KRW. Had some breakfast at the Seongpanak bus station (base camp), got a bottle of water and a snickers then started the hike. Read that it would take 8-9 hours roundtrip, got to the top in less than 3, a very slow and steady rising hike firstly through the forest and later up the mountain. Stunning views from about 1800m and up, saw some water also in the crater, quite crowded at the summit. Ate my chocolate bar, took a selfie and started walking down. Total time return trip to the bus station was 6 hours. Best tip is to not pause at the middle camp which you must reach before 12:00 if you want to get to the peak, but instead just walk on to the top and have some lunch or break up there, you will then skip most of the crowd, try to head back down before 13:00, as you need to leave the peak before 13:30 it does get crowded on the descent and will just increase your time spent by waiting for slow groups.The views are spectacular, do recommend, no fees.

Took around 6 hours up and 4-5hours down the volcano. Really pretty with all the snow around, but on the way down snow started to melt and the ground is slightly muddy. traveled there in the winter period from December to January. You should go and reserve an entire day for this winter hike!If you choose not to climb to the peak, at around half way mark there is a crater which is around 3 hours up and another 3 hours down. The crater is filled with water but is frozen in winter. But i would recommend heading to the peak for the best views! There is a rest station at 2/3 hours mark with toliets and 2nd rest station at the 4/5hours mark near to summit. The 2nd rest station has a small shop that sells coffee, instant noodles, gloves, small tidbits. But best if you bring along some gimbap along to fill your stomach.

Took a bus from Seogwipo early morning and it takes around 1 hour 40 minutes to get there as the bus stops on all stops along the way. Once there, it is a short 10 to 15 min hike up to the top where you will be met with a green crater. Unless you have a drone, its not possible to capture the beauty of the place unfortunately. On the way down, we waited to see the women diving show, but it got cancelled which was a let down as we only got to know after the show was supposed to start.

Too fascinating when seeing all the traits of massive lava flow in the cave, which is actually part of the lava tube. Must bring along a powerful torch if you want to enjoy from the ceiling to the ground. Relying just on the phone torch or the lights inside will hinder your enjoyment and appreciation of this natural masterpiece as you will be only focusing on your steps. Do walk the entire 1 km so you can see the big massive lava lumps which stretches from the ground to the ceiling. Water drippings and water patches are common, wear a cap and windbreaker will help. In fact the temperature inside is a few degrees lower than the outside

Too dark to actually take any nice photos inside. The paths are quite moist and therefore slippery, so have to take extra care when walking. The scariest part was the path down from the entrance as it was pretty steep, so have to be careful of your footing.

Too crowded.  Trail very rough - they   improved   it by adding very large rocks that make it difficult to traverse. We saw several examples of people who had hurt their ankles because of these rocks. We liked the Olle Trails very much but Halla not.  Okay view at the top. To see the sunrise, one has to wake up early and hike along the stairs and some stone steps and must remember to bring along a torchlight or use our smartphone's torchlight as it can be still very dark during the hike. My husband & I took 30 min to reach the peak, while waiting for the sun to rise there were many people waiting and getting ready their cameras. During that moment, everyone started exclaiming with delight as I believe it is not easy for some of us who do not have strong stamina when comes to hiking but it was worth seeing such glorious sight. If I have the chance to visit Jeju, I would want to visit this place again.
To n fro distance of 1km apart. The underground lava cave is natural and unspoilt, unlike some with artificially colorful lightings to spruce up the area. Overall a great place to explore

To make sure hikers are able to return to base before sundown, you have to enter the trail no later than noon and must reach the final section of the approach by 12:30.  Gwaneumsa trail was about 8.7 km long taking about five hours at a leisurely pace.  Most of the hike was in a shaded area which would make it comfortable even during summer.   The first 3 kilometers were just a stroll with nicely laid out boardwalks for some stretches.  There are railings parallel to the trails in case an injured person needs to be transported from higher elevation, which made it extra reassuring for me.  Although steep, it was still a relatively easy hike and I made it through the last section without much problems.  From about 1600 m above and onwards, the trails were covered in ice and snow which slowed me down a bit as I didn?t even think about carrying crampons in late March.  As I got a late start the summit area was a little crowded with hikers having lunch or taking breaks.  Luckily, the Baekrokdam peak is a crater and there was a relatively wide area for people to sit around at the summit.  Unlike the Baekdusan Cheonji Lake, Baekrokdam is devoid of any water except a small patch of water that looks like a small puddle from the top.  While not particularly scenic, it is nice to stand at the highest point in the country.  Because of the strong winds, I didn?t stay long and started to head down the less steep Seongpanak Trail which was about 9.7 km to the parking lot.  Few kilometers from the summit was easy with boardwalk paths and steps.  There was a three kilometer stretch of snow covered trails that made the descent quite stressful though.  Once the snow covered area was cleared, it was a long but relatively flat walk rest of the way which my knees were thankful for.  The entire round trip took about nine hours total without much rest.  Having crampons would have shaved at least an hour off of that time.

To go there: take bus #710 bound for Sheongsan Ferry Terminal. You have to tell the driver where you're going before boarding the bus. Buy a ferry ticket from the ticket counter (5,500?? - round trip).We were there on 2nd May ~11am, the weather was windy but there was sunlight. We bought tickets for hop in and out bus from the ferry terminal. It will take you to 4 different attractions on the island, we only managed to enjoy the first 2 because it started raining (good thing we don't have an international licence, because u can rent a motorbike there too), and it was already windy, so the cold was too much for us. But I would recommend this place. Come once you're here, come at least once. I love the view. Too bad it was raining so we have to keep our trip short.

To be honest, I wasn't quite sure what to expect before I saw this show. I knew generally it was about performers who drew and entertained the audience somehow on stage. BUT IT WAS AMAZING! We saw   Team Chaplin,   four   hunky   young men, all dressed in decidedly stylish paint-splattered black clothing, complete with Charlie Chaplin bowlers. It could best be described as a multi-media show in which the performers draw using charcoal, paint, LED touch screens (I think!) and other art mediums and techniques to create a wide variety of images from pop culture and the classics, most of it set to contemporary music. They dance plus do a little martial arts, mime and comedy, and they use audience participation very effectively. Among the images are Michael Jackson, the Little Mermaid, Bruce Lee, Beethoven and Jeju's own icon, Dolhareubang, or   Stone Grandfather.   Even after seeing the show, I am not sure how some of the effects were achieved. I'm not going to do any   spoilers   here of the action, because the element of surprise is important for this show. But trust me, you WILL be surprised. It has many entertaining moments. If you live in Jeju or plan to visit, you should make time for the show, which is performed on the campus of beautiful Cheju Halla College...you'll be treated there to one of the best views of Halla Mountain anywhere on the island...take your camera for that, and for the photo/autograph session at the end of the show.

To be honest, I didn't expect much at first, but when I started walking up the stairs, OMG! I was really awed by the clear blue sky, silver grasses, wind, everything! The view of the crater was just   so-so   to me but the view of the other side with the silver grasses was just way too amazing! I would say, it's not something that's so special that you must go to see no matter what but still, it's something that you won't be able to see everyday or everywhere. First of all, you must go at the correct timing. I went during mid-October, the view was magnificent! You can even see Hallasan from afar (check out my photo). Thereafter, you can walk through a small road where you literally being surrounded by silver grasses. That's a perfect place to take photos as well (photo attached).This can be a romantic place, or it can also be a peaceful place where you go to relax your mind and to see something different.

To be blunt, I couldn't see the dragon's head in the Dragon Head Rock, and I'm not alone. Apparently a portion of the formation fell off during a heavy storm long ago, so perhaps it was once more impressive. Currently, it has become iconic for a rather tired trend in Korean tourism. Pointing at the sky and finding clouds that look like other things is childlike. Officially naming rocks and then designating them as   important cultural artifacts   in order to manufacturer tourism is crass. In much the same way that the Korean government has become intimately involved in generating the so-called   Korean Wave   of K-pop and Korean television dramas, there is a constant rush to capitalize on landmarks, events, and experiences that will help distinguish Korea in general and Jeju specifically in the competitive marketplace of global cultural value. This push to invent cultural significance is monopolized by a predominately male class of older Korean bureaucrats who have capitalized on Confucian values in order to override younger, better ideas, fueling their own, often tedious marketing concepts despite the existence of far better and substantive materials from which to draw inspiration. Take for instance Jeju's rich history of folklore and deities. Sure, you can dawdle about with stories of a dragon stealing jade or herbs of immortality from Halla Mountain and being shot by a celestial arrow as punishment, turning it to stone; but the fact is there are literally hundreds of far better stories that have some basis in local lore rather than the distinctly artificial details surrounding the Dragon's Head Rock. If you're interested, look for books on the subject, some of which were written by expatriates in an attempt to save this rich heritage from being slowly whitewashed away by modern fabrications. A book called   Spirits: Jeju Island's Shamanic Shrines   by Joey Rositano comes immediately to mind. Or you can go to any number of local beaches and walk along paths where every 20 yards or so you can read a plaque that tells you what a large stone vaguely resembles if you squint hard and suspend your disbelief.    That said, there's nothing wrong with taking a nice stroll along the seaside in this part of town if you only have a short amount of time to spend and you need to get to the airport soon. There are some passable restaurants along the way, a couple of good caf챕s, and some great views of the ocean. However, make no mistake - this is an authorized conduit for tourists and as such you will be subject to a conveyor belt of people on the same walk, as well as an abundance of stores whose sole purpose is to extract money from you by selling tawdry bits of plastic.

TLDR:Long hike, not that easy if you're not fit. 8-9 hours, 19.6km in total.Bring at least 3L of water each. They do sell water at the checkpoint, though only in 600ml bottles.Wear shoes with good sole and ankle protectionConsider taking a small towel (or two) to wipe away sweatBring a warm jumper and possibly a clean, dry shirt. Even in summer it's cold at the topStart the hike before 8.30am if you want to reach the peak because if you don't make it past the checkpoint at around 7km in, before 12.30pm, you won't be allowed to go to the peak.Bring a plastic bag for your rubbish because there are no bins at all on the hikeFor those who want moreRemember that this hike is longer than an average work day and you will need to replace water lost through sweat. Pack around 3L of water per person. Also pack some protein and carbohydrate heavy snacks such as nuts and dried fruits to keep up your energy levels. If you sweat a lot, consider bringing an electrolyte drink sachet to use halfway (or buy a can of Pocari sweat at the checkpoint). At the checkpoint, you can buy instant noodles, 600mL water bottles and Pocari sweat. If you don't want noodles for lunch, bring lunch. But keep in mind it's cold at the top so some warm noodles can be perfect. The noodles are a bit spicy though, so if you don't like spicy food, maybe bring your own lunch. There are absolutely 0 facilities for heating or preparing food. They won't even give you hot water for any noodles you don't purchase from them. Also there are no rubbish bins on the entire hike so you'll need to bring a plastic bag to carry out your own rubbish. The toilets are pretty gross and may or may not have toilet paper so consider bringing tissues. Also the toilets generally have no sinks, so bring some hand sanitiser gel.A small towel or two to wipe away your sweat wouldn't go astray, and a warm coat/jacket and clean, dry shirt will make your time at the peak much more comfortable (addressed in a later section).We took the 781 bus from Jeju city hall at around 6.55am. We arrived at the Seongpanak stop around 7.25am.Make sure you give yourself enough time to get to the Jindallae Shelter (checkpoint around 7km into the hike) before 12.30pm. If you don't make it to the shelter before 12.30pm you will not be allowed to continue up to the peak. It's very disappointing, I'm sure, to hike for 7km, hoping to see the peak and then be told you can't go because you missed the 12.30 deadline. I can't stress this enough. At the shelter, we heard some Americans complaining that they had missed the deadline by 24 minutes (they had started the hike at 10.30am) and that there was no information available on the trail or online about this rule. They were wrong on two counts- there are at least 5 signs along the trail up to the shelter stating that you need to pass by 12.30pm (in English). Also there are a number of blogs about this hike online which also talk about the rule. Now we started at around 7.30am and made it to the shelter by 10am, but we didn't stop to rest at all before the shelter. The walk up to the shelter is 90% easy level with gentle slopes and a few short harsher sections. If you are fit enough to contemplate doing a 19.4km hike then this section should be fine for you. If you start the hike around 8.30am, you will have no issues making it to the checkpoint in time and you should make it back to the bottom by 6/6.30pm. Earlier if you don't rest too long and are relatively fit.Note: there are several places that you can stop to rest just after the shelter. If you are running close to the 12.30pm deadline, just get past the shelter and then stop to rest once you've gone past. Just make sure you don't rest too long because you've probably got another 5-6 hours before you get back to the end of the trail including the rest of the walk to the peak, and you don't want it to get dark or have to rush on the way down.The next section after the shelter is graded as 'normal' by the signs along the route. This section does have a few challenging sections but also some easier stretches as well. If you have regular short rests then it's manageable for people of minimal to moderate fitness with some huffing and puffing.The last 1-1.5km of the walk to the peak is where it starts to get difficult. By this stage you've already hiked uphill around 8km and for probably 3-3.5 hours. The way to the peak is hundreds and hundreds of stairs often with many oddly shaped rocks to navigate around whilst traversing increasingly steep steps. If you're not super fit then you will struggle on this section. At one point we were setting ourselves goals to make it up 3 sets of staircases before we would rest for 1 minute then start again. But the important point is you are so close to the top now, so just keep pushing.The top can be quite crowded. We made it by around 11.30am and hung around for about 30mins to take photos and admire the view. My next piece of advice is- bring a warm jumper because the wind is cold up there and if you're anything like me, you will be sweaty which makes the wind even colder. Another point: if you're a sweaty person, consider bringing an extra dry/warm shirt (or two) with you to change into at the top (and possibly on the way back down). If you're prone to sweat a lot, this can make a huge difference to your enjoyment at the peak because you will by dry and warm. Your photos won't look so sweaty either. Make sure you take a picture of all members of your party with the peak stone marker or the crater to prove that you reached the top.Keep in mind that the way back down can take longer than the way up because you are now passing many people on their way up and going down is very hard on your already exhausted legs and feet. It can take 4-5 hours to get back down from the peak. We started going down at 12pm and made it to the bottom by 4pm, but we stopped several times.The path is quite narrow so on your way down, you will have to stop to let people pass in the other direction many times (unless it's significantly past the 12.30pm deadline, in which case everyone will be going down). The section between the peak and the checkpoint is very hard on your feet and legs. It will feel like forever but just remember that the track gets gradually easier and gentler the closer you are to the end. Stop at the checkpoint for lunch if you haven't already had it, or you feel like some hot noodles to warm you up.Keep on all the way down, being very careful not to slip. There are many rocks and if they are slightly wet, they are very slippery. Eventually you'll make it to the bottom. Then you can take your photographic evidence of reaching the peak to the little tourist office and for 1000 won each, you'll get a certificate saying that you reached the 1950m summit of Mt Hallasan. Congratulations!Sore feet and legs and weary bodies, you can catch the 782 bus back to Jeju city for a well earned rest.

Tips & things to take note:- Bring LOTS of water. On average 2litres per pax.- Bring sufficient food - basically breakfast,lunch,dinner.- Got to reach the checkpoint by 1pm to be allowed to attempt summit- Got to start descent from summit by 2.30pm- Gets cold and windy at the peak so bring a windbreaker.- You have to carry your own trash down. No bins on the mountain at all.We took 11hours and took the Seongpanak trail up and Gwaneumsa trail down. Seongpanak is easiest as its gentler but its the longest trail. Gwaneumsa is much more scenic. We were beginner hikers and hence probably took longer. The tourist  centre told us it would take ~9hrs. Spotted a deer on our way down on the Gwaneumsa trail. It was pretty scary though, we walked for 1hr+ without spotting a single human. (probably cause we were slow)My legs ached for 4 days straight but I have no regrets. My knees and ankles were insanely sore by the end of the hike. If you've even the slightest knee/leg issues, please think THRICE before you attempt Hallasan.Also, toilets are only available at the bottom (before the hike) and at the checkpoint. The toilets are GROSS. I couldn't do it no matter how hard I tried. Toilet was damp and stinky and lots of flies. No water system & its a squat system for ladies. Basically peeing into a hole filled with other people's waste. Saw another lady peeing in the woods instead...Also, all the announcements are in Korean, though signboards are in English.Aim to start hiking by 7am-8am. Any later, you may not reach checkpoint/summit in time unless you have a good enough stamina.Hiking sticks and shoes would help tremedously. Though we did it with regular sneakers. LOTS OF BUGS. Bring insect repellent though again, we didn't have one.Overall, its worth it and wouldn't do it again but have no regrets.

Tip: if you are not coming for the sunrise like us, come early enough though, we arrived at 8 and it was pretty quiet but got crowded very fast when we left past 10 there were bus loads of Chinese tourists everywhere plus many Korean families. The way up is steep and you'll get a bit tired but the views from the top are fantastic, particularly over the sea since the shore is already getting seriously overdeveloped even in this part of the island which is comparably much less developed than others.

This well set out and very informative museum recounts the history of how many of the Jeju islanders were killed and repressed during the late 1940s and early 1950s.  The visitor passes through a series of rooms, each explaining in Korean and English a different stage in the tragic events.  Apart from the actual events themselves, two things shocked me most.  Firstly, that I had never before heard of the April 3 Uprising, although some 25-30,000 people were killed by Korean government forces and their supporters.  Secondly, that even well into South Korea's democracy the events continued to be hushed up and only relatively recently has the truth begun to be told.  Just a few years ago, mass graves were discovered near jeju airport.  The museum provides such a valuable insight into the island's past that I think no visit to Jeju would be complete without coming here and learning about the events and their aftermath.  Entry is free of charge.  The peace park around the museum provides a place for contemplation after visiting the museum.

This waterfall lies in the southern part of the island, specifically in Seogwipo. Pay an entry fee of 2000 KRW and you can experience it up close for some photo-opportunity but just remember to wear a good air of shoes and be very careful when walking around or climbing over large rocks for a closer feel of the cool breeze. It's worth the trip.

This was the same village that Dae Jang Geum (鸚㏝룝) was filmed. It looked like a huge place in the show but in actual fact is that this place is really tiny! It should not take anyone more than 10 mins to complete. We were shown how water was collected from the rain by wrapping a rope on the tree that links into the water pots. The tourguide said that in those days, women in Jeju island work while the men stay at home. The lady touring us in the area carried the water trout to show us how Jeju women in the past used to carry water. There is one small house that according to the lady, is still inhabited. We were not allowed to enter but we can take pictures from outside the house. The house smells of the aroma of freshly cooked rice. We were told that someone is actually cooking. After touring the small compound comes the main part of the program - promoting honey. It seems like there are many version of how real honey should be. For this version, the honey doesn't melt in water. One can see the hives when it's placed in water and swirled around. We were given different honey to try: Pure honey, lingzhi and 5 flavors. For some reasons, they also sell handcream made of horse oil. It smells quite nice though. But I still have a whole box of lanolin cream at home so decided not to buy. They are not cheap either.

This was the most fascinating and beautiful experience during my two week stay in South Korea. The long, winding path to get to the coastline to see the Women Divers Show is gorgeous from beginning to end. The mist hovering over the black volcanic sand was unlike anything I have ever seen. I never wanted to leave. The hike up to Sunrise Peak was sweaty but worth it. The long, windy path to get the the top of the peak is fairly easy to walk and offers many wonderful views along the way. The fog was too dense to see anything from the very top, but I'm still glad I did it. This was such an amazing part of my trip; one of my most fond travel memories ever.

This was the last stop on our vacation. Unfortunately it was also the only grey/cloudy/cold day. The island was still a must see for us. The ferry ticketing area can be very confusing, so be prepared if you don't know any Korean. We figured it out after about 5 minutes of standing around, staring in confusion. Once we reached the island, we rented an electric car (from Gulliver's Travels) with side-by-side seating for 占35,000 for 2.5 hours and cruised around the island following the path. The beaches were incredible. White sand, crystal clear water at the shore, turning into turquoise water a little farther out. Even with the grey sky, it still looked amazing. We didn't climb out to the lighthouse (if you climb to the top of Hallasan on your visit, you'll understand why. Ow.) but we got some great photos of it. Peanut ice cream is way overrated in my opinion, but it was still a must since we were on Udo! My husband got the hallabong ice cream. We liked that one more, but the stuff they put on it tastes like mashed up hallabong peel, so it was bitter and we just scraped it off. There is a restaurant that serves (I forget the name, I am guessing) Hallasan fried rice. They make it look like a volcano! We really wanted to go, but needed to catch the ferry back. Overall, if it had been warmer and the we could actually see the sun, it would have been much more enjoyable. We talk about going back and spending a night on the island so we have the time to walk around it, instead of having to drive/rent a bike.

This was part of a day tour. After climbing a mountain and being someone who doesn't exercise, this place was too much for me. Like mentioned in other reviews, this place is dark, the path is naturally uneven with puddles of water from rain and natural water. I came out earlier to enjoy some hot ramen at the convenience stall and didn't regret it.

This was our first visit to a lava tube, and we enjoyed it very much. The lava tube cave is maintained in natural state. Hence the floor is uneven and you need to watch your step. It is also very wet and little cold in side. Apart from that the walk is very enlightening. We learned many new things about lava tubes.The lava column at the end of the cave is a must see and is the highlight of the whole walk.Must visit.

This was our first stop during our weekend trip to Jeju. I had heard about these women before but didn't know much. First, they showed us a video (in English) all about the history. I was immediately hooked! The rest of the museum is so interesting. The pictures and artifacts tell a great story. I just wish I could have met the Haenyeo personally! Also, the women working at the museum were nice and helpful as we tried to get to our next stop.

This was one of those places on earth that fascinates me... It was a rare opportunity to see and walk through a lava cave!  There is no place like this where I'm from, so I thought it was delightful! The day I went, it was hotter than Hades outside. Once we were inside, the air temperature immediately dropped. The farther down you went, the cooler the air. My hands were actually freezing cold.  Although its not necessary, I recommend you bring a light jacket and explore!

This was one of the only attractions that was open the day after Typhoon Bolaven moved away from Jeju this summer. On the day after there was still some strong wind and it was overcast, but people were out clearing debris off the roadways and sidewalks. Our hotel called ahead to this Botanical Garden and they said they were open, so we took the bus over and sure enough it was! It was a huge greenhouse building with an observation area at the top you can climb stairs to and see all over the area including the ocean. There were different climate areas inside with plants from that part of the world (jungle, dessert, local climate, flowers, etc), a small cafe with coffee and ice cream, some shops, and restrooms inside. Outside there were nice grounds with a big grassy area where people could sit, and other themed gardens (Korean, Japanese, French, Italian). Very pretty. Signs inside in English and Korean and Chinese describe some of the plants.? There were lockers inside for rent with coins. They weren't huge but we saw some backpackers taking a medium sized pack out of one.They were renovating part of the building but we didn't smell or hear anything bothersome. All in all it was a nice place to visit if it's raining or just post-typhoon outside, if you love plants, or have some extra time to see sights on Jeju.

This was one of the most popular things to do in jeju and we stayed close by so was a no brainer. Cost $11,000krw to get in, and had heaps of different plants and flowers from different parts of the world etc. overall not too bad, october is the off season to go so was very quiet. If you love plants you?ll love this if not properly not the place for you.

This was one of the most expensive tourist attraction that we did, at 6,000 kw per person. There was a lot of hype related to this attraction and I was not impressed with the crater. There should be no charge for this site as it is a concave valley in the earth. If you like hotdogs, then get a hotdog.

This was one of the highlights of my trip. In autumn there is a sea of pampas grass swaying in the breeze on the slopes of this volcanic crater. If you walk up a little you get an amazing view of Halla Mountain and it makes for some great photos.  We went early in the morning and it was amazingly quiet - we could just hear the rustling grass.As we were leaving tour groups started coming in so could be nicer if you beat the rush.Entrance is 6,000 won which is a little expensive on Korean terms for a small attraction like this, but I thought it was well worth it.

This was one of the few places in Jeju in which I wished I had more time to explore and actually take the trail up the the crater.  Moreover, the place is a UNESCO World Heritage site.The attraction is located on the eastern edge of Jeju Island.  I've heard the place is good for sunrises (why it's nicknamed Sunrise Peak).  However, that may be difficult to do if your hotel is in the Jeju City or Seogwipo areas and so far away from the attraction.  There is also a trail that heads up to the edge of the crater - which I unfortunately did not have the time to walk - but I would definitely advise anyone to take that trail if you have the time.  There is also an opportunity to go horse riding, but it looked like it was more for kids rather than adults.I did have the time to walk on the lower parts of the attraction - near the bay/harbor/cliffs area.  Notably, the area is extremely windy and cold, so be sure to bring the correct clothing especially during the off peak season.  There are some spectacular views of the cliffs and of Udo Island if the sky is clear enough on that day.  There are also some female divers that   perform   at 1:30 PM and 3 PM - although I did not get the chance to see them - if you take a trail to walk down to the bay/harbor area.This is definitely a must-see place to visit in Jeju and you'll get a lot of great photos here.

This was one of our stops in our taxi tour for that day.This is a small place showing the traditional homes of that area a long time ago.  It?s free. An English speaking guide will tour you around.  Some interesting facts, like two separate doors (one bigger for the male I think.) They will offer you a drink made of honey and some fermentation of some berries.  It?s like juice but with some tart aftertaste.  Taste good though that we spent I think $40.00 for a bottle.  In hindsight, maybe a bit too much considering it?s not an alcoholic drink (tongue in cheek).  But while drinking that juice at home, it sure brings in mind our visit to Jeju.  While there we saw a black pig with a small companion rat.  Well seems the rat was hovering near the pig pen.  Interesting place and the guide did tell some interesting stories and tidbits! (Can be done in half an hour).

This was one of my favorite parts of Jeju. We went during the sunrise which reading everywhere said was most ideal, and it was gorgeous. It?s a lot of steps to get to the top. I would suggest bringing a bottle of water.

This was not part of our main itinerary but we visited it as it was raining in other parts of Jeju.We saw the acrobatic performance, it was rather entertaining and sometimes hilarious though some parts were boring for us. The kids enjoyed it though. There was some reenactment of a story but it was all in Korean so we only got the gist of it.

This was my best experience in Jeju. I went in October 2013 and we went up Yeongsil and down by Eorimok. The hike was not the most difficult, but can be quite crowded. We arrived by car around 8am and there was a queue to the carpark. Note that there are two carparks, one on the lower level (where buses drop you off) and one at the start of the trail. We waited about 45 mins to get into the first carpark, and when we saw that there was another queue to go up, we just parked at the lower carpark and started our hike from there. This is a good idea if you plan to go down by Eorimok - you won't have to climb up to get your car after taking to bus from Eorimok to Yeongsil.The hike in autumn was wonderful, the foliage was awesome and the weather was perfect. There is a rest area between both trails where you can buy cup noodles and chocolate bars. It took us around 4 hours to go up and down.

This was an interesting experience. I am usually ok in small spaces and felt this would be a great thing to do. But once I was in the middle of the first maze I felt a little uneasy. They provide a map and the maze itself is pretty easy to do. You also hear people walking around, but just something about the possibility of making a wrong turn made me not want to do the second and third maze. But there are really cool towers and a museum where you can take amazing pictures. the museum is free, they have trick art and a puzzle art. Getting here was a little bit difficult. Ask around your previous destination at the bus stop perhaps some people are willing to share taxi with you. Since the bus that goes around this area takes almost 45 minutes. And once you get to your destination you sometimes still have to walk a while to get to where you want to.

This was a very interesting Lava Tube cave.  There were signs in English as well as various other languages describing what you were looking at.  The signs were informative.  The cave is cool, so I recommend a zippered sweatshirt or windbreaker.  Also, the floor of the cave is uneven, so you definitely want to have good walking shoes.  I was just fine wearing old jogging shoes.  We went as part of a guided tour - I would have liked to spend just a little more time there, but that's how it goes on bus tours...  There may be more beautiful caves, but overall, it was the nicest cave I've been in - very nice Lava Tube - you will enjoy it.

This was a really enjoyable hike up the highest mountain in South Korea @ 1950m, and I recommend it as a great experience of the outdoors and physical activity.  However I saw a lot of people (both locals and foreigners) struggling with various aspects so please take note of the following points:WEATHER:  If you have the flexibility of several days from which to select, review the weather in advance and aim to choose the best day.....otherwise for example you may have no views when you emerge from the trees and at the summit.TIME, PACE & TIME-LIMITS:  This is a long hike, 19.2km round trip to be exact or about 12 miles, but is a relatively gentle incline.  The general consensus in many reviews is that it should take 10 hours total including breaks and lunch.  I would consider myself slightly above average fitness and took 6 hours total, however being solo it makes a difference because I could walk at my own brisk pace and take breaks (typically quite short 5-10 mins) when I wanted.  There are 2 shelters (with toilets) on the route located at approx 4km and 7km, and it's very important to note that for safety reasons they do not allow anyone past the second shelter (which is 2.3km from the summit) AFTER 13-00 HRS, no exceptions.  Furthermore everyone must depart the summit to start descending by 14-30 HRS latest.  I did come across quite people between the 2 shelters who appeared to be rushing to make the 13-00 deadline.  This is not recommended because either you could push yourself too hard and get exhausted, or get injured walking on the rocks, or simply miss the deadline.  FOOTWEAR:  At minimum bring sturdy training or trekking shoes, preferably hiking boots to provide ankle support. Some sections of the hike are on hessian mats and wooden walk ways which of course are very nice to walk on, however probably 30% or more is on large volcanic rocks which are not comfortable to walk on and requires some focus and concentration (especially descending when your legs are tired).  I was surprised to see some walking in sandals and they suffered.  A walking stick can be helpful but is not essential.DAYPACK:  Bring a small daypack to carry water, snacks, clothes etc and to keep your hands free.  Even in summer bring a light jacket or sweater because it can get cool at the top with the wind and elevation.  In Winter I'm sure it's really cold at the summit.PROTECTION:  Bring a hat for the higher elevations (when not in the forest), sun cream and lip balm.HYDRATION/SNACKS:  There is reportedly a source of mountain water half way up but personally I did not see it near the sign, and staff at one of the shelters advised me that no water is available.  Hence suggest that you bring at least 3-4 bottles of water or isotonic drink in your day pack per person (maybe 1.5 to 2 litres), and be sure to conserve it wisely because you'll need some on the way down.  I encountered some people on the way up who had no water left.  Muesli bars, chocolate and fruit are good sources of energy.  As well as fruit, the locals tend to pack rice & meat lunches and have communal picnics at the summit.TRANSPORT:  I used a rental car and got there early, before 8am.  The car park was already full and people started parking on both sides of the main road, which is allowed.  The bus stops are right there beside the car park for those using public transport.CERTIFICATE:   There is small office hidden away near the Seongpanak car park which will print your name on a nice certificate for 1000 Won. (US$1).IN SUMMARY: Please take the time to prepare properly and get there reasonably early so that you can enjoy the hike at your own pace.  During the walk I saw several deer, lots of beautiful butterflies and other insects and loved the great views ....Jeju is covered in 300+ volcanic cones so its amazing to see all of these.  HAVE A GREAT DAY ON HALLASAN!

This was a part of our Yeha bus tour - East Course - and felt it was worth seeing.  It is a lava tunnel/cave, which makes it kind of unique.  Visitors are limited to how far you can explore, which is fine as you do need to watch carefully where you walk - it is a lava tube and the floor is very uneven.  It is known for   Stone Turtle   because it is shaped like Jeju island.  Be sure to have a light jacket.

This was a great visit!  There is a hidden gem that people didn't seem to know about or decide to see (I'll mention later in the review).  The entrance fee is nominal and you get to see so much.  Even from the top, you get an awesome view and picture with sort of a bonzai tree at the top of the stairs.  Then walk a little further down and there is an alternate path you can choose to walk on large stones and there's some locals selling fresh seafood.  We didn't partake but a lot of other people were purchasing and eating the fresh seafood.  Then we walked all the way down to the falls using the stone path.  Be very careful if you choose to do this as the stones can be slippery.  Once we got down to the base of the waterfalls, you could feel the mist from the waterfalls and just hang out there to take pictures.  It was pretty cool to know this is one of the few waterfalls in the world that fall straight into the sea/ocean.  We walked back up after relaxing a bit near the waterfalls and we saw a path to the Castle of Shell near the edge of the parking lot.  You should take time to walk through this and visit the Castle of Shell.  It's free and you get a very picturesque view from the 2nd floor inside the castle.  Ok it's not really a castle but a small house but it's still very neat to see and just relax on the 2nd floor with the breeze and the nice views.  Then go around the house and there's a relatively unknown path leading down to smaller waterfalls and another great view of stone beach and cliffs around the corner.  I actually liked these falls the same as the main falls.  Smaller but more greenery and there were small little ponds you could soak your feet into.  We took some wonderful photos there and spent a long time wondering why very few people knew about coming here.  There were a ton of people at the main falls but we were at these smaller falls around the Castle of Shells for a good hour and literally saw just 2 other groups of people at the smaller falls.  Take a look at the pics.  It's worth the extra walk!

This was a first time visit for us...and we found it to be cheesy with a capital 'C'. However, who would have thought that CHEESY could be so COOL!!!!Yup, we had fun here...the place was amazing. Nature in harmony with recycled glass and plastic. it's very well maintained, good to spend a few hours here taking pictures...as well as soaking in the various exhibits on display. I particularly enjoyed the walk in the Enchanted Forest, a bit creepy though...as it was secluded from the rest of the complex, and this added to the excitement of being in the forest...talk about a vivid imagination!They have a shop selling souvenirs as well, clean restrooms and a cafe. I would recommend those looking for some fun to drop by here, and just let your inner child run free!

This was a building to commemorate those who perished when an uprising was brutally put down.  It is part of Jeju's history and should interest history buffs. As we're not history buffs, we just paid a short visit here in October 2016. The building was of fair size and the surrounding park was quite big, but not much to see. It has a serene atmosphere and a solemn place and reminds me of a cemetery.  We saw lots of local school children visiting when we were here.

This was a beautiful climb, but let me tell you, it's a climb. Granted we seemed to go on a particularly hot day at like 1:00 pm so that didn't help.I recommend taking water with you, but if you don't feel like carrying it, there is a store about half way up that you can get water and snacks. There are also lots of souvenir stores and restaurants at the base to stock up on supplies before heading up. I also recommend sunscreen and bug spray.There was a short line to pay about $2.00 for an entry fee. You received a ticket stub with a pretty picture of the volcanic crater on it. The trail is one-way: meaning there is one trail that goes up to the peak and one that returns down. This cuts down on congestion and ensures a scenic route the entire way. There are lots of places to take pictures and rest along the way. The time it takes to complete the trail all depends on your fitness level, but it is advertised as a 50-minute round-trip experience. At the peak, there are numerous places to sit and relax. You can see a beautiful 360-degree view of Jeju and Udo. Other items of interest: Horseback riding is available here and you can see the famous female divers of Jeju.

This village was very interesting. A lot of people still live in this village and they make a living off of the products that they sell. The village is free to go to, so we made sure to purchase some things in the village. We encountered a couple English speakers that guided us and explained some things to us. They were so sweet, they held onto some of our belongings at their home while we walked through the village. When we were done they offered to call us a taxi. When we told them we planned on taking the bus they insisted on driving my entire family to our next destination. They were so sweet, it was very heartwarming!
This tourist attraction quite interesting for the beginning of introduction after that, they will try to sell anything start from honey, tea and ginseng.

This tiny, delightful island feels miles away from anything familiar and mundane.  I highly recommend renting an electric scooter (for about 25 bucks for 2 hours) and driving around the entire island.  Driving around the island only takes about an hour, but give yourself extra time to stop for photo ops.  The place is dreamy and laid back - you can even spot the famous haenyeo (women divers) at work, and see their   dressing stations.    There is no   one particular amazing   thing to see on Udo, but rather it's about the whole experience of exploring this off-beat place and losing track of time.

This rock is really popular location in Jeju and also  Olle trail part.We have seen it just from quite far apart, but that was worth as well.Don't miss an opportunity, because it doesn't take a lot of time.

This Rock is believe as a Snake want to be a Dragon, so according to the local story there are God who live a the Sea.  And the Snake should have the Jade from the God and Snake steal the jade while the God is sleeping but before the snake escape the God Woke up and put an Arrow to the snake.  Half Body (Upper Part) already come out from the sea at it's become a dragon but the lower part is still below the sea and become the rock.  That's why the upper part that we can see looks like Dragon Head Rock.  This area is very near from the Parking area, here we can find Orange Seller, Snack seller, restaurant also, souvenir shop.  Nice place to see and near from Jeju Airport.. 10 Minutes from the airport.

This review will be written from the point of view of a middle aged woman of average fitness, not someone for whom a 20 km trek is a walk in the park.Mount Hallasan is the highest peak in South Korea and if you are on Jeju island it's definitely worth visiting. We took the Seongpanak trail, a scenic , easy route which reaches the summit. Plan on one day for the trek up and down. Here are some tips:1. It goes like this - You take a bus or taxi to the Seongpanak trail, and start climbing. It's a mix of  some steps and an easy trail. After a while you reach the first stop - I forget the name - where you can use  the restroom. There's a small shelter where we had our packed sandwiches. After this, the trail becomes a little steeper, and you reach the next stage - the jindeballat rest stop.( Times by which you must reach the Jindeballat stop and when you must start your descent are posted on the trail). There are restrooms here - but inspie of information to the contrary , there was no food for sale. After this the climb becomes a little tricky , and you need around 2 hours to reach the summit . The views are amazing from the summit. The Koreans hiking the mountain were not only super fit, they were the sweetest people I've met. When I became tired near the summit, so many encouraged me with words like   Fighting!     Turn around and see how far you have come.  Tips :1. Wear good hiking shoes - at points , the trail is slippery, and good shoes with ankle support are helpful.2. Carry a stick. You can get your own hiking stick or buy one from the store at the bottom.3. Carry plenty of water and snacks.4. Take a selfie at the summit and you can get a certificate at the bottom stating you have completed the climb ( costs 1000 won)5. You do need a certain degree of cardiovascular fitness to make the climb comfortably. But apart from that, the uneven  rocks and boulders are a little tough to climb, so make sure you do some core and lower body exercises too. 6. If you climb down slowly, it gets a little dark by the time you reach the base. Carry a head lamp.

This post is about logistics and what to expect from the hike. My partner and I hit Hallasan around 6:45 in the morning on a Saturday to avoid the crowds. We drove to Seongpanak parking lot (free and was filling up quickly. A tour bus with dozens of hikers was already there) which was about a 30-minute drive from Seogwipo. From there we took a $15.00 taxi ride to the Gwaneumsa parking lot. As this was not a loop trail, we wanted to take the steeper/harder route in and have gentler descent (easier on our knees) back to our car. Turns out, doing it this way we avoided what felt like hundreds of people ascending when we were heading back later in the day. The Gwaneumsa parking lot has a fee. (Sorry TA fans, I didn't get the amount since we took a cab --- I am sure it is nominal, like all fees in RoK:) People are allowed to camp at the Gwaneumsa section of the park and I saw a few people starting their day as we marched to the trailhead. We were under tree cover and walked along a dry river bed for the first couple of miles. At this time of day, we only ran into seven other hikers on this trail. After you cross the river via bridge, the hike starts to get a little steeper. About two hours in, you hit a large, modern shelter and toilets. Good time to take a break and snack. Or keep carrying-on as you will get a chance to sit, eat and gaze at another resting place. After the shelter, you will cross a much larger, newer suspension bridge. Fresh water available here. The climb will get a bit harder for next half quarter mile. Continue past the foundation of the destroyed shelter. After you ascend the 18-22 inch tall stone steps, you will reach a ridge which is the other good stop.  No shelters (in fall you should opt for the shelter), but a nice wooden platform from which to gaze at how far you've come. Crows will land in search of scraps. At this point you are very near the top, only a couple more hundred feet to go.The crater was dry when we visited (first weekend in October), but still a wondrous site. The seasoned, local hikers brought burners and ramen and were happily chowing down near the crater. Darn! That would have been nice. The  t-shirt, fleece jacket and windbreaker I was wearing barely sustained me, so the hot ramen sounded freakin' great.The hike down Seongpanak was not nearly as enjoyable since we were bombarded by the late starters heading up. At one point, the hikers coming up were in a jam ? seriously, no one could move, there were so many people. There?s a large shelter a third of the way down. As another reviewer noted, be sure to wear supportive shoes with rigid shanks as you're constantly stepping on uneven rock.  I had on trail runners, which was fine going in, but heading down, my feet were pretty battered. The boardwalk was a nice breather when we could get it.*Seongpanak gentler ascent, (and descent) but be prepared to share the trail with dozens and dozens of other people.*Free parking at Seongpanak -- fills up quickly as early as 7am on weekends.*Toilets available on trail.*Take bimbimbap for a nutritious, affordable, and portable snack. Mandoo is another good one -- good balance of carbs and fat.*Listen and look Nuthatches, Wrens, Great T*ts, and other winter birds on the Gwaneumsa trail.*The park states you must hit the summit by noon. I think this is why so many people were rushing to hit the peak at the same time.

This place will be good for nature lovers and those who are in Jeju to relax and get away from busy city life. It only takes 1hour to cover the area at a slow pace. You may get a chance to see autumn foliage here from mid to late Nov as there are quite a number of maple trees in the forest. (Note: Autumn is mild in Jeju, while northern parts of Korea are having colourful autumn foliage, we hardly see any colourful trees in Jeju till we came to Bijarim forest)

This place was one of the highlights in my jeju trip and it did not disappoint me. Seongsan area are small and stroll-able with mostly seafood restaurants. I stayed in a guesthouse that's literally right at the entrance of the peak. So took me fifteen minutes from getting up to reaching the peak. The stairs was not for the fainted heart and Or who has knee problems. If you think the stairs may concern you, come little early and really take your time there are a few platforms you can stip while climbing up.

This place was gorgeous! It is a Korean beach so it is crowded please keep that in mind. I am a Floridian and we have some of the best and most peaceful beaches on earth. But this, even for me, was truly an experience. One the amount of people was impressive but less crowded than Busan beach. Try to get here early and pay the money for the umbrella spot. They all cost the same, but you wanna be in the first row so you can see the water.The water is truly beautiful. The color is very different than floridan green blue waters. The ocean here is the deepest darkest blue I've ever seen, and the part that meets the beach is a light bright crystal blue. There are many families and watching the kids is really cute. We spent a lot of time floating around. Next time I would bring a float so we could inner tube around like the locals did.You can order food and the vendors or restaurants will bring them to your umbrella.Fried chicken is a must for Koreans on the beach. We actually were super hungry before going (next time we will do it differently) so we went to Korean food chain Mom's Touch that serves amazing crispy fried chicken in bbq glaze with pickled radishes. So on the beach we got ice cream and fresh fruits.Warning for travelers: more of a cultural heads up. There are showers- like beaches in America have...you do have to pay to use them, but there are no private changing rooms or showers it's all a show for anyone to see. Now it is gender separated, but don't be shocked to find you'll have to strip down in front of strangers. My husband is Korean and didn't warn me, but it was too late once I walked in, plus he already paid for my shower and I really needed a shower. But here's the thing you'll notice that no one cares about you, and no one looks at anyone. Just shower off, do your thing and you'll be outta there in no time. If this is too much for you to handle...then skip the shower and head back to your place to shower in your comfort level.

This place was breathtaking! After getting a yummy octopus pancake we walked around the cliffs admiring the beauty and the ocean. We started on the west and ended on the east it was a beautiful, windy, gorgeous day! Great place to get fresh seafood from the lady fishermen too.

This place starting to get famous in my country when Korean drama 'Princess Hour' was aired, never thought that someday I will visit this place. If you're a Teddy fans, take your time ^^ to enjoy the dioramas and various Teddy collection. They also have garden that full of teddy bear statues.

This place is such a gem ? literally ?? awe found it by accident and were blown away. Seriously one of the best parts of the trip! Highly suggest as a couple or with friends. (Solo is fine too, honestly)

This place is small but surprisingly occupied us half a day. Largely it?s because of the photo moment and also the activities it has to occupy the kids. These activities are drawing, taking self portrait, kids playground, and watching cartoon etc. There is a small cafe to rest your feet while your kids spend sometime at the indoor playground.

This place is name the world 7 wonder of nature, and defintely live it up to the name. I love the Jeju woman's diver perfomance, they are so lively and bubbly... Climbing up the stairs is totally panting (however nearing to the top, the stairs are very steep so be more cautious) but wait till u reach the peak of it, you will find it totally worth it. You can see the blue sea from this side and the other part of Jeju on the other side. The curve in volcano is amazing too.Totally recommended but please dun go there during noon when the sun is hot...

This place is just so amazing! All the displaying items were made by glass, the butterfly, the chairs, benches, pumpkin car, etc..... Not just clear colour and its colourful! I think they have done the check frequently because I can't find any defects, broken part from the displaying items. Best visit for lovers, family with elderly or kids...

This place is huge, with lots of plants, flowers, caves to see. Though it may not be extra especial since it felt so artificial, it is still a cool place to visit. Stroll and take lots of pictures with friends or family. Don't join the tour because they only allow 1-1.5 hours and you'll end up just walking and not really appreciating the things that you will see.

This place is huge!If you like nature, do visit Jeju Stone Park.  The English audio guide was excellent.  The exhibits were really interesting.  There were indoor and outdoor exhibits.  Do be selective if you have limited time.  One could easily spend up to half a day at this place.As we were a bit short on time, we browsed through the indoor museum rather quickly and still managed to pick up some interesting information.The outdoor areas were really nice and comfortable.
