Within minutes I was on my way back down.The reason why you need a photo with you and the summit stone (even if it over your shoulder in the distance) is to claim your Certificate of climbing Mt, Hallasan. On the Gwaneumsa Course you can self print your certificate at a booth just past the QR-cord booth at the trail head  If like me you are clueless with mobile phones you can go the manned QR code booth and them to do it for you.  There have a printer in the booth and was very happy to do it for me.   It costs 1000 won (around 1 us$) Facts and figures, I am a 73 year old Englishman on an extended holiday in Korea.  Start time 7-50am, summited at 11-05am.   Started down at 11-15 and back to the trailhead at 12-55pm. Yes I do class myself as a bit of a mountain walker so these times  are maybe a little faster then average, but mountain walking is about enjoying yourselves and not about how fast you can get up and down. I took a litre of liquid, in hindsight I should have taken more and I did finish it off when I was within sight of the carpark. There is a shop across the road from the carpark.   Food, I took no food just a few sweets and a couple of chocolate bars.  So the bottom line is you have to take all the food and drink with you.  It does say that you can get drinking water at the second WC (shelter) but I could not find any so don't depend on it. Getting back to Jeju City.   There was no buses so I started walking the 8 miles back to my hotel on the seafront. Pleased to say that  I did manage to flag down a taxi after around a mile.  All in all a very enjoyable day out on the mountain.

I do feel some surprise during our visit here, but probably we expect so much. Mysterious road is a part of the road, amazing. But after i tested with two bottles of beer, it just normal. i don't understand so much. But overall it's worth visit to Mysterious Road, Jeju.

I do a fair amount of hiking in the Green Mountains of Vermont, and I found Seongpanak trail to the summit of Mount Hallasan to be enchanting and beautiful! Though the hike may be challenging for folks with knee problems, it is a very well maintained trail (though long) that is worth the effort.Start your day out early and bring plenty of water!

I didn't reach the summit but hiking the Eorimok and Yeongsil trails didn't provide amazing views as far as I was concerned, but it's definitely worth doing.Take the 740 bus from City Bus Terminal to Eorimok (krw1800, 45 min) or Yeongsil Ticket Office (krw 2800, 60 min). Bus leaves CBT at 07:00, 08:00, 09:00, 10:00. You don?t want to set off after 10:00 as you won?t get back! Last returns are 17:36 (Yeongsil) and 17:55 (Eorimok) April through October.I took the Eorimok trail up (there?s an easy 1km walk from the bus stop to the trailhead) and reached the Witseoreum shelter in 2 hours, including stops. The first 2.4km are quite tough but it gets much easier the further you go. If you?re worried about your ankles then wear hiking boots but trail shoes are fine. The descent down via Yeongsil was a leisurely 90 mins but it feels like it would be a slightly tougher climb compared to Eorimok. There?s also a 2.5km downhill walk from the trailhead to the bus stop, so bear that in mind if you decide to start from Yeongsil. The scenery is much better on Yeongsil, although those with vertigo may find it tough, even with the very good safety barriers on the route. Eorimok doesn?t have those problems but the first 2km is under forest cover, with little scenery to admire for most of the climb.If you want to hike to the summit start very early, which probably means you'll need a car in case you miss the last bus back.There are clean, normal toilets at both entrances and at the Witseoreum stop. You will have to carry all trash back down as there are no bins anywhere on the mountain. You can buy hot instant noodles at the Witseoreum but you?ll have to carry it back down. I bought several buns and pastries at Paris Baguette for my hike.

I didn't get to see the sun rise there. We started the climb in the afternoon at about 2pm and it was pretty warm!To me, the highlight was taking in the views as we climbed up to the top to see the crater and back down. When we reached the top, it was quite an anti-climax actually. The crater looked like a huge green field. The climb was pretty easy for an unfit person like me. I saw a very pregnant lady successfully climbing to the top as well.Our tour guide took us to a beach area to take photos of Seongsan Ichulbong from a distance and that was really lovely as well.

I did the hike just 2 days back from the Seongpanak trail and I was really glad for the   gator   spikes that I rented from the guesthouse that I stayed at...the snow was thick such that you hardly see any steps at all. At the early part of the hike, the snow is hard and easier for grip but as you go higher, the snow gets soft and with every step, you will slide a little down. The last part was the hardest being very steep but with the summit in sight, I don't anyone is going to give up at that point. Going down proved even more tougher as the tendency to lose your footing and slide down is very real. Hiking stick is necessary. For a city person like me without much exercise and preparation, I took 4hrs to reach Jindallaebat shelter and 1.5hrs to reach summit and 3.5hrs to come down. The view is gorgeous and worth the hike but do not underestimate the difficulty especially in winter.

I did the hike in January, and it was amazing.  Parts were pretty difficult so you may need trekking poles or crampons.  The views from the top are stunning, but be sure to leave really early (before sunrise) as you'll be sharing the views with hundreds of your closest friends if you don't.

I definitely recommend this place altough it's popular among tourists. Anyway, the view on the top is absolutely amazing and for me walking on the top wasn't too hard. It was very windy but sunny day (and I burned my nose) so I recommend to remember the sun lotion! Or if it's cold and windy to wear warm clothes. On the top there were many places to sit and take a brake. The journey down was also lovely because of amazing views. Before you start to walk to up remember to go to toilet and eat something (there are toilets and food in the same area). If you haven't used to walk lot of stairs it can be quite challenge but it is definitely worth of it.

I decided to go with Seongnapak trail, and was planning to go up to the summit!Rocky and stony path made me really exhausted, I managed my breath okay and left the last 1.5km as my keens!You will be accompanied by many people along the trail! It?s highly recommended to start early, I arrived by 8am, reached the shelter around 11:00am!Weather was mild as you?ll be covered by trees most of the time!

I couldn?t resist visiting this place on our way from Jeju city to Seogwipo. It made me giddy as a child. Entry fee is now 14,000 won per adult, and either 11,000 or 13,000 for children. This place has optional guided tours and accepts credit cards. Small room of Hello Kitty history and how her image has evolved since 1976. Original design merch on display. Lots of interactive rooms for kids and 3 floors to play. As an adult I still had fun and enjoyed a Hello Kitty hot chocolate (her face is in the cream), and Hello Kitty-shaped strawberry mousse cake in the cafe. You?re paying for the experience, here, so if you or your child is not a Hello Kitty fan, don?t waste your time. The maze on the roof is shaped like Hello Kitty from an aerial view and is strictly for children?the maze walls are only about 2 feet tall. My favorite part was the art exhibit (2nd floor) and all the small, unexpectedly perfect details (heart shaped straws, Hello Kitty toilet paper!). Souvenir shop: a mechanical pencil costs 7,700 won (more than $6)?I guess this is slightly more than American Sanrio store prices. But, if you?re willing to visit this museum, you?re probably also willing to pay for a momento of your experience.

I completed every single course over a period of a year so the following comments are just my opinions. If you are staying for a short period of time in Jeju courses 6 and 7 are the most popular and will probably get the most from. Both are very scenic and you will get to see some of the major sights. If you start at one of the information sites, you can pick up a Jeju Olle guide which has maps and information of the trails, guides for the Buses, to get to and from the starting points. Also I'd recommend downloading Kakao Maps app on your phone and you can zoom in and see the actual trail that you are following when you are on it. It comes in handy especially for me when I made a wrong turn on my trips. If your doing the entire course I'd recommend buying a jeju Olle Passport. Carry it with you and get it stamped at the starting points and halfway way points of the trails. I was living near jeju city and caught most of Buses from the Jeju inter city bus centre. The 101/201 express buses will take you to/ or near a lot of the starting points but I'd recommend picking up the Olle Guide first and the info in that is invaluable.Most of the Starting points are close to the roads unless you are going to one of the 3 islands. I used booking.com most of the time to book places to stay overnight as I don't speak Korean. Jeju has a lot of places to stay and there would be abundant places to stay except for maybe a couple of the more remote locations on the trail. There are offical Olle trail Hostels throughout the trails to which are very nice. If planning for no Korean speakers just check before hand that you are not traveling on a Jeju holiday as a lot of paces close down and might be harder to find a place to stay. Of course take plenty of water and there's usually 7/11 of CV's around the place where you can get snacks to eat.The trails themselves are very beautiful , Different scenes ranging from Black volcanic rock on the coastlines, Forest trails, Beautiful beaches, Hill sides, a lot of Oreums (Jeju extinct volcanoes) small towns with a chance to see wildlife and a lot of friendly people. For myself my favourite trails were routes 11, 18-1 Chuja-Do island), 1-1 (Udo island), 7. For me the stronger trails were on the southern eastern point of the island starting from route 6 through to 15.Getting to the supporting islands it you might take note you will need your Passport to catch the ferry to Udo. You must show it when buying a ticket. There are a lot of ferries going most of the day to Udo. They have a very nice Peanut ice cream there. The smaller island Gapado at the time I went there were only 2 ferries in the day and its not the most reliable service and the ferries can be cancelled due to bad weather can be cancelled due to bad weather so check beforehand if you can. Chuja-Do island was one of my favourites. When I done it they had 2 ferries a day and you can not do the whole trail in time to catch the next ferry back so be prepared to stay over night. I have heard of instances when the weather turned bad and people had to stay a couple of nights on the island because the ferries were cancelled so just plan for that just in case. it is a beautiful Island though and one of my favourites.I would also recommend going and joining the Olle Walkers Facebook group. They take guided walks along certain courses and have great information about weather and so forth. all you need to do is contribute to the group from time to time.

I chose Seongpanak as the starting point from 7am, I managed to arrive the top before noon. I took Gwaneumsa to go down. This track is difficult than previous one but the view is beautiful. Make sure to bring lots of water and your own food.

I choose the most difficult route (Gwaneumsa Trail) as the website said it offers the best view of the mountain and I stupidly assumed their difficult is not too difficult if compared to Malaysia's route (because Malaysia's one is not a proper/well maintain path).And so I was wrong :p It is all the way up up up and up, stone path (which I hate most) and wooden staircase (so descending is definitely more blessing but very challenging to your knee). I hike @ 26 April, didn't get to see much fantastic scenery as I guess I'm not at the right season as I saw some other people's review they saw great scenery. So this was more like a physical training to myself. To train the mind especially. But, the sound of the wind is like ocean waves, this was indeed very beautiful, I even record it down during descending. It took me 4hrs 10mins to reach the top, in between there are... 2 toilets I think, and if you manage to reach samgakbong shelter (1500m) not later than 12.30pm (spring/fall) you are allow to continue to hike to the top, else you'll need to return. Cross this check point there is a spring water ahead before the bridge for you to refill your water! Then what's lying ahead is the super strong wind and the sturdy steep stone/wooden staircase path ==|Long story short:1) Hike at the right season I'm sure you can see more than what I see2) choose the trail wisely. I would say as long as you have a strong will, even you are not very fit also you can do this trail, just start little bit earlier than others to give yourself more time (say 5hrs to the top). 3) Make sure you are well equip to keep yourself warm. Windbreaker and glove is a must. I had 4 layers (t shirt, thermal, windbreaker & sweater & I was still shivering at top, the wind is just too strong that we couldn't even stand still) 4) Bring water, food, chocolate and candies! 5) Good shoes is a must for less struggling during descending & less stress to your knee. Personally I don't use hiking stick so suit yourself for this. 6) count the time and familiar with your own pace if you want to reach the top. Just make sure you reach the check point then you can take your own sweet time to get to the top.Last but not least, just don't under estimate this well develop stone & wooden staircase path. Although it's only 8.7km, 1950m height, it took me 4hrs plus up and 3hrs 15mins down (with very little time rest at top coz its just too cold!)Good luck!

I chanced upon this wonderful beach along Ilchul-ro Road while my family and I were on our way to Breeze Bay Hotel. I returned to the beach in the late afternoon and my family and I went to the same spot again the next day early afternoon. On both occasions, I parked our car at a car park that’s got just a few cars. Gwangchigi Beach is very long and the spot that I was at was near to a erected stone put up by the Rotary International. The good part was that there were very few people on this secluded beach. The better part was that Gwangchigi Beach is a black sand beach (yes, we finally experienced a black sand beach). The best part was the beach offers a marvellous view of the south-western face of Seongsan Ilchulbong. Using a pair of binoculars or a telephoto camera lens, you could see visitors climbing the stairways as well as the summit of Seongsan Ilchulbong.Moreover, walk along the beach and you will find unusual rocks and rock terrain just beyond the black sand. I believe the rocks arose from the explosion of an underwater volcano long time again that created the Seongsan Ilchulbong. During the late afternoon or sunset, the sunlight produced a beautiful array of black, brown, orange and green (algae-covered) colours of these rocks. Because late afternoon is where low tide occurs, the sea water was trapped within the rocks as ‘ponds’ ? and there were beautiful reflections of Seongsan Ilchulbong on the still water. Alternatively, you could walk on the rough brown ‘mat’ (not sure what’s the material) that was laid on the grass. It was along this mat path that I saw a horse that was tied to a pole. I guessed the horse was used for horse-riding but I didn’t see such activity as it was already past 5 o’clock in the afternoon.Gwangchigi Beach is one beach in Jeju that is under-rated and not well known. It warrants being among the top 10 beaches in Jeju. Anyway, I recommend visiting it as part of the Seongsan Ilchulbong experience.

I can wholeheartedly recommend everyone visiting Spirited Garded. Even though I came in winter, it was really beautiful, actually exceeded my expectations. I enjoyed the relaxed atmosphere and learned a lot about about bonsai trees and this garden. The staff was more than kind. I really appreciate this experience and will remember it for a long time. :)Doporuuji v큄em, i v zim je to kr찼sa, atmosf챕ra kouzeln찼, pracovn챠ci neskuten mil챠. Dozv챠te se plno zaj챠mav첵ch vc챠 o bonsaj챠ch, i o dlouh챕 cest vzniku t챕to zahrady.

I can imagin Udo is a quiet and beautiful island to stroll or bike sometime, but the day we visited was full of people.  We arrived there already at noon and rented electric bicycles to start rounding the small island.  The road was full of small vehicles and bikes moving or stopping by the road, I did not feel I was in the nature but a hustle corner.  There were quite some restaurants and cafes along the route, the one we went was full of people, price of food/drink is in high end.  It took us 3-4 hours to round the island due to time for camera and lunch.  Back to the electrical bike, which could power to assist you, but battery did not last long, it usually fails in the last up slope (the last check point with a cave and cliff) - and it is tough for rider to move uphill without gear.  So I suggest you rent a normal bike, it is cheaper, more reliable, and rider can wear hat but not the heavy helmet.  I will say if you want to visit Udo, visit in low season, not summer, which is really crowded and extremely hot - no tree, no shelter along the road.

I came here expecting mundane rock formations. Ohh how wrong I was. This is one of the most beautiful places in Jeju. The rock formations are gigantic and so artfully formed. Be careful when walking as you're walking beside the water and it can get slippery. We even sampled some fresh raw seafood like sea squirt, sea cucumber, sea snails and octopus with rocks as table and small children chair as our seat! No soju for us as we're driving!You park at the base of Sanbangsan and walk across the road to reach Yongmeori Beach. Entrance fee varies depending which location you want to visit.

I came here by chartered taxi, I got rate 130k KRW for 8 hrs use. Not sure how to come here with public transport though. For a first timer underground trip like me, it's quite interesting. The track is not very long, not suggested for Claustrophobic person (like my friend) as it's dark,wet and getting smaller inside. Suggested to bring a raincoat with you, if you forgot don't worry you can buy on convenience store in there.

I came here by bus .. so I waited for the bus and cars to go on neutral and watch them drive up he hill hands free.Some people poured water while other rolled a water bottle.Since this attaction takes less than 15 minutes, i would suggest also going the Jeju Art Museum next door :)

I and my boyfriend traveled here by public bus. We visited the place at the end of October not really December but I did a very late review. It was very easy to get to the place by public buses. The bus stop right in front of the entrance and crossing the street the take the return bus. I researched the bus number, it was wrong. So I asked the bus ticket woman for help and she was really helpful.It was a very challenging hike. Be prepared with a lot of water bottles with you and really exercises before the hike. The trail we took was Seongpanak trail, which is the easiest one. It was early of the fall season. Leaves started turning into different colors, chilling, not so cold, sunny and very enjoyable.We just finished 1500m of height and ate a noodle in a shelter. Then, we turned back (blaming non-stop walking in the previous days :D) and took a quick turn in a shortstop in Saraoseum (beautiful lake, nice view of the mountain).Overall, really enjoy it! Will try it again one day.P/S: it is a natural place so not clean bathroom. A very natural way of toiletry but I really don't like it but can't blame!!

I am really unfit and the hike up to the peak is painful to me. But once i reached the top, all of my pain seem to go away. The view of the sunrise is so beautiful. I know i will take longer time to reach the top so i begin the hike up earlier. I started at 5.30 a.m and reach the top after excruciating 1 hour.

I am not much of a teddy bear lover but I still found this place interesting. The entrance fee is a bit pricey though at KRW7,000. However, compared to the Tricky Art Museum, I think this place offers better value. I can imagine kids and teenage girls going ga-ga at this place. It lives up to its name in that there are hundreds of teddy bears in various settings and themes.There is a small park outside of the museum building with some more teddy bears but it was rather uninspiring. If you want to grab a quick bite, there is a Lotteria inside the museum.

I am not a teddy bear lover, but I found the collection very interesting. First of all, these were the collection of a Ms. Joanne Oh, a teddy bear artist. The bears date up to generations of collectibles. The design varies with time. The size of the bear are from tiny to bigger than man size. There were several hall showing different themes. Of course it will end with a souvenir shop showing many bear designs. In the international bear, there was even one of President Obama, with a letter of President Obama to Joanne Oh. The museum also has an advocacy of bear conservation. All in all, it was interesting with plenty of Photo opportunity for my wife who loved it so much. By the way, the materials used in Ms. Oh's bear were all made of ecological-friendly materials, another advocacy of this fantastic bear artist.

I am a resident of the Seattle metropolitan area so I have to compare it to the Chihuly Garden and Glass museum.  The Jeju Glass Castle is very different in concept as it also focuses on small to medium sized glass items.  Conversely, Chihuly Garden and Glass focuses on large scale items produced by Chihuly in small quantities.  That's not to say it was disappointing, but it wasn't that impressive in the sheer quality of the items.  However, you do get a very large variety of glass items from throughout the world so it does make it up in quantity.  Unlike the Chihuly museum, the glass castle is a very large complex.I did notice the museum seemed a little run down in a few areas - it really did seem it needs some upgrades to its infrastructure.  However, there is a maze, nicely manicured gardens, glass shoes, and a large variety of other takes on glass items.  There is also a nice trail to walk that showcases certain glass items as well.Perhaps the most interesting part of the museum is near the entrance.  You'll find a glass making room there with windows you can look through to see glass artisans at work.  It was quite interesting to see these people create glass items by sculpting it, putting it in the oven, and more.

I am a huge fan of Udo.  I have been numerous times and I never get tired of exploring a new road or a new cafe.At times it is soooo overrun by tourists that it can be a little overwhelming, but if you are smart and plan your trip during quiet times of the year, it is really rewarding.  The roads are quieter, the stores less busy.  There are numerous ways you can tour the island:I usually take my car.  I have heard that NO rental cars are allowed on Udo anymore.  so be aware of that.But once off the ferry there are so many scooter and electric bike shops* around.  *Foriegners be aware that you do need a license to rent these!ProTip:  I absolutely recommend you get off the beaten path and go explore the inner part of the island. So many cute cafes and splendid views!

I absolutely recommend you to take a day trip and hike up Hallasan if you are in Jeju. Even though if it takes the whole day, since it is about 20km walking, it is worth it. If you are in okay shape I'd recommend you to go up on the Seongpanak trail. It is longer but easier than Gwaneumsa trail. The hike has a lot of stairs, so don't expect climbing. Once getting up, the most thing that shocked us what the loads and loads of bugs, since we never heard about that. They don't bite but they do get on you which is annoying. That said, the view is beautiful, to the island but also to the crater. Going down I'd recommend Gwaneumsa trail since it is a lot more beautiful and more to see. It is only the first third part that is the hardest, after that it gets okay. Remember to start climbing early since you have to reach the checkpoint before a certain time depending on the year. It takes about 3 hours to get to the checkpoint so try to check what time you have to be there before. The time is there because it takes a longer time to get down than you expect. Also bring water with you. There is only one point where you can buy going up, and only one point where you can fill your water bottle on both trails!

Hyeopjae is a beautiful beach with everything you would want in a beach it's very long with thick soft sand. But, the best thing about Hyeopjae beach is the Ollhe trail that starts at the Northeast end of the beach and goes for ever. The trail runs along the shore so close to the sea that at high tide on a windy day it becomes inpassable because of the waves submerging the trail in some places. The volcanic rock along the trail forms different things. If you look at the rock closely you might see a dragon or a horse or maybe a bird. If you stay on the trail long enough you walk by G-Dragon's cafe. If you go even further you will come across a Smoke Tower that is hundreds of years old used to send a signal of a enemies ship approaching.So, while Hyeopjae Beach is 1st rate when you are done swimming take a walk through history down the Olleh trail.I'm an American that has been living in Jeju for the last 12 years and I walk this trail 3 to 4 times a week and it never gets old.

Huge, lots to see and easy to get lost in the maze of stalls. For a glimpse into local life with products ranging from clothes, fabrics, sundries, cooked/fresh food, seafood, dried goods and everything in between. Local souvenirs definitely cheaper here than duty free shops and touristy spots. Check out fresh tangerines, Jeju chocolates, hallabong jam/honey vitamins; even dried anchovies (great as Korean soup base) and ginseng roots for DIY ginseng chicken at home. Do compare prices at a few stalls and bargain with the kind ahjummas when buying several items. Souvenir hunters, moms and senior relatives will definitely love exploring the colourful atmosphere of Dongmun market. The covered market is good activity during rainy or hot days. Nearby attractions: Jungang underground shopping street, E-martNote:Street parking just outside the market can be difficult at peak hours, suggest self-drivers park around Black Pork Street or nearby hotels and walk to the market.

Horses are a big part of the Jeju culture  and Jeju Horse Park is a pretty cool place. Its museum includes many photographs  artifacts and a video telling the story of the Jeju   ma    or pony  which is descended from the ponies brought to the island by Mongol invaders. The island was considered a good place to raise horses  and the Mongols used it as such. At the park  you can also ride the horses. There is a great giftshop with lots of local handmade items. Children or even adults can make related crafts in an activity room. The building itself is round like a ger  the traditional nomadic tents used by the Mongols. The top deck includes a fabulous 360-degree view of the   oreums   (small cinder-cones or parasitic volcanoes) that literally ring the area of the park. Inside the railing  an artist has painted the oreums  along with their names. So  you can know exactly which oreums you are viewing. There are also some actual Mongolian gers (also known as yurts in other nomadic cultures). I believe tourists can actually spend the night in one of the gers. One thing to consider: If you want to visit  you must either have your own transportation or go with someone who does. It's kind of far from anywhere  and bus service may not operate in that area. Likewise  taxis don't just happen by. But  it is a beautiful area and interesting for the entire family We visited in the spring  and there were also lots of colorful wildflowers. Plan to spend a few hours there  especially if you will ride the horses.

Honestly I never know that Kpop will be this fun after visited this place. Not only like indoor theme park, but also like a museum. You can learn about music industry in Korea from time to time. There are memorabilia for Korean musician too. The fun part is, if you are a VIP (fans of Big Bang), you have to and you must watch GDragon hologram performance. You can be GD's girl and be the part of it (I was chosen and it was really fun). After that you can take pictures with GD (using chromakey tech) and pay around 5usd to print it. Well, so much you can do here even for not so Kpop mania like me.

Hmm... Where to start?Well, Jeju Island, being volcanic in nature, must really have places like this!Honestly saying, it wasn't something so jaw-dropping and spectacular!Just more like a place with rock formations due to the cooling of lava!The trek inside isn't hard and what I really liked was that it was chilly while we did it!It was a nice sidetrip nonetheless if you like walking and if you like all these geo stuff!If you're in Jeju, maybe you can give it a try

Hiked to the top of Hallasan yesterday morning through the Gwanmeusan Trail - started at about 7:10am and were back in our car at 2:30pm - so this start and finish time includes breaks, and you'll need them even if you are in okay or good shape. It was a bit disappointing to see the majority of water bodies in the mountain are dry at the moment - just a few ponds on the early parts of the trail, and the crater lake at the summit, which we expected would be much deeper. The trail has a combination of dirt, rocks, and steps/bridges. I wish the steps and parts of the trail didn't include so many sharp rocks - your feet WILL feel them! We did the hike in running shoes because we don't have hiking boots here. I can see the climb being a lot easier with hiking shoes. Some parts of the trail are very steep so if you have serious knee problems, I don't think this is the trail for you. Do bring lots of water and snacks - we had two liters of water for each of us and I still think my husband got dehydrated rather badly. There is really nothing to eat on the trails so bring snacks. Visibility yesterday wasn't great - pollution has been pretty high in Jeju the past couple of days - but it's still a GREAT, BEAUTIFUL view from the top. I loved all the flowers you see growing in the rocky sides of the mountain in the last third of the trail. Very happy I did it and it's a great hike, but there is not a lot to see before you get to the top. We went down the same trail, so a total of 17.4kms. It'd be interesting to see what the other trails are like, but I don't think I need to summit again.

Hike the mt thru seongpanak trail (Gwaneumsa trail was closed due to rock slide) These are the only 2 trails that lead u to the summit. Took a taxi there, cost was 30,000won from somewhere near the airport. There is a bus stop at the foot of seongpanak but not Gwaneumsa. Overall, it was not an easy course for me and my hubby as we were not prepared. It's better to wear hiking shoes & have a walking stick. Do start early, I was told that it opens at 6am & we arrived at 7am. Go for it if you enjoy hiking!

Highly recommend everyone to do at least one of the Jeju Olle trail routes. We chose route 6 as it?s being classified as the easiest route. The route is filled with beautiful sceneries. Some part of the route takes you onto the roads, into the bush, along the coastal and up some hilly roads. We meet a lot of locals along all way and they are helpful & friendly. Lot of cafes for one to take a rest too.

Here is the best was to try the experience of climbing up the hill Come from the loveland (from the north) and stop at what seems to the bottom of the hill (there will be a sign on the other sign of the road)Stop your car, go in neutral put you warning signals on.Make sure there is no pedestrian and car behind you and release the break The car will start climbing the hill in reverse mode It is a bit dangerous as there are lot of pedestrian and potential drivers that dont understand what you are doing but really the best way to experience the illusion

Here at the Jungmun-Daepo Coast, you see the very unique and naturally beautiful Jusangjeolli!These are basically volcanic rocks that have been naturally formed by winds and waves into what seem like artisan-sculpted pillars!It was astounding and amazing to see how nature can create something that you could only imagine a person could do!Usually, there are a lot of people so you can't really stay long and soak on the view and the soothing Jeju breeze!But hey, it's worth the stop!

Heaven on Earth - volcanic stone sculptures abound - every tree a bonsai - cedar, pine, maple and more.  Azaleas were in full bloom and a delight in colour.  The birds, in particular the white peacock who posed displaying all his feathers fanned out.  Then onto the water garden with its lotus blooms, fish and waterfalls.  I would do anything to have a garden like this in which to spend my days.

He has quite a collection of his paintings exhibited in this museum.? If you have an eye for such artistic talent, then you would really appreciate this exhibits.? It is sad that a person has to die before his paintings can be recognized and treasured.? It would had been nice if his talent had been recognized earlier so he didn't have to be separated from his family.
He can also speaks a little bit of English, so no need to worry about the communication part.

Having visited limestone caves in other countries before, what was different about this experience was the stalactite or staglamite looking structures were not made of limestone but lava.  The walking surface was very interestingly grooved unlike limestone caves but called for very careful walking at parts. The lava stack at the end of the section open to public was pretty awesome and is helpfully bathed in lights so one can see.What I wanted to point out is that we happened to visit at a time when many Korean schools send their students out on educational trips (we visited in early April).  So the lava tube was full of noisy teenagers who seemed more interested in shouting out to each other and seeing who could run through the tube fastest than in appreciating one of nature's wonders.  Seems like Korean teenagers are just like teenagers everywhere else!  So if you are going in early April, be warned.  If it is going to bother you then better give this a miss because you will be in a dark confined space where sounds are magnified.

Having never seen a lava tube cave before, we were very keen to go here. We live on Jeju Island so it wasn't a terribly long trek to get there. Not exactly on the beaten path, but not too far off either. Once you arrive, there's a small information center that explains the history, science, and mythology surrounding the cave. There's also a restaurant on site, which we didn't use, and then there's the short walk to the cave entrance. Here's the only reason I didn't give this a rating of 5. I have some minor mobility issues stemming from multiple knee surgeries and the entrance to the cave is a fairly lengthy and sometimes steep set of stairs that can be wet and slippery. Once you're in the cave, however, it's not too bad to traverse unless you have much more significant mobility issues. There are a few places where you have to go up ramps or small sets of stairs, all of which are industrially produced. The cave itself is quite dark and damp, and I'd recommend long sleeves if you're prone to feeling cold. Definitely wear good walking/hiking shoes as the cave does not have a full walkway installed. You're walking over ground that is solidified lava. It's about a 1km walk to the end of tourist access where there is an impressive lava column, which they claim is the largest in the world. There's an observation deck approaching it, but you cannot go past and actually touch the column. Along the way, there are decent informational placards in multiple languages, including English. The explanations are reasonable for most people, including children, to understand. Our kids, ages 7 and 5, enjoyed the experience, particularly because you could get right up beside the cave walls and touch them, along with other artifacts inside the cave. For anyone interested in geology or volcanos, it's a great experience. Price is reasonable too. We paid 12,000 won, which is currently a little over $10 US, for four people. Supposedly children under 7 are free with ID, but we didn't ask about that for our younger one.

Having just visited the newly opened Teddy Bear Museum in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China (by the same group), this original museum in Jeju was a little underwhelming, even for a solid teddy bear fan like me. Unlike those in Chengdu, I didn't appreciate the fact that all teddies in Jeju were enclosed in glass cases. Impossible to take a decent pic with them!There was a good collection of antique bears. Great for a collector like myself. Also there was the supposedly most expensive teddy bears in the world. The LV bear and the diamond bear.For sale of their Elvis bears I believe, there was a small theater on the second floor showing 4 mins Elvis teddy concert every quarter of the hour. Perhaps I went at a later hour (5pm), I was the only one in the theater. Appreciate that the museum is opened till 8pm in the evening, so it's great as a quick destination pre or post dinner, if you are staying or hanging around the Jungmum Resort Area. The museum was located right next to Lotte Hotel. There was a Lotteria on the ground floor but it was closed during my visit. An attractive and well stocked teddy store on the ground floor too, unlike its sad and sparse Chengdu cousin. Happy that there were some collector grade Korean handmade teddies for sale. Their house brand   so-called   limited edition replica made-in-China white Alfred bear (real limited edition would come with serial numbers) came in a nice copycat Steiff look alike gift box and a photo with a Korean prince. At only USD 35, it's great as a souvenir/gift!I like the outdoor park area. Great for kids to run around. Overall not a very big place. Whole place would take about an hour.

Having been to the sex museum in China near Shanghai I was somewhat disappointed by this one mostly because I found it more biased and sexist than I would expect a museum to be.  It started out good with a fairly progressive and balanced presentation albeit almost entirely in Korean talking about sexual freedom and equity.  But the vast majority of displays were very...vanilla and heteronormative.  There was very little depiction or discussion of anything besides sex between one man and one woman.  Furthermore the depictions of women and closeups of vaginas far outnumbered depictions of the male form with many showing women in very submissive poses such as on all fours and wearing a leash!  There were even a few instances where the English text accompanying a display used rather judgmental language describing certain sex acts as   abnormal   or   depraved   which I found very shocking.  I think it's great that Korea which is typically very conservative has a museum about sex at all.  But to a more sexually progressive westerner it will probably seem outdated and disappointing.  It's also hard to get to if you don't have a car.

Having always wanted to see the cliffs off of Northern Ireland, it was a pleasant surprise to see these interesting hexagonal basalt column shapes on the coastline of Jeju Island!  There is a wooden walkway/stairway with informational signs along the way.Restrooms are near the entrance/ticket booth.  There are typically cart/street vendors hawking various foods/fruits/veggies and other items here and there throughout.  There was a local photographer with his work (varying in size from postcards to poster-size photographs) which were of breathtakingly beautiful scenery around Jeju Island.I would definitely recommend this as a stop on your trip around Jeju Island.

Happened to pass by & decided to visit. It's my most expensive entry (so far I only paid between KRW2000-3000) at KRW10000 (adult) KRW9000 (senior citizen). The route is entirely guided. While it's generally relaxing to look the various glass artifacts, there's little much to do except for taking pictures. I won't recommend coming here unless you have nothing better to do which is not likely.

Hamdeok is perhaps the most popular beach in Jeju but this was the first time I visited the island on summer during peak season. The beach is packed with families who took advantage of the low tide during the day (about ~30cm of water in a 50m stretch, at least on two weeks while was there) and let the kids in the water for a very enjoyable and risk-free time at the ocean.However I was surprised by the amount of   lifeguards   there. They will drag a security rope marking a no-swin zone after it starts getting   deep   (just after the water reaches your chest) which ok its a security measure specially with so many kids, but for adults who want to take a dip is horrible. They will start blowing their whistle and order you to go back even though half my body was above water.But the worst part is that they -- the lifeguards -- place beach umbrellas all across the beach and charge you ??20000 (~20USD) to open and use them! It's already very weird that the lifeguards are also operating a rental service at the beach, but thing is they will NOT allow you to sit anywhere near them without paying (even not using the damn umbrellas) unless you look foreigner (white) so they don't loose face. I don't so I got reprimended like if was a Korean and they wouldn't leave my side until I moved.Isn't the beach a public space? This didn't happen just once but every day during my time there, overall an awful experience due to these threatening and autoritharian lifeguards.

Hallim Park, located western 33km away from Jeju City and west of Mt. Hallasan along the beach in Hallimeup, is one of the most popular tourist spots on Jeju Island. It faces the pleasant scenery of Biyangdo Island, Hyeopjae Beach and Geumneung Beach. The park was established on barren land in Hyeopjaeri, Hallimeup, and covered with tons of earth and began planting assorted subtropical plants in early 1971.

Hallim Park was definitely one of my favourite spots in Jeju.There were so many different areas to visit within the park and so much to do and see. Of course, I went in May and the weather was superb. Bright and sunny with clear blue skies.I liked that there was a bit of everything to see and do here. Do take note that it can get quite chilly in the underground lava tubes, so bring a jacket when you go in. Don't say you weren't warned! Pleasantly surprised to see peacocks, some were even let loose and just strolling around us like it was the most normal thing on earth.

Hallim Park is privately run, which would explain the cost, which is 5x the cost of entrance to Sunrise Peak, a must-do in Jeju.There are many parts to explore within the park. The most interesting sections to me was the albino peacock enclosure and the rapeseed flower garden. The cherry trees at the cherry blossom section were okay (we went during the cherry blossom festival) but why would u need to pay for that when the rest if the island (and Seoul as well) is full of cherry blossom trees.The tropical plants, wildflower and grass garden section were disappointing. There were lots of potted plants which looked unhealthy and unkempt. I really couldn't tell if the garden was supposed to be manicured or wild.Overall, I think the park is quite passable. I wouldn't visit it again, nor would I strongly recommend it to a friend.
Hallim park is part botanical garden, mini zoo, and culture center. The majority of Hallim is mediocre, but the jewel of the park is its rich bonsai collection.An hour is okay

Hallim park is part botanical garden, mini zoo, and culture center. The majority of Hallim is mediocre, but the jewel of the park is its rich bonsai collection. There's an extensive range of bonsai trees at display, some of them are over 300 years old. To those unfamiliar with bonsai trees, they may just be miniature trees; but to those who know the value of these works of art, these bonsai trees are literally priceless. In fact, it's almost unbelievable how openly accessible these trees are to the guests, considering their value and need for extreme care.If you're planning on visiting, briefly study the artistry before your trip to enhance the enjoyment. This is a one-of-a-kind collection.

Hallim Park is located at the West part of Jeju island, approximately 20 minutes drive from Jeju City. The park is pretty large as it has a wide range of gardens (cactus, bird park, flowers) and it also has a couple of lava caverns. The park does not have spectacular sites but it is a great and cozy place to spend time especially for families. Do wear comfortable shoes.

Hallim Park is huge and has many sub-theme parks inside, including subtropical garden, wild grass and flower, two lava caves, bonsai and Jeju stone garden, a Jeju folk village, a bird garden, a stone exhibit hall and a water garden.  Plan to spend 2-3 hours.  For me, the best was the bonsai display, many 200-300+ years old.  Most in plant containers, some growing in natural ground, well maintained.  I've never seen a bigger or better bonsai display (maybe you have to go Japan?)  Caves are nice, but if you really want to see lava caves and explanations, don't miss Manjungul Cave -- World Heritage stuff!  Stone exhibit is good, but I prefer the Jeju Stone Park.  Other sub-theme parts rate a 3 on my scale.

Hallasan was a good challenging climb, with the hike splits into 3 parts. The first 2 hour or so, we were hiking through mostly level ground, some rocks and little steps. As we reach the middle ground, the trail gets steeper, more rocky and almost half are made up of steps, mostly made of rocks. Using a hiking stick at this time really helps in making the climb easier. When it rains, which happened the entire day when we went, the ground gets covered with puddles and pools of water, so it was extra effort trying to choose the rocks to step on to avoid getting our feet wet. Towards the top, there are flights and flights of steps, followed by a trail made of rocks where u have to use a rope to climb up the steep rocky surface. It was challenging but overall, felt good.As it was raining, we didn't manage to get any view of the crater or lake at the summit. But the sense of accomplishment making it up was great!The way down was more challenging as after a day of rain, the trail became wetter and what used to be steps, some were submerged in water. Hence, even with a good waterproof shoes, ur feet could still get wet. Also, note that the sky turns dark at around 5pm in winter and there's no lighting in the reserve. Hence, make sure u buffer enough time to reach the foot of the mountain before that time. Otherwise, u would be hiking in the dark. Nevertheless, there would be a ranger moving down the rail lines in a cabin moving on a rail line, looking for stranded hikers. So no need to panic. However, I would still recommend planning well, checking the weather and choosing a clear day to climb. Start early so as to buffer enough time to reach the 3rd rest station by 12pm, as anytime after that, they do not allow hikers to go up to the top. Think it is for safety reason to buffer enough time for the ascend and descend. Also, to wear waterproof shoes and if available, bring a hiking stick along. Do standby a raincoat in case of light drizzle. Also bring some food along. Though they sell instant ramen and some bento at the resting stations, it closes by 2pm or so and you don't want to end up hungry.  Lastly, enjoy the climb!

Hallasan National Park is a fantastic place to explore. Firstly, the vegatation between Spring and Fall is beautiful. As you hike to higher elevations the landscape and plants slowly change. Numerous rare and even some endemic species are found here. Concerning wildlife, what visitors are most likely to see are the Roe Deer. These small deer are found throughout the park, and as I hiked quitely we came upon 5-10 throughout our 6 hour trek.In 2007 Hallasan became part of the Unesco World Heritage site calle   Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes  . This honor is only bestoyed on the most unique and important natural and cultural sites on Earth. Hallasan is a geolocial wonder, and is comparable to some of the most iconic national parks in the United States. The park probably deserves 2 days as visitors will want to hike to the crater lake on Hallasan peak, but the entirity of the park holds many exceptional sites. Many trips to Jeju island are scheduled around their trek at Hallasan. Make sure to bring plenty of water, and keep an eye on weather conditions. Hikers must start early if they want to hike to the peak, late arrivals will not be permitted to make the full trek as it takes anywhere from 6-10 hours depending on your pace.

Hallasan is the tallest mountain in South Korea and even though I was not in the best shape .. i had to do it!  In preparation i got two bottles of small water, some snacks, and the clampers for the shoe.  There is a store beneath the mountain if you forget anything .. like a hiking stick or rain jacket on a rainy day.I started at 830 am because you need to get to a certain point before 12:30 pm during spring or you're prevented by the park rangers from going to the top.The last stretch was pretty painful as was the last stretch going down the mountain.On a cloudy / rainy day, there is nothing to see up top.  However, I did get a nice sense of accomplishment :)

Hallasan is Jeju?s massive mountain, and was once a volcano. It peaks at 2000 meters, and from 700 meters up, the only way up is by foot, and you?ll have to drop your car at a designated area to begin the climb. The best place to start the trek is Seongpanak, on the East side of the mountain. Going up takes about 4 hours, at a normal pace, this trek will take all day. There are two checkpoints that you much reach before a certain time of the day to be allowed to go all the way up (and come back down before sunset). This means that you absolutely have to go there early. I was at the foot of the mountain at 9am, and I wouldn?t advise anyone to start climbing after 9:30 if you don?t want to be turned down. Also, since this can be exhausting, pack beverages and food before going up. There is a small shop at Seongpanak and another one at the 1500 meter checkpoint, but they have very limited choice. Just stop at a convenience store in the city before going up and you should be good for the day. The climb is relatively uneventful for the first 2/3rd of the way, with fairly little to see because you?ll be surrounded by vegetation. But once you reach an altitude of about 1600 or 1700 meters, you?ll start getting a great look at the top of the mountain and more importantly at the rest of the island.  Once you reach the top, the view will be amazing. The volcano?s caldera feels like being on the moon, and you can also see Jeju?s coastline as well as its major cities, Jeju and Seogwipo. Absolutely breathtaking! Make sure to check the weather if you plan to go there, because the tall mountain tends to attract clouds, which could completely ruin the awesome view you?d get on a clear day.

Halla Mountain or Hallasan is one sadistic hike. For the month of May 2018, Gwaneumsa Trail is the only trail open that summits Halla. Seongpanak is having maintenance done.We did Gwaneumsa Trail... with one slow hiker... we got to parking at about 7:30am and we were walking by 8:06am. It is beautiful and green, especially in Spring. There is one restroom stop about 1/4 way and another 3/4 way at Samgakbong shelter. There was no other support. Take water, take food, take toilet paper just in case.READ: There is only one potable water stop. It is after Samgakbong about 3.5 hours into the hike at the last downhill before the bridge and start of final red part of trail. There is a hose at the corner at bottom os stairs before the bridge. Fill up here both going up and down.Also wear good walking or hiking shoes. We witnessed two people's shoes rip up and one guy had to walk back 2.5 hours with no shoe. There is no rescue for small issues. There is a supply cart that goes up once or twice a day but only for serious rescue. There is AED in Samgakbong shelter too. No food for sale when we went in April 2018.The reason for the difficulty is the climb and distance... mostly on volcanic rocks... large ones... and lots of stairs of wood and of stone.We left at 8:06 and back in the parking lot at about 5:30. All day event. 9.5 hours going slow up Gwaneumsa Trail.

Half science, half art. A museum dedicated to the formation of the igneous rocks in the area, tectonic plate movements, volcanic eruptions, formation of lava tubes, and various methods of making craters. Extremely interesting!Then rock art. Lots of interesting rocks from around the island, arranged in a way that makes them just so fascinating.Budget a couple of hours here for a leisurely walk through these sections. Add a couple more hours to see the historical village section (which we didn?t go into as we had seen these elsewhere already).

Haenyeo Museum which is dedicated to the female sea divers of Jeju was an excellent museum about the matriarchal culture of Jeju that used to exist.  Despite the large building that houses the museum, there isn?t that much on display.  However, visitors get an idea about the amount of responsibilities the typical haenyeos had, basically raising their children (some dived until the day before their children were born) and running the family finances while going out diving everyday.  The donated artifacts on displays were interesting but the information about the lives of haenyeos was fascinating.

Had a mixture of nice gardens, some birds and lava caves. When I entered and started walking, it did not sem like much, but then impressed me as I went on. So enjoyed it quite a bit, was a good pleasant walk. Worthwhile if you go to Jeju.

Guide is good explaining about the village and oldtime Jeju. We came here by chartered car, not really sure how to come here by public transport. For me this place not very special, it's just different with typical hanok house that you ever see in Seoul or Jeonju.

Great place to relax and take shelter form harsh weather condition.It's very peaceful and quite beautiful, particularly on the inside. The temple is spacious and also has a little garden, with a lake and several tangerine trees.We got? there by taxi but you can also take bus 600 from Jeju International Airport (Bus Stop 1).

Great place to gawk at all the live seafood that Jeju has to offer. All manner of sea creatures, alive and dead, to be savoured & haggled over if you so wish to partake of feasting on them. Besides seafood, there are also veggies, Jeju souvenirs (mainly foodstuffs), a couple of seafood restaurants (which charged seating fees per person so we skipped going in) and some cooked food stalls. Great to stop by to check out the local market scene.

Great natural parc. We've done the trek suggested by the lonely planet guidebook. Going up from eorimok and down yeongsil (which is really breathtaking). It was a little hard, but we succeed though we aren't particulary trained, thank to the stairs and timberworks all along the path.

Government run, the Jeju Peace Park is set out over a large area with a variety of things to see. The main building contains a movie theatre, a cafe, information desks, and amenities as well as the main museum. The museum itself contains not only an amazing arrangements of information, exhibits, artworks, detailed memorabilia, personal video stories and recreated scenes of important sites, but also photos of the lost, current excavation efforts and modern artistic representations of the era. There are several other building that house additional memorials and scenes that are both emotional and historic. It is very worth a visit or two and should be given the time it deserves.

Got a tour of the village for about 5 minutes, then they herded us into a room to hard sell their crazy product made from the bones and other parts of the horse. The products were crazy expensive and we were not allowed to leave the room until they were finished. What a waste of my precious vacation time.

Good, peaceful trail, starts slowly, then is quite steep for a while, then flattens out, nice views of a dome on its side. The path is well maintained, steps or planks lead almost all the way to the top. How to get there? By a taxi from Jungmun Beach (approx. 30,0000 Won). There also is a public bus. We went up on an overcast day, it was quite windy and chilly on top.

Good show for young and old. No need any knowledge of Korean. Theater is located in the middle of nowhere so make sure you have your meals before going. There is a convenient shop (GS25) in the hotel nearby but limited food selection. There is also a restaurant within the hotel but only opens at 7pm (our show was 8pm) when we were there. Be punctual, the show starts on time.
Good range of artefacts, models and audio-visual aids to really illustrate the story behind this unique group of women.

Good 8 min video to start and then interesting museum that makes you appreciate the island much more.  There are many statues around the island of the Haenyeo and this museum helps educate you about them.Entrance fee, but inexpensive.

Going to Hallasan by bus #701 from our hotel in Hamdeok area, through Jeju Intercity Bus Terminal, change to bus #740 departing every 1 hour.  Stop at Eurimok Trail point. Walking from bus stop to the gate for about 5 minutes. There was a nice facilities at the gate: clean toilet, small convenient store with drinks vending machines, and police station too.Please be aware that   sleepers   are not allowed to be use for trekking due to heavy terrain. Including our son's crocs shoes. Unfortunately, the shop run out shoes stock so He can't join us.Eurimok trail quite heavy for untrained persons, we just only reached 1.300 meters before deciding to turn back to base.The bus #740 was picking us up at 15:35 back to Jeju Intercity Bus Terminal.

God?s beauty with unique rock formations and the waves crashing. Short boardwalk to see the beauty. We bought a bag of oranges and explored a bit more on the side paths but it was so hot, we didn?t enjoy that part as much as cliff viewing.

Geumneung Beach and Hyeopjae Beach are the two beaches of Hallim located about a kilometer apart from one another.  While swimming is not allowed for some stretches, both areas are absolutely stunning during sunset.  The stretches of the camping area looked like a great place to spend the daylight hours and at low tide, there was plenty of space for kids to run around and play.

Fun and exciting. Go through once without the map and get lost. Then try the second time with the map. Finally, the challenge starts. Go individual or in teams. Shouting and screaming and laughter will fill up the maze.

From the prices I?ve seen for pork dishes in other parts of Jeju and in the rest of South Korea, I fear that some of the restaurants in this strip are somewhat overpriced (even for black pork). The restaurant we ate at required us also to order two portions of the meat (of the same type). My impression is that this is a bit of a tourist trap. This street is very close to the beachfront promenade in Jejushi and some restaurants seemed to accept guests even after 10 p.m. There is also not a huge number of restaurants lining this street. More often than not, you will have to grill / prepare your own meat over the grill at your table with minimal help from the waiters. So if you do not know how to prepare and eat samgyeopsal, it would be a good idea to read up about it a bit before eating at one of these restaurants (or any samgyeopsal restaurant for that matter).

From Segiowipo (Jangung rotary) the park can be reached in a little over an hour on the 231 bus which will drop you at the front of the park.   Fare 1200krw. Park admission is 5000krw. I spent 2.5 hrs here doing course 1 and 2. I think you might enjoy it more if you were an artist but I liked it all the same. The stone museum, which is the first stop on course 1 tells you all about how lava rocks are formed, their different types and would be a geologists dream. After that you'll walk around the park and see the different stone sculptures, most of which are natural,  some manmade. There are also a couple of replica traditional jeju houses and local pottery too. The Obaek gallery has some driftwood on display along with 1 hall of art but it is mostly empty. I thought there would be more info on the local traditions and how they lived but the park is still a work in progress. Its not due for completion until 2020. Rug up because it seems to be colder here than other areas of the island and you will be outside most of your visit. Recommend you go on a sunny day as this area gets very heavy fog too.

Friends, my husband and I rented ATV's, Scooters and a Golf Cart to check out this island. It was so much fun touring around and stopping at the beaches and different view points. We even saw the diving ladies who dive by only holding their breath! This wasn't the most spectacular views of Jeju we saw but the adventure was a lot of fun!
Free stamping art in paper , handmade soap you have to pay , No make up for sale here , only mask , perfume , hand creams, skin care . Love the view outside from this cafe .

Four young entertaining painters give a 2-hour long show of slap-dash painting, sketches, dance and pop to enthrall groups of teenagers and school kids. Audience participation is strongly encouraged!!

For the ones who believe they are in good shape:Why struggle, why do it the hard way? because it is much more scenic and maybe only one tenth of climbers going that way. Taxi from town to starting point (approx 20 min) was 11.000 won on taximeter from my hotel in Nohyung-dong (near the int. airport) or take the bus but only on sat and sundays). Bus stop at Seongpanak when you come down from the mountain on the road. Check schedule and bus no. Taxi back 20.000 won (not on meter..)This is by far the most important place to look before you set out. THE WEATHER! http://www.mountain-forecast.com/peaks/Hallasan/forecasts/1950 I wouldn't call my self an experienced climber but I did it in 3h10min up and 2h down. This is in a pace where I overtook and was not overtaken, and very short breaks, maybe only 2 min in total 5 times. The track is changes between rocks or stairs, I think it's well kept. Two toilet stations up and two down. None at the top. Bring 3-4L of liquids minimum, no passport nor entry is needed for the mountain (aug 2013). A windbreaker for the summit can be nice to have. The weather can change every minute so rain is likely. I did it in old worn-out runners. Bring food and nutrition - no shops. Good luck and enjoy

For the adventurous and those seeking a different experience. This place is located quite out of the way, however close enough to Halla arboretum as well. Quite challenging to find as Naver and googlemaps does not have this location up to date. If you are looking to find it, look for a bus that will take you to Halla arboretum stop and you could find it by following the street direction towards the arboretum. When you see a building with   playbox  , you've found it!There's an ice sculpture display area with an ice slide you can experience. Next level on is your VR experience that you could choose to experience (cost of entry varies depending on what experiences you would like to add on).As reference we chose the Basic A experience which provides us entry into the ice sculpture, Trick art area, 5D movie experience and 1 VR experience of our choice - cost 22000krw per person.You could spend at least an hour here and rest at the cafeteria before moving on.

For teddy bear lover, you should visit this place, there is a lot of thing to see. Don't forget to visit the outdoor and fully explore the place. This is kinda combination of art and humor. Visit my youtube channel and get more in sight: (search by title) - EN CHANNEL#2 TRAVEL BLOG DAY 1 JEJU-DO

For people who loves green tea, can check out the variety of green tea products they have; it's nice to 'chill-out' at the yard with hot beverage in hand.It will be good for the kids to try out their self made soap and they felt very good with their artwork. However, if you would to make your purchase at Innisfree, please do note that they DO NOT give out any free samples or gifts for your purchases (even thou I've purchased about KRW500,000 worth of products) unlike those in Seoul or Busan, they are very generous with their samples and gifts with purchase.

For only $10 (10,000 KW) you can spend an afternoon wandering around a carefully manicured small park that exhibits outdoor glass work. As you walk in there is a place to watch professional glass blowers blow bottles in the traditional way, and if you are taking a school group there, the kids can have ago at making something, and then return the next day to pick up their handiwork. After that you follow the path around the exhibits until you get to the other end.In this mainly outdoor museum, there are glass plants, flowers, and an eclectic collection of glass made curiosities that make a very pleasant way to spend a couple of hours. There is a small cafe in the middle of the exhibition, and the gift shop just before you exit. The bathrooms are at the entrance exit, so go before you start!

For most people, this place is kind of hard to reach because the public transportation in Jeju is not really comfortable. But if you rent a car, you really need to visit this place.You need to take ferry from the east part of Jeju Island. Inside of the island, you can borrow a bicycle to travel around the Udo Island. Don't miss the authentic ice cream of this island (see the pictures).

For a teddy lover like me, this place is heaven I?ve been collecting different teddies and seeing all sorts of teddies here, big and small is like a dream come true. Kids and kids-at-heart will truly enjoy and treasure time spent here.

For a start, if one is looking to purchase Innisfree products, it would probably be better to get them from their numerous stores on the island. Almost a quarter of the floor space here is set for people to try their hand at making (or shaping) Innisfree natural soap. The product selection is limited and they don't provide any free samples or special offers (like in their purpose built stores or counter in shopping malls). On the plus side, the store offer instant GST deduction for all items purchased here (min 30,000won).There is also a cafe here. But if one is looking for the famous Green Tea Latte or Green Tea ice cream and cake, those are only available from Ossulac Tea Museum Cafe next door.

For 1st time hikers climbing Mount Hallasan, take note of the different hike trails AND the closing time for each trail. This is especially if you drove on your own and parked at 1 of the 5 (one of the locals told me there are 5 different car parks at different foot of the mountain)If you are climbing Mt Hallasan to reach Baengnokdam (the crater top), do not take the Eorimok trail as it does not lead there. I made the 1st mistake taking this trail and the trail ended 3 quarters way up the mountain and you only get to see the side of the mountain top. I made the 2nd mistake not watching my time and could not descend Hallasan from the trail (Eorimok) where I came as apparently it closes at 2pm, and there was a park warden stopping me from taking the trail back and kept ushering me to take the other way (towards Donnaeko trail) to descend. The descend took 4 hours and the trail was treacherously full of rocks. You could tell that it was a trail less taken as there were over-grown bushes covering parts of the trail. Your only guidance of where to go was a      thin cord string tied from tree to tree and red strips of cloth tied on the string. If you weren't too careful and lost sight of the guiding string, you may actually go off tangent of the trail. There are no lights, very few signage and are all in Korean, so if you are like me with no understanding of Korean, good luck. And that wasn't the end. Donnaeko trail actually ends up at Donnaeko cemetery. So when I got to the foot of Hallasan, it was pitch dark (6pm+ and no street lamps), by myself, and I had to walk for 1 hour through the cemetery to get to Donnaeko car park (which was 30 mins driving distance away from Eorimok car park where my car was T-T).

First off maybe because of the trail I chose the first part after about 20mins was walking, is really quite tough (even for a person like myself who walks and runs up to 3 times a week).  The uphill staircase hike that took almost an hour up, with little stops.  But after the uphill hike, the top is rather flat.Just being in the mountain, breathing in the nice mountain air was simply a joy.The only issue I had about Hallasan from a non-Korean speaking person driving to Hallasan, is there is no telephone number / GPS code that we could key into the GPS found on the official websites (whether English or Korean).

First of all ensure you hike on a non rain day.  We were worried all week because it was raining.  We got a non rain day but cloudy. When got pass 1 km up it was beautiful sunny weather.Know there are 6 trails and they start in different places and not all go to the top. We took the Eorimok Trail (Northwest). It was one of the shortest. We didn't do good research and started too late to do a longer trail.I'm moderately fit. The trail was steep! I was definitely challenged for the first 2km. It was balance of even and uneven ground. Anyone can make it up but it might take you a bit longer if you were unfit. There isn't a drone restrictions and was able to take some great video. Bring water and food.  There are places near the top to grab instant noodles and water. There is no washroom on the way up.  Bring some tissue and wet wipes just in case.Although we didnt get to go to the summit, it is a must do while visiting. Jeju.

Few hundred feet of road that makes you feel like your rolling uphill with the car in neutral.  Best is to begin at the start point from a full stop place the car in neutral and release the brake, the car will begin to roll very slowly and it appears that you are going up a slight incline.   I would not go out of my way for this... although I did.  If you have plenty of time or nothing to do because of rain then why not.
Fascinating glass art,nice for photographing,but too bad I went was a cloudy rainy day..entrance ticket is 8000Won for adult and 5000Won for children.

Experience狩狩狩Price狩狩狩The Glass Castle is highly recommended for glass artefacts enthusiasts, so definitely not recommended for families with children. Extremely boring except for the mirror maze, an extremely small maze reminiscent of the one at the Trick Eye Museum. Only if you're trying to kill time or collect false eyes as a hobby.

Experience狩狩Advisable not to go in winter as there's nothing to do except explore a dirty, sandy   shipwreck   and ride a train ride. Probably the train ride was the best part. The pond has some fishes but that's about all...

Expected the place to be bigger. Only reason we went here was to kill some time before heading to the airport. Could have gone to the Ripley's museum instead which was just across the road. As expected, lots of teddy bears in the museum. Only interesting part was the history section. They had teddy bears from as old as 1905 on display. The bears were still kept in good condition.

Except for the tulips which do not bloom in Singapore and the caves which are special to Jeju, this park is not impressive. It does not have good landscaping on a whole. I understand that tried to grow flowers of all seasons so there are naturally trees and shrubs not in bloom. But still the landscaping could be improved so we don?t have to walk for such long periods with nothing much to see. I liked the statues and water feature, the tulips area which was very beautiful, the part of the park where some peacocks could roam around. However the enclosures could be done better for more visibility of the animals. I read some reviews that they were ill treated but I didn?t see any evidence of this. We have very good displays of succulents at Gardens by the Bay in Singapore and Yeomiji Botanical Gardens was also more impressive than Hallim park. For April, I would recommend to skip Hallim park and go for Yeomiji instead for a better visit in general unless you really like tulips. Have to admit the tulips display was very beautiful.
Excellent. Recommended for KPOP fans. Will be return if I visit Jeju again. Nice staff, have many photobooth with artist.

Excellent view especially at sunrise. Hiking was good for a beginner level. Many places to stop and take a rest if needed. If not an experienced hiker, it takes maybe 40 minutes to get up to the top. No entrance fee if you go super early. Lots of lovely places around to grab coffee or some food after you hike down as well. I would do this again in a heartbeat!

Everything about our favourite bear and its history. The museum has 3 floors, where you can see many different displays of teddy bears and animatronics, in a different setting. One floor is for displaying teddies from different times, another one shows teddy related artworks and finally there's a floor where you find a souvenir shop and some cafes. In the outside park you can view Jungmun sea while seeing human-sized teddy sculptures. The whole surrounding area is beautiful. Ideal for friends, couples and families as well!

Even with the crowd, it's still worth it. We took Seongpanak trail to hike up to the top in mid March and still needed snow sparks. Make sure start your hike by 9am and bring food/snack to survive for 8 hours or more. The trail is mix of rocks and boardwalks with little soft surface to walk on, so be mindful with choice of your shoes or socks.

Even though my family and I stayed in Breeze Bay Hotel which is within 3 minutes? drive to the Seongsan Ilchulbong (Sunrise Peak) car park, we couldn?t wake up so early to hike up to the summit to catch the sunrise. Eventually, we were at the base of the Seongsan Ilchulbong at 10am, together with hordes of tourists and locals?nd the sunny weather.Getting there and fees: GPS coordinate/code for this UNESCO World Heritage and South Korea National Monument site/attraction located in the east Jeju is 7830959. As the parking lots are limited, I suggest you drive (arrive) there early (before 9am). Parking is free.  The entrance fees are 2,000 won for adults and 1,000 won for teenagers and children.The attraction: A non-stop no-rest ascent for a fit person takes about 30 minutes, but with my young children and with stairs-climbing not part of our daily routine, we took about 1 hour to make complete the 182 metres climb to the summit. There are several pointers that you may want to take note:(1)
address: If you can, go on a weekday. We were there on a Wednesday mid-morning and already it was quite crowded, so I cannot imagine what the weekend would bring(2)
입력주소: Wear a pair of good-sole and comfortable walking shoes and bring enough water to hydrate yourself (you could still buy water at only one place during the ascent)(3)
X: On a sunny day, you could bring an umbrella or wear sunglasses or a cap and preferably put on sunscreen lotion(4)
Y: Take note that the ascending trail or route is different from the descending trail or route, so do take lots of photos and selfies along the way. (5)
CLSS: Hike at your comfortable pace (although I understand that may not be possible when the tour guide requires you to be back at the bus within a certain timing) and do rest at the benches and the viewpoints or points of interest (e.g. huge rocks) whenever you are out of breath (give you an excuse to take photos and selfies)(6)
PNU: There is no need to bring a jacket or sweater unless the weather becomes chilly or windy or cold (e.g. winter) or you are hiking in the wee hours of the morning to catch the sunrise. In fact, it was scorching hot when we reached the crater summit at around 11am(7)
주소구분: When you reach the summit, remember to pose with the signage says ‘Top of Seongsan Ilchulbong 180m’We started the climb after the 4 bronze round inscriptions (one of them is ‘New 7 Wonders of Nature’) on the uneven rocky or bumpy uphill sloped path. After a certain distance, this sloped ascending path became one that comprises of proper (stairway) steps. Look for the signage “Ascending Trail” and continue your ascent. Somehow the last stretch is a steep climb on continuous stairway steps and with so many people behind you, you simply cannot stop to rest. But once you reach the top, before you have time to catch your breath, your breath will be immediately taken away by the breath-taking panoramic views! You could see the flora-covered 600-meters diameter crater with 99 jagged rocky spires that resemble a crown, in addition to the Seongsan town (village), Seongsanpo-hang harbour, Cheju Haehyop (Cheju Strait), Mount Hallasan and others. It amazed me when I considered the almost symmetrical tuff cone crater was created by the explosion of an underwater volcano thousands of years ago. Due to the barriers, all visitors cannot walk into the tuff cone crater.Of course, the descent was relatively easier along wider wooden stairways with railings. When near the bottom, there are two directions to take. Going to the left, you could ride a Jeju pony (Jorangmal), which we didn’t go. Going to the right (signage “Women Diver Performance”), you would come to a black basalt rock cliff and also to a place to see the famous female divers (Haenyeo). To the right too, you would come to a lookout point for Udo Island (South Korea’s second largest island)Comparing with the only other tuff cone crater that I have climbed ? Diamond Head in Honolulu ? I find the Seongsan Ilchulbong more challenging to climb but it offers more breath-taking scenery.  So don’t miss Seongsan Ilchulbong on your Jeju itinerary! Start the ascent early to avoid the crowd.
표준구주소: If you can, go on a weekday. We were there on a Wednesday mid-morning and already it was quite crowded, so I cannot imagine what the weekend would bring(2)

review: Even in March, Udo is beautiful--and in March, there are few visitors. When we were there, haenyo were out at low tide collecting seafood among the lava rocks, banging the rocks to bring them out. We stayed at a traditional hotel (thin mattresses on heated floor) near the lighthouse on the main road. Eat al fresco at the nearby restaurant across from the healing-stone throne is and check out their fresh   ginseng of the sea   (slices of a raw sea-cucumber-like animal).
