Didn't expect the lava cave to be that long. But it was an interesting experience. Wear waterproof non-slip shoes as the floor is always wet.
Cute museum for families and teddy bear lovers. Two floors of exhibits plus more outside. A fun place for an hour stop over.

Chocolate land  is an interesting place to visit  it is close to Teddy Bear museum  they charge 3000 won for enterance  & give you coupon for the same amount  so when you buy chocolates the amount is deducted. It consists of 2 floors  the lower level has workshop where I saw people experimenting with chocolates  I did not because the did not know english.They have exhibition where chocolates from all parts of the world shown.They have samples on both levels to taste & then decide which flavor to buy. The upper level has cubicles with history of chocolates  & nice statues made of chocolates.The upper level has coffee shop where you can rest & have hot or cold drinks  icecream & chocolates.
Bring your jacket: is super cold as walking into cave. Entrance fee is KRW 2000. Wear sport shoes: cave floor is slippy.

At 12usd per pax and with the first floor being all in korean we think it's a rip off... It's the first time we've been to such a museum and we were quite disappointed to not be able to read a word of what they're saying. The second floor has english though so it was slightly better... But 12usd... we wouldn't recommend people who do not understand korean to go...

A good place if you love tea.They have a tea plantation that you have access to and take pictures. Not bad but when we went it was pretty hot. So we opt out of that. The museum itself was alright. It has the teacups from around the world.On the ground floor itself you have the cafe as well. The cafe sells ice cream the roll and other light food. A very good place to escape the heat.Innisfree Jeju House is just next door as they are run by the same Group.

A  unique cave with 70 cm lava stalagmites and lava tube tunnel . Lighted with dim lights. Floor rocky and slippery but manageable  with comfortable shoes . A kilometer long but takes about 20-25 minutes one way . The Lava  formed at the end is a beautiful one worth seeing.

You can discover your favourite teddy or safari animal here. With 3 floors of huggable and adorable animals there is much posing, hugging and choosing. You can even get a teddy to propose marriage to you.Teseum should not be confused with Teddy Bear Museum located in Seogwipo (near Alive Museum), a more 'serious' museum.

Yes I did it! Even though I almost fainted half way, wore skirt and wrong shoes, everything was worth it when you were at the top! It felt like I was climbing stairs of 50 floors building and every steps on the way full with regrets like 'why, why i'm here climbing this!' However, all that thoughts were gone when I was on the top. The view was breathtaking, all my tiredness went away. It was so beautiful and it was worth it!

Yakcheonsa Temple? is a famous Buddhist Temple located in Jeju, a small Korean island south of mainland Korea. It has been built in 1981 by Buddhist monk and has the largest Buddhist prayer hall . and? miniature gold Buddha statues all located on the second floor encased in glass.The main temple has Two -three floors and balconies that overlook a beautiful three-meter-tall Buddha. The view from the top floor facing the sea is awesome.

Whilst I'm giving the Teddy Bear Museum just 2 stars for quality, value for money, class of exhibits, and any actual worth as a proper   museum  , I have to admit that my visit made me laugh. I'm not sure though that derisive snorting sarcasm was what they were looking for.This museum is a pile of pants, masquerading as teddy bears.. The   attractions   are about 15 to 20 poor quality adult-human-sized bears, dressed in various outfits of clothing, with a challenge to guess   who   they are dressed as. Military uniform and two medals apparently is enough for a bear to resemble Prince William, for example - and a grey wig and   E=mc2   to represent Einstein.Then there are the bear portraits. Frames containing bears dressed to vaguely resemble famous portraits. Mona Lisa teddy bear, anyone?There's no   history   of the teddy bear, no collection of historical bears, no pictures / video clips of teddy bears being made, no maps showing where different types of teddy bears originated from - nothing educational whatsoever. There are no audio tours, no leaflets or signs to show the visitor around, and certainly no staff available to talk to about any   exhibits  , whether you are Korean, English, American or anything else.The gift shop on the lowest floor contained the largest number of bears - none of them particularly special, all just your usual cheap mass-produced bears, but at slightly hiked up prices.By far the worst part of the visit was the funniest. Your ticket includes entry to the   Elvis Stage Show  . Oh dear Lord, where on earth do I start? The show is on every 15 minutes. In a room with about 12 benches in it. There is a curtain at the far end, hiding the   stage  . On the quarter hour, the announcement is made -   The King of Rock and Roll, Elvis, is in the house!   The curtains open, and there it is. The Elvis Presley Show. Six, sad, lonely looking teddy bears, dressed in stage show outfits, rocking gently on their animatronic sticks. The three backing singers sway gently on the right, the drummer's arms flail up and down towards the drums, the guitarist's arm moves.Elvis meanwhile gyrate and swivels his hips, the crowd goes wild. Oh, no, sorry, that last sentence was a lie. Elvis sways and looks like he almost falls several times.Worst animatronic puppetry in the world. Hilarious. Hilariously BAD. Less than two minutes later, the curtains shut, and   Elvis has left the building   - until the next showing in approximately 12 or 13 minutes' time....Don't go to the Teddy Bear Museum thinking you'll have an interesting visit. Go to see the absolutely bizarre vision that South Koreans have of   entertainment  .

When we arrived in jeju it was raining so we needed to do something that was more indoor.  We drove out to the cave.  The entrance fee is cheap at 2000 won per person.  Then you walk down some steps and enter the lava tube.  It is really dark down there and the floor can be slippery.  I think we spent most of our time looking down at where to walk rather than looking around.  You walk 1km to the end and there is a rock formation.  Nothing too special.  Then you turn around and walk back.  Overall it is a nice cool 2km walk, perfect to escape the heat of jeju.  Just watch where you walk

What a fun little island! Exploring the island on a motorized bike/trike was an awesome experience. To rent the trikes an international class A drivers license is needed (US Military living in Korea can use your ID card and Korean drivers license). No license is needed for the motorized 2-wheeled bikes. This is the easiest way to travel the island making frequent stops to see the scenery or stop at one of the many cafes or restaurants. We saw tour busses, and a few regular cars, but seems like the majority of visitors chose the motorized trike to see the island. The ferry from Seongsan Port on Jeju to  Cheonjin Port on Udo runs every 30 minutes and the ride was about 15 minutes. There was an air-conditioned room on the upper deck but it was floor seating only. It is possible to see the whole island in a few hours.

Went out here because it was recommended via a coworker. Would definitely recommend! Keep in mind the cave was much colder then outside so don?t be surprised. Also, I don?t know who needs to hear this but wear appropriate shoes. Kitten heels are not it. The floors are wet, uneven, and just not for cute heels. I?d recommend visiting the Information center first there was a lot of good information.

Went in August, so it was really hot outside. Was so pleased to be welcomed by the cool temperature of the cave. It will take you about 2 hours to go in and back out with some stops to take pictures. Recommend everyone to wear proper shoes as the cave surface is really uneven since it used to be flowing lava coupled with low visibility of the cave. The floor is also wet, so advice to wear something non slippery. I wore normal slippers and i got my feet wet and dirty, no worries though, there's a place near the toilet specifically to clean you feet outside the cave.I saw some locals even wearing heels inside, not recommended, but i guess it's possible to come out unharmed.

Went here with a tour package bought from Klook. Entering caves experience feels great however, for it requires like 30 minutes walk to the Lava Coloum and you have to walk back (there is no other way out) so you need to make sure to wear comfortable shoes because the floor is uneven.

Well worth the visit, especially if geology is your interest.Plenty of stairs in and out of the cave so not too advisable for elderly, or families with babies/ toddlers. (though i did bring both!) Being a lava tube, the flooring can be uneven and slippery within the cave so wear proper footwear.It will be cold and dimly lit down in the lava tube, so bring your sweaters if chill is a concern.The walk long to and fro the end, so be prepared.After the first half to the end, it can get boring for some especially the kids. That said it is still a unique experience for many.

We were there about an hour before closing so there weren't many people in the cave. It's pretty dark and wet in the cave. The floor is also uneven. I must say that it's quite an awesome cave (different from the ones I've seen in NZ, USA & Switzerland) though I can imagine that it would be quite boring if there was no one to explain to you the different features of the cave.If you don't have a local guide with you and are not a Geography fan, you might want to give this a skip. But if you are into caves/rocks/Geography, I think you'd love it!

We went there by taxi from O'Sulloc Tea Museum. It's interesting when the displays are made of glass but nothing impressive. The entrance fee costs 9000 won but my friend and I got a discount thanks to the taxi driver uncle, and we end up paying 7000 won each.. The displays are mostly outside. On the 2nd floor, there is a gift shop..you can buy some gifts there and the cost is acceptable for some (e.g. accessories, keychain, etc) certain products (e.g. glass displays) are more expensive. It was raining when we visited the museum, but we just went around the museum and took some pictures. It is good to visit once but not more than that.

We visited this just because it was rainy, and realized that it would be great to visit otherwise.  It was interesting because of the theme-based teddy bears in thousands, spread across 3 floors.  Loved the Gandhi bear, Times square scene, Mother teresa bears, Charlie Chaplin bears, most expensive teddy bears (Louis Vuitton) and so on.Do visit if you can fit it in your schedule!

We visited on a very wet day so it was good to be inside even if the inside was the lava cave.  The lighting is very low in the cave and the floor, made by lava flow is very uneven so close attention needs to be made to where you are going. Its one kilometre each way to the end of the public bit and you miss quite a bit watching where the feet go so not to fall over.mAn interesting place to visit but take a torch!

We took a local bus from Jeju City to Manjanggul Cave. It's 2,8 km walk from the bus stop to the entrance of the cave. You can hire a taxi, if you don't feel like walking. Just outside the entrance you can find a restaurant and a kiosk. The entrance fee was very cheap (2000 won). There are quite many stairs when you go down to the cave. The floor of the cave is a bit uneven, but still quite easy to walk on. The cave is quite dimly lit, moist and cold. I recommend bringing a jacket with you. All that said the cave isn't maybe a best spot to visit with small children or elderly people. For healthy adults the cave is a nice experience. There is information in English about the different formations and the history of the cave. There is only one entrance to the cave, so if you walk to the end and back, it's total of 2 km of walking. I recommend visiting Manjanggul Cave, if you're interested in Unesco heritage sties and natural beauty!

We stayed at Seowipo, near to the seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal and took bus 110 from Jungang Rotary bus stop to Jungmun Tourist Complex. The bus journey about 30 minutes and cost less than 2000won one way. The bus driver could provide change if needed. There was a TV screen at the front of the bus that will flash and announce the current and coming stop in english clearly (Although I did not see Jungmun Tourist Complex on the TV screen, therefore I used GPS to locate instead. For my other bus trip, the stops were annoucne correctly and was reliable). You can press the bell to alight. Just to note that the bus ride can be a nausea one as the driver usually travel at a high speed as there were many stops they need to embark on. The Teddy bear museum is a small two storey museum. The famous personnel, movie and cartoon characters were dressed in bears to make those bears special. You can expected toy bears moving their limps as some bears were mechanically  wired. There is also a small outdoor park with some display of bears. There anShort 5 to 10 minutes elvis show at level 2 theatre. 30 minutes would be sufficient to finish the entire museum. The ground floor has a large souvenir shop where you can purchase teddy bear. A small palm size teddy key chain about SGD$15. A 10? bear cost about SGD$50. As I am not a bear fan, I rated 3 stars as I personally feel that SGD$12.50 for the entrance fee was a little pricy. However, I am sure the teddy bears fan would love this place and rated 4 stars and above. Anyway, the museum is close too many other attraction that is walking distance (Eg: Cheonjeyeon Falls). If not, you could also take a bus 702 to many other attractions like the Hyeopjae Beach. If not, you can take bus 782 or 110 back to seogwipo-si (former) intercity bus terminal.

We spent the afternoon at Hallim Park and thoroughly enjoyed the statues, the bonsai garden, the rock sculptures, the caves and the traditional village.  The grasses section appeared to be very dry and in need of some immediate cleaning up.  We were shocked and saddened by what we saw in the bird section.  The ostriches were clearly in distress as they had lost many feathers and were showing signs of balding.  They were enclosed in an area devoid of greenery and appeared to be desperately seeking out food by nipping the air.  The enclosure did not allow for these beautiful birds to run and get the necessary exercise.  Yes, there were food dishes in various locations however they didn't seem to meet the needs of the ostriches.  The peacocks were also showing signs of stress as their plumage was rather thin.  They were enclosed in an area where the floor was of interlocking brick.  This is as far from a natural setting as possible. Our visit ended on a sour note and it is our hope that the dire situation of these birds will be addressed by those in charge.  We highly advise anyone who visits this park to make his/her concerns known as it is the only way to rectify this sad situation.

We love this place!!! It is so so so so so so so beautiful! Travelled with my hubby and 2 kids and took the earliest ferry to Udo. The ferry we took is those that doesnt come with seats and we have to sit on the floor like the Koreans do. Rented 2 scooters and rode the around the entire island for 2 hours with our kids sitting behind us. It is really safe to ride but you need to make sure you have your international driver license with you before you can rent a scooter. My hubby doesnt know how to ride a scooter, but no worries, simple instructions and quick lessons were given and within 10 mins we were off to our adventure. Though it was winter when we visited, the wind did not stop us from visiting every checkpoint to take photo and of coz, eating the famous peanut icecream. I really felt like I had jumped into a K-drama, especially when I have my Oppa with me, haahaa! It was quite cold so we din manage to get into the water. But already we had spent like 4 hours just wondering around the island. The fun part was to get lost into some residents farms and got directed to get onto the right path. The sceneries are breathtaking! I cant describe better. Really beautiful. Definitely highly recommended, even for people with young kids!

We had the best time at the 3D Alive Museum.  As you walk through there are pictures on the walls and floors that you pose in certain ways to make it appear the picture is   alive  .  You can be sky diving riding on a magic carpet in King Kongs grip etc.  We edited our pictures once home and they are wonderful!  Highly recommend this museum!!

We chance upon this on our drive from Seogwipo to Hyeopjae.  The pink building is big and visible from the highway. They should have repainted it as it looks washout and faded pink. But once I step in, it?s totally new! Infact it is even newer than Sanrio Puroland which I visited in Tokyo and bigger than there! I am a true blue HK fan since 40 years ago. Once HK fan steps in, I am sure you will be transformed to a little princess at heart and you?ll be so excited again! There are a lot of Instagram worthy area to take photos. As others pointed out, it has a section that talks about the evolution of HK from 1970s till now.  There are HK rooms, dining room, bus, living room, wardrobe, dressing room etc. Even the toilets are so pretty! Level 2 offers some purikura area, a restaurant and some other HK displays.  There is a 3D dancing room too. On the 3rd floor, there is a open air rooftop HK small maze. On level 1, you go through the souvenirs shop to exit and a notice states that once u exit, u can?t go in again. So it?s best that u buy yr souvenirs when u are ready to leave. I swear I could stay there for 3 hours but as my husband is with me, it only took us about 1.5 hrs to complete our visit. Overall this place is small and not much for non Kitty fans. For us Kitty fans, it is definitely a must visit.

Walking 2km (to the end of the section open to the public, and back) in a lava tube is a cold, dark and wet affair, but it's a unique and educational experience. The floor is very uneven and there are many puddles to step around. There's not a whole lot to see, but every now and then, features of a lava tube are highlighted and explained. This is not for everyone but if you can appreciate that it's rare to get the chance to walk through a lava tube, go for it. Just be ready for the slightly challenging conditions

Visited this place as part of a tour group, and spent slightly under an hour at this place There are a total of 3floors to explore, starting with a history tour to the current entertainment scene today. Several interactive booths and kiosks allow you to experience things such as singing, makeups and dancingAnd of course you can take photos of all these experiences

Visited this museum with my kids.  There were hundreds of Teddy bears displayed over 3 floors. We saw Teddy bears in all sizes,  different era and occasions, celebrity characters dress up, themes etc.   Kids were excited to watch the free performance theatre with teddy bears dressed up as Elvis and his supporting singers singing. Every floor has different group of bears on display.   Entrance also allowed visitors to venture out to the back garden which boosted more Teddy bear statues.   Garden was well maintained and worth a visit.  Near the main entrance,  it also had a 2 storey high wooden Teddy bear which is a real attraction for the kids. The entry ticket is not cheap,  unless you are a real Teddy bear fan,  in my view,  it is not a must see destination.

Visit the lava tube only if you are easily awed by geological creations. 4 of us went, and not all were impressed as they thought it was just another cave. We read the description boards, and tried to spot the highlights to better our experience in the tube. As we went during winter, our coats were suffice for the low temperature within the tube. Wear sturdy footwear as the floor is uneven and wet.
Very nice, also very cool inside. Walk is pretty light but the floor is uneven so wear your walking shoes.

Very interesting inside and out. The first floor is mostly modern about sexual preference health and rights but it is 95% in Korean. I would recommend to bring a Korean friend who doesn't mind translating if you are interested in that part. There was also a big wall of history at the very front which was all in Korean that would be worth translating. It wasn't very busy and some of the   hands on   things that would show examples were broken so I started with a mediocre impression. The bigger and more impressive part though is the number of historic sexual things they have on the second and third floor. Lots of artifacts about sex in Eastern cultures with some in Western cultures but a lot of things have their English translation. This part is much more impressive and interesting to look at. A lot of phallic objects and   traditional   pieces but it's historic and that is how people viewed sex in history. The more modern section is more modernly-styled and was a bit confusing (a lot of sex dolls...? kind of weird) and included more fetish stuff than I expected. Not much on queer and non-hetero there was a small section (in Korean) on the ground floor and then one very gray area display on the top floor but not a whole lot can be expected of Korea (where homosexuality is still viewed very negatively). Overall it was worth the price and was pretty interesting to look at. Having a translator or understanding Korean would make it more memorable.
Very dim, and  pools of waters on floor. Understand it is UNESCO site but it should be properly lighted up as least to what are showed in the photo which attracts us to come and visit.

Unless you really love Teddy Bears, this place is not worth it. The place has two floors of teddy bears, It is full of history with all the teddy bears from all over the world. All of the ancient teddy bears is well preserved but with relatively minimal background story. Some of the information are written only in Korean, so there isn't many interactive attraction here.My advise is SKIP this place if you're not Teddy Bear lovers.
Unique geological features.  Definitely worths a visit. We were quite impressed.  Yet wet floor, can be getting cold inside the cave.  Need sturdy shoes and warm clothings.

Udo is a really small island, you can go around by bicycle in several hours. Udo is a volcanic island, so it has several nice beaches with white and black sand, impressing lava rock formations, caves etc. We went there several times, every time for 2-3 days, and every time it was just wonderful. You should go and spend a few days there if you want to relax in a quite and peaceful atmosphere with no nightlife, co crowds, no big attractions but with beautiful nature. Still, if you want to get in touch with the rest of the world - no problem here, our Korean mobiles were working fine, Internet was available right in the   arrival hall   of the port and in many   minbaks   (small Korean-style hotels).You can get there easily from Seongsan port  (＿?깆??고) of Jeju island by ferry in just 10-15 minutes. Ferries depart every hour from 08.00 till 17.30 or 18.00 depending on season. Most accommodations are found on on the White Coral Beach (Seo-bin-baek-sa, ＿?鍮諛깆?? or  Sanhosa, ??고몄?? ), 10 minutes walk from the port. They are all small 1-2 floor buildings located directly on the beach with seaview (Pensions, Minbaks). We never booked anything in advance, but found a room on site, but we went in May and October - not highest season. The rooms were always nice and big, also with kitchen and all the necessary kitchenware. Also there are small shops with snacks and some Korean restaurants.So, what to do in there?- swim in the pure emerald water of White coral beach, see the special kind of sand, it really feels like you are in tropics ^^- rent a bike and go around the islandThe road goes nicely along the shore, there were almost no cars except on the busier Jeju-facing side, and we enjoyed the scenery very much!  - Geommeolle Beach (寃?硫?)This is a black sand beach with very beautiful and unusual rock formations and caves, and we spent a very good time there. You can go in caves and see small rocks piled up on each other. And once a year they have a symphony concert in the caves!!Also, if you are a diver with a certificate, there is a diver center there. We tried to do it, but we did not have a PADI certificate so they refused, they do not do fun dives.And  we took a motor boat (10 000W/person) to see farther caves with a spectacular view of Udo cliffs (Hu-hae-seok-byeok, ＿?댁＿?踰). If you are lucky, you can also see a peculiar site called Ju-gan-myeong-weol - sun reflecting at the ceiling of a cave giving a   moon shape  . We also went up the hill, nice view of both Udo and Jeju!!What problems you can encounter in Udo?- languageLocal people are friendly and try to help, but they do not understand English!!So if you do not speak Korean, print out Korean names of what you want to visit and some basic Korean phrases (preferably in Korean, not transcriptions, because pronunciation may be tricky). BUT! the owner of the LOG-house speaks English very good!- foodThere is no Western restaurants on the island, only Korean!! The shops on the beach only sell snacks like Ramen, but there is a bigger mart inland called Hana-ro Mart with fruits, vegetables, milk, etc. (??濡 留, try to ask locals for directions and go there by bike, you will find it, there is no place to get lost ^^). And it could be a good idea to bring some food with you from Jeju, especially if you want something like cheese, wine etc.
Two floors of teddy bears for display and one floor for selling them. Outdoor park is nice to walk around. But due to hot weather, we only go out for a short while and hide indoors.

This was probably my favorite attraction - it wasn't a place where you go and just take pictures but also get to learn something. Throughout the cave, there are display boards highlightng the different lava formations. Plus, it's pretty awesome to be walking in a cave formed by lava flow. I felt like Indiana Jones! If you walk all the way to the end of the cave, you will see a pretty magnificent lava formation.Wear proper shoes as the cave floor is wet and being a jacket as it gets fairly cool underground.

This was our first visit to a lava tube, and we enjoyed it very much. The lava tube cave is maintained in natural state. Hence the floor is uneven and you need to watch your step. It is also very wet and little cold in side. Apart from that the walk is very enlightening. We learned many new things about lava tubes.The lava column at the end of the cave is a must see and is the highlight of the whole walk.Must visit.

This was an interesting place that was well preserved. Wear a good pair of walking shoes as the place is quite dark with very uneven floors so watch your step. The air in the cave is kept at a constant temperature of about 19-20 degrees all year round, not a problem as we went in winter. Very good if you have not seen anything similar to this before.

This was a very interesting Lava Tube cave.  There were signs in English as well as various other languages describing what you were looking at.  The signs were informative.  The cave is cool, so I recommend a zippered sweatshirt or windbreaker.  Also, the floor of the cave is uneven, so you definitely want to have good walking shoes.  I was just fine wearing old jogging shoes.  We went as part of a guided tour - I would have liked to spend just a little more time there, but that's how it goes on bus tours...  There may be more beautiful caves, but overall, it was the nicest cave I've been in - very nice Lava Tube - you will enjoy it.

This was a part of our Yeha bus tour - East Course - and felt it was worth seeing.  It is a lava tunnel/cave, which makes it kind of unique.  Visitors are limited to how far you can explore, which is fine as you do need to watch carefully where you walk - it is a lava tube and the floor is very uneven.  It is known for   Stone Turtle   because it is shaped like Jeju island.  Be sure to have a light jacket.

This was a great visit!  There is a hidden gem that people didn't seem to know about or decide to see (I'll mention later in the review).  The entrance fee is nominal and you get to see so much.  Even from the top, you get an awesome view and picture with sort of a bonzai tree at the top of the stairs.  Then walk a little further down and there is an alternate path you can choose to walk on large stones and there's some locals selling fresh seafood.  We didn't partake but a lot of other people were purchasing and eating the fresh seafood.  Then we walked all the way down to the falls using the stone path.  Be very careful if you choose to do this as the stones can be slippery.  Once we got down to the base of the waterfalls, you could feel the mist from the waterfalls and just hang out there to take pictures.  It was pretty cool to know this is one of the few waterfalls in the world that fall straight into the sea/ocean.  We walked back up after relaxing a bit near the waterfalls and we saw a path to the Castle of Shell near the edge of the parking lot.  You should take time to walk through this and visit the Castle of Shell.  It's free and you get a very picturesque view from the 2nd floor inside the castle.  Ok it's not really a castle but a small house but it's still very neat to see and just relax on the 2nd floor with the breeze and the nice views.  Then go around the house and there's a relatively unknown path leading down to smaller waterfalls and another great view of stone beach and cliffs around the corner.  I actually liked these falls the same as the main falls.  Smaller but more greenery and there were small little ponds you could soak your feet into.  We took some wonderful photos there and spent a long time wondering why very few people knew about coming here.  There were a ton of people at the main falls but we were at these smaller falls around the Castle of Shells for a good hour and literally saw just 2 other groups of people at the smaller falls.  Take a look at the pics.  It's worth the extra walk!

This teddy bear museum is one of a few around the world.  Located in Jungmun tourist complex in Jeju, Korea, is this tiny museum for teddy bear fans alike.  For 8000 KRW you have unlimited day access to 3 floors of teddy bear exhibits and the outside grounds.  This museum carries interesting themed bears like the Mona Lisa bear, the Leonardo Da Vinci bear, a Marilyn Monroe bear, and so many others.  Currently they are displaying the Elvis bear.  On the ground floor there is even a really nice restaurant if you get hungry.  Not much choice in  terms of breakfast, they do offer mostly burgers and different types of coffees.  Also there is a gift shop if you are interested in taking home one of the really cute teddy bear souvenirs.Well worth the visit and few hours for both teddy bear fans and those with just a passing interest.  Remember to use the lockers next to the admission counter.  We didn't and carried all our jackets and bags for the entire exhibit,  It will make the visit a whole lot lighter and more fun.  Enjoy!

This place is a must-visit not only because of its UNESCO status, but also because it's really fun!!  Entrance fee was around 2000KRW.  It took me for around 60minutes to have a round trip between the entrance and the lava tube, while browsing and looking at some of the information lined scarcely within the cave.  If you have children or elderly, it'll take longer (I won't really recommend people with walking difficulties to go).  It's quite a walk and be sure to wear comfortable and non-slip shoes.  This is very, very important because there's water puddles on the floor, and the rocks on the floor are actually quite smooth and can get very slippery when wet.  The lighting was very dim but it makes it more fun, but do be careful.  For those who might be wondering, I don't know whether it's allowed, but you definitely cannot use a baby stroller in the bumpy walkway in the cave.  Little tip:  At the information centre (near the bathroom/toilets), there's a photo-booth that costs around 1000-1500KRW for a photo that can allow you to take photos with backgrounds of different attractions (including the Manjanggul cave) within Jeju.  Given that you ought not to take photos inside the cave, why not give the photo-booth a go?  It's not only quite cheap and easy to operate, it's actually a lot of fun!

This place is a must-visit if you visit Jeju. It was a pretty long walk from one end to another end. Inside the cave, it was quite dark and you have to be extremely careful while inside as the floor might be slippery. It was a magnificient cave and if you are a nature/cave lover, you will definitely love it!
This place has variety of teddy bear. Upon entering, they have a zoo theme on the 1st floor. They have many zoo animals made of stuff toys. The 2nd floor is more of a theme section.

This is the sort of cave one would visit on a tour , decend down into the bowls of the earth , in fact it's not too far down , but be prepared to walk for some 2 km there and back , this is in fact a Lave Tube run then an underground river , all along one can see the water line marks that have cut into the lava ;The floor is VERY uneven , bit slippery if not careful , you are in effect in a huge underground tunnel , rather dark , somewhat damp and water is dripping from the roof all of the time , not sure how wide or tall it was but, shall we say huge . At the end of the tunnel there is a spiral of volcanic rock that has shot through the earth and been frozen by water ( I suppose ) One of UNESCO World heritage attractions in Korea , To be honest I think one has to like this sort of visit to enjoy it , whilst I somewhat enjoyed the visit , I have seen better in France ; however if you have travelled this far around the world and find yourself in Jeju Island then make the effort to visit , entrance fee is 2000 won

This is quite an interesting place to visit. Do remember it's a long lava tube cave.Take note:1) Stairs to the cave can be steep.2) The floor of the cave is in its natural form. It's wet, slippery, jagged and uneven. There are large puddles everywhere so watch where you step.3) When we went, there isn't really any special colorful lighting in it. It was quite dim. We used our cellphone as our flashlight in some of the darker and very uneven floor areas.4) It's cold so wear some warm clothing. There may be water dripping from the ceiling as well. Overall we enjoyed the lava cave.

This is probably the wonderland of 90% of the female population. The place is not huge but if you are going to watch the 3D movie, you have to queue early coz they only have a certain number of 3D glasses. We only have less than 1.5 hours in Hello Kitty Island thus wasn't able to watch the movie. The toilet is cute!! I so love the mirror and of course the cleanliness of the place. Saw a lot of very cute exhibits in the museum. I especially like the bedroom. Wish it was mine. There is a caf챕 on the second floor. The deco is all pink and white. Didn't eat coz we were rushing for time and the snacks aren't really cheap. The gifts are expensive too. I can actually get them cheaper when I'm back in Singapore.

This is NOT something to do on your own. Going with a small group is best because you will need someone to take photos of you/your friends interacting with all of the   art  . It's a silly good time with lots of themed rooms each one with loads of photos or interactive displays. Watch the floor for markers of where to stand to get the best angle for the optical illusions!

This is my first time visiting a cave and this is an extraordinary cave where this is actually a LAVE Tube which was formed 1million years ago. The open to public is only a section of its 5km length as a protection to its other natural environment and that is why it is labelled as the UNESCO Natural Heritage. The entrance to the 1km tube is a 100m long flight of stairs. Upon entering, the internal is wet and cold when visiting at this season (starting of spring). Other days would be still wet but temperature would be around 10-20degree C. The length of the tube excursion is just nice for family of elderly and young. My family (Mum, brother, wife and me) had a nice time inside the tube and although it is quite hard to take beautiful pictures, the experience is definitely immense.However, most of the time my mum is trying to avoid the water on the floor (do not worry it is not as slippery but it is on some areas), she did not notice much of the natural formation of the lava flow and lava stalagmites. The tube is well lit but it is recommend to bring torchlight to shone on areas above to see properly. Beware of the top water flowing down, that is why there is water on the floor. Overall, i feel that it is educational for the young and good walk for the elderly. To tour the place, i recommend to wear tracking shoe or covered shoe to prevent water or slipping. Else you will not enjoy the beauty of the tube. We had lunch at the nearby restaurant and it is a hearty meal. Lastly, i really enjoy the visit and definitely visit again in future, i hope you too!

This is for the female Merchant who saved people in Jeju island 17,18 Century, Joseon dynasty. Very carefully and beautifully made. However, it is limited for 3rd floor. 2nd floor is for kids' experience museum. 1st floor is for some special exposition from time to time. It is FREE, worth to visit for an hour. It is located near by Jeju coastal international port and Dongmun traditional market. Actually from this market, exit/entrance #3, it is just 500 m away. In those times, people in Jeju island could not get out of the island, however, since she saved whole population in the island, The King Jungjo wanted to give a awards but she refused. Instead, she asked him she would love to visit the peninsular once, and wanted to travel in Diamond mountain(located in North Korea now). So she could get the chance to meet the King and travel inland. Under the Patriarchal system, it must be very hard for her to work as a merchant, but became the most rich person in Jeju, then when there was big famine, she released whole rice and food for free to Jeju people. Any way, it was great fun to enjoy each section from her birth to death. All explanation are in English and in Korean both.

This is enormous highly worthwhile visiting. While I've visited caves around the world this is the first time I've seen lava tubes. They are huge you could drive a semi trailer through most of them. Defiantly worth seeing just for this aspect.It's quite wet on the floor of the cave, while you won't get wet, there are puddles of water. The ground is extremely uneven in places so good footwear is essential.There is heaps of signage in English on how they were formed.Highly worthwhile.

This is a UNESCO World Heritage listed site. It is indeed one of the largest lava cave/tube I have ever seen. It is awesome, dark, wet and huge. Its floor uneven, wet and slippery. Artificial lighting is minimal and don't attempt to take photos as it is too high to be lit by ordinary flash lights. You need to watch where you are going. The result of a fall can be serious. Minor twist ankle is common. The experience is well worth the trip. Do not forget to take extra clothes and be prepared to have a thorough shampoo and shower that night as it drips everywhere.

This is a really cool place to visit, one of the best activities in the Island.  Inside the cave it can be a bit cool so do not forget to bring a jacket or a sweater. We went inside the lava tunnel all the way to the end, at least to the section where you are allowed to walk. It will take you about 45 minutes walking, then we came back running, it was fun and a good exercise but you have to be careful as the floor is uneven.  Some of the views are quite spectacular.  The whole experience will give you a sense of peace and adventure.

This is a most unusual feature on the North-East coast of the island of Jeju, South Korea. Although there are a few around the world, these tubes are some of the best preserved ones and it is a Unesco World Heritage site. It is also accredited as a Global Geopark.You can walk 1km of the tube at Manjanggul (there are over 7 km but not open to the public)- it is damp and dark so go prepared with shoes that won't slip and also have an extra layer. The temperature drops quickly: it was 28C outside when we visited in late September but only 15C inside. However, they are very 'manageable'.The caves are well-preserved and present themselves as a long tunnel which displays various features. Though it is dark and so difficult to take photos, you can clearly see the lava flowlines and the lava shelves whilst the floor is ropy lava. At various points along the walk, you are directed to other features such as lava columns and lava stalacmites. Only one entrance of the 3 existing ones is used by the public.Well worth a visit, and especially so if interested in geography/ geology.

This is a good location you should spend time to visit, nice and you can see some different kind of cave, some of the cave have spotlight follow so amazing. friendly reminder, please wear a shoes instead of slipper or sandals because the floor very wet.

This cave is actually a volcanic Lava tube, not limestone cave. So don't expect to see amazing things like what you see in Guilin and Yunan.Same as reviewer ggkoh, I visited there after a day of persistent rain. The cave is wet, filled with small pool of water here and there. The floor bed is rocky and uneven. So be equipped with a jacket comes with hood (or raincoat) and a good pair of track shoes.

This ?Unesco? lava grot is quite nice. You can walk a kilometer underground in a dark cave with lots of information panels in English and Korean/Hangul. The Floor is uneven and the temperature is ten degrees Celsius. We did not expect something special, but overal it was a nice experience with a rewarding pilar at the end of the walk.

There's two Teddy Bear Museum in Jeju Island. One is Safari Theme that has an entrance fee of KRW 8,500 (Php 369) for adults. This has a safari theme great for pictures but on the second floor, there are more which has a variety of themes. The other Teddy Bear Museum where the most expensive Teddy Bear is on display wearing a Louis Vuitton outfit costs KRW 8,000 (Php 347). This one is better because it has so many display that you will be amazed, famous scene, characters, celebrities from different industries. Very nice! This is also the museum where Princess Hour was shot, a Korean novela. I will go back!

There is a huge greenhouse with 7 separate areas of different plants including desert, aquatic, floral, jungle, and tropical fruit. ? The tropical fruit area had platters (examples)? of many different types of the fruit of the nearby trees. ? There are a couple small shops in the greenhouse selling different items as well as food and drink.? ? There is also an elevator going up to a 5th floor observatory. ? We went on a very rainy day.? ? Couldn’t see a thing. ? The greenhouse was extremely busy, I’m sure moreso due to the bad weather.? ? ? 10,000 won to enter.

There are a few attractions within the same area. The teddy bear museum has 3 floors,with teddy bear exhibits and also it's history. There where some with themes and also resembles idols and famous people  and some that moves. There is also an elvis show with teddy bear on level 2 theatre. The outdoor photo taking area has a few exhibits too.

there are 2 buildings to visit;1) the main building where you can see 3 big Buddha statues. on the second floor there are thousands of small Buddha statues.2) the side building where there are 100   lohan   statues are placed. Each lohan is different.Very peaceful and serene place to visit No admission fees.You can also donate/offer 3 packs of rice/grain as you pray to the Buddha which is available at the main hall for 10000 won

The Teddy Bear museum is a fun stop. There are many displays of teddy bears in various historical, cinematic, and pop-culture type settings. Take your camera and visit each floor. The gift shop at the end is full of fun teddy bear treasures as well. Definitely a good stop for anyone. We went on a rainy day, but it would also be fun on a hot day if you are looking to get out of the heat. Fairly easy to find, it's located in a popular tourist area.

The stairs down into the cave system are steep and plentiful, so if you have trouble with stairs then you should skip it.  Also, if you don't like walking on uneven ground then you should skip it, because most of the cave floor is natural stone, so it's rough and uneven in many places.  There's also small standing pools of water in places, so watch where you step.  You don't have to walk the whole cave length, since it's very long indeed, so you can just do what we do and walk part of the way and then back again.  But you do need appropriate footwear, and no, high heels are NOT appropriate footwear.And remember, this is a natural cave system, not a fun park, so don't go expecting anything beyond what it is.

The site was the best part of an all day trip covering the eastern end of Jeju Island. Such places are always fascinating. As soon as you enter, the temperature drops to the lower double digits C.There is a one kilometer stretch you can walk. I like that it has not been jazzed up with a rainbow of colours. The floor is naturally uneven with some sectors covered in wood. The cave is 18 meters as its widest and  23 meters as its tallest. At the far end is located the world tallest lava column at 7.6 meters. When you appreciate the force of Mother Nature to cause such formations, it only adds to the visit.

The prospect of walking through a cavern formed by lava was extremely exciting for my wife and me. So although we were staying in Seogwipo and wanted to see Udo Island and Ilchulbong on the same day, we decided to visit Manjangul. It was a 3.5-hour long journey by bus and another 15-minute walk from the bus stop. It was a hot and humid day, but as we entered the cavern, it was cool. Droplets of water trickled down on us and the deeper we went, the cooler it got. The cavern is lit up just adequately to help you find your way around and read the signages about the different formations inside the cavern. Watch your step and mind your head. The floor is wet and slippery and there are low rocky ceilings in places. So have a safe and enjoyable experience. It's cool, in every way.

The previous review states that the climb was in 20 minutes but for a relatively unfit person like myself, it took me 30 to 40 minutes with numerous stops beginning from halfway till the top. Much to your agitation, we see older citizens and children alike happily and easily climbing the steps and overtook you to the top. Nevertheless, the view on the top was well worth the tough climb (according to my unfit status). Managed to take some photo shots of the surrounding and the crater itself. As it was just beginning spring, the crater floor was covered with brownish grass and vegetation, not the greenish color you would expect in summer. What I most remembered was the real cold buffeting wind of 2 Degrees Celsius blowing and you could really feel it even with winter jackets and caps worn while climbing the steps. But it was most memorable. Wife did not want to climb the steps but decided to go shopping for the famous Jeju orange chocolates in the shops at the foot of the park.

The place was rather quiet when we visited (it was on a Sunday morning) despite the heavy traffic from Seoul the day before. We were given pamphlets in English, while most of the displays were in Korean language. There are many teddy bears in display and most have been displayed/posed in accordance with certain themes (like Hollywood, Snow White, landing on the moon etc). It was interesting.There was an Elvis show, with teddy bears swaying their hips to Elvis's concert in Hawaii (if I'm correct) and that was entertaining for the kids.Outdoors is a small park with human size teddy figures, great for picture taking. Remember to take pictures with large teddy outside.There is also a cafe but we did not stop by since we had breakfast earlier. In the pamphlet, we saw a train ride but we couldn't locate it anywhere. May have missed it.There was one floor for shopping and there is a large selection of teddy bears to bring home. Maybe pricey but the quality is quite good.The place is convenient for families with small children (the kids were not terrified) and stroller friendly as there is an elevator available. There is also free parking outside.As usual, for Korean tourist attractions, there are discount vouchers available. Just have to know where to get it :)
The place is nice and well maintained, it was a bit cold down there so i would suggest a light sweater and comfy shoes as the floor was uneven with lava stone and made it hard to walk

The museum is located next to a please area of town with multiple artists in various media as well as tea/coffee shops - which is how we found the location.? There is a small entrance fee (1000 Won per adult at the time).? In addition to the small, but nice collection of paintings and sculpture, there is a great view of the city and see from the 3rd floor.? If art is your thing, then definitely go.? Otherwise go only as weather or your schedule dictates.

The Manjanggul Lava Cave was a very large lava tube cave.  A 1km section in the middle of the 7.5km lava cave was open for groups to tour.  We found it an amazing place to visit, and an outstanding example of a lava cave, but since it is a lava tube cave, visitors should expect the following when visiting this attraction:1) unlike limestone caves, generally created by water over long periods of time, lava caves do not usually have the stunning formations (ie ? stalactites, stalagmites, etc).  They have their own unique, highlights, but are not as colorful.  Such is the case with this lava cave.2) the cave is very softly lit (not brightly lit) and has a very uneven floor, so walking takes attention and concentration.  Anyone with mobility problems should be very sure they can handle all the steps, uneven ground, and low lighting.3) the cave is cold and damp and the ceiling drips constantly.  The amount of dripping is directly related to the recent rain amounts received.  Since lava rock is very porous, the rain drips through the rock into the cave.4) the cave lists that it is ?restricted? access.  I don?t know what that means but I recommend finding out if you are trying to visit it on your own.  We were the first group to arrive that day and we had the cave to ourselves for about 30 min before other groups started showing up.  It made our experience even better, but it is possible that only groups with pre-purchased tickets have access?5) aside from the sheer size of the cave (again, huge for a lava tube cave), the coolest feature for us was the large lava column at the far end of the cave.  The dark hole in the ceiling, where the lava flowed into the cave and made the large column was quite impressive.We visited this cave as part of a cruise ship tour.  For those looking at things to do from a ship, there are 2 cruise ports on the island, one in the south port and one in the north port.  Where you port could determine your itinerary since various and impressive sights are available close to either town/port.  This lava tube cave is in the north-east part of the island, and is listed as   restricted   so, again, before you try to visit on your own, you might want to make sure you will be able to get into it.Jeju Island has so much to offer ? large lava tunnel caves, waterfalls, craters, mountains, cliffs, black sand beaches, incredible fresh seafood, and more but they are spread throughout the island, so it is impossible to see all of them in one area or in a short amount of time.  Also, some of the attractions are restricted, so they might require group access to enter.  We concentrated on the east end of the island during our visit and found it to be similar to Hawaii in many ways other than the temperature, which was quite a bit cooler than Hawaii during our visit at the end of March (55 deg F was our high temp).

The Manjang Cave was one of the   must-dos   in my itinerary. I can only say it was somewhat a disappointment. It was not quite as spectacular as I have thought it would be. I was with my mum and dad both 60. My mum did not take the walk well and headed back halfway. My dad stayed behind to do some photo-taking, Here's the bottomline:- If you have never ever been in a lava cave before - go for it!- If you are traveling with young children / older folks / people with bad knees and weak ankles - give this a miss. The initial flight of stairs can be quite a walk. The floor of the cave can be wet and uneven- If you have been to lava caves before and if you do not have a mental benchmark - go for it if you have time- If you have seen the most wondrous lava caves and already formed expectations - skip it... more than likely this might underperform

The longest lava tunnel in the world and designated as a natural monument.  Plan to spend a couple of hours here and wear study shoes with traction. Also bring a flashlight.  Walking in and out, over a mile distance.  Some light provided in the interior of the cave, but fairly dim.  The floor of the cave is rippled, uneven, sharp and unpaved, with occasional stepping stones placed in areas.  May cause injury, if you stumble, so you need to walk carefully the entire way in and out of the cave.  The entrance of  the cave requires you to walk down about 3 flights of stairs, which you will have to climb up to exit the cave.  Not reccommended for elderly, frail people and young children.  See some different lava formation along the way.

The longest lava tube in the world was sitting in Jeju and I didn't even know! Stumbled upon it on my fourth trip to Jeju. If you like caves, geology, or nature in general this place is fascinating. If you aren't, it's simply an interesting/unique cave that stretches 7.4 km (1km of it walkable). It's a 30 minute round trip in and out if you don't doddle. If you take it all in, give it an hour. It's about 10-15 degrees celsius inside so it's warmer than outside in the winter and cooler than outside in the summer. Perfect place to get away from the elements either way. It can be kind of dark so mind your footing on the uneven lava rock floor!

The lava cave was dark and spooky but then, that is part of the fun and adventure.  I took the long walk in the dark cave, looking at the various lava formations and reading the information that was provided about them. The cave is not completely dark, subtle lighting from lanterns are provided to show us the way into the cave. Some areas are brighter than others. The floor is very uneven, wet and rocky so you have to wear sensible flat shoes.  I got to see the Turtle Rock (Lava Raft), Lava flowstones and the 7.6 meter lava column at the end of the cave which is the highlight of our subterranean adventure. I saw a couple with flashlights and wondered why I had not thought of bringing one. I will definitely bring one next time.  It was a lovely adventurous experience at the Mangangul lava tube. I recommend it to visitors to Jeju Island because it is not every day that you get to see a geological wonder like this  UNESCO World Heritage site.

The lava cave is like a small adventure if you are keen at exploring. Bring a torchlight or make sure you have one installed in your handphone as the cave floor is uneven and slippery. Wear good shoes and a warm jacket with hoodie or wear a cap as water occasionally drips from the top. There is a short trek up a flight of stairs to reach the cave entrance. Lockers available near toilets. Set aside one and a half hours to finish the cave and return as it is slippery at certain sections. Wear good shoes and walk slowly and carefully. I was apalled at how some kids manage to walk pretty fast without their parents holding on to them. In summary, I do not find this cave spectecular, not much for photography too. Just a straight tunnel like structure. We were tired out by the time we went to the cave as we climbed seongsan ilchubong in the morning. Not recommended to combine the cave with other trekking activities in a day. Imo, I find the cave interesting but not a must visit.

The floor is uneven and the lighting is dim, not for those with walking issues. Nice place to see the strange wall formation due to lava. Only 1 km and mostly even.  The tourists can be a bit noisy, hope the bats in the other parts are not too disturbed

The entrance fee was 2000W . You descend down about three to four flights of stairs to this Long tunnel cave. Temperature drops to about 15 degrees . No toilets in the cave so go to the bathroom before you descend . The floor of the cave was wet , slippery and uneven not suitable for young children and elderly. Most of the time you are looking down to avoid stepping into puddles and holes. A torchlight or handphone light is a must unless you have amazing night vision . Also the ceiling drips water constantly so can get quite wet so bring a hat. The walk to the end takes about 45 min to an hour . We gave up after about 35 minutes though some of our friends made it to the end to see the giant structure . If you do not want to do such a Long walk , do 10 minutes . The cave looked the same all the way through.

The cave takes about an hour, nice walk. Wear sensible shoes as the floor is not even and take a small jacket as it gets colder the further in you go. It was an interesting walk and we got to see bats at the end.

The cave is very dimly lit. The floor was very uneven (we are not blaming.. it's the natural formation of the lava) and slippery. I could only look down to make sure that I am walking safely and properly. I had no time to stop and look up and admire the caves. The cave is also very dimly lit, which makes the walk more challenging. We decided to turn back after 20 mins.

The cave is really nice, and amazing as it was created by the lava tunnel, thus the floor is the original ground where the lava froze. The journey is 1km one way, butnthe cave is lit, so you dont need torchlight or guide inside. There's interactive exhibitions too inside about the structure of the cave that was created by lava, unlike any other limestone cave.

The cave floor is uneven combined with inadequate lighting makes the winter walk very uncomfortable and after some distance, we gave up. Our youngsters were bored as the couldn't see the cave's beautiful features. Rather disappointed.

The bus ride from the bus terminal is near an hour and the bus stop you alight at looks like a bus stop in the middle of a highway. From the bus stop, walk 2km to Manjanggul cave. It's a very long walk and not if you are on a solo trip (my mistake as i thought there would be shops and things to see along the way!) as it can get quite scary. Cave is very dark, not well-lit, cold and vey wet. The floor and stairs/steps are very uneven with puddles of water so will suggest covered shoes. Will need a jacket or shawl as the cave gets colder as you walk further in. The lava/cave formation is amazing but I couldn't properly enjoy the sights as I have to keep watching out for puddles of water and the uneven floor to avoid tripping.Will only suggest this if you like to see lava formations, have a group of friends to go with and have transportation to bring you to and fro.

The building looks a bit old. There re space for parking. Inside the castle, there's hello kitty tree at the middle for photo shooting. When you walk inside, there're few theme of hello kitty for photo shooting and walk up the stair to the 2nd floor you will see a few rooms theme of hello kitty including the kitty cafe which sell drinks,Desserts and cakes. The restroom also there. The price is not high. The restaurant decorated in cute seating with hello kitty design. On the way back on ground floor you need to pass the souvenir shop. The price is not cheap for stuffs but if you are hello kitty fan it may worth.

The building itself was amazing and the indoor gardens were impressive. You can take an elevator up to the 5the floor lookout for a nice view through windows that need cleaning. The outside gardens were mixed. Japanese garden was the nicest overall but smaller than I would have guessed. The Italian and French gardens were impressive by scale alone but the details were far under kept. Green water, weeds??? And I between the larger gardens were under kept areas like a? garden that looked lame at best.? With all that it was still worth a quick stop but don't get your expectations too high.
Summer is very hot and visiting the cave is a relief from the hot weather .Very nice place and well maintained , slippery floor .English translation of the plates were very helpful .

Spirited Garden is the #1 place to visit in Jeju in my opinion. I strongly recommend paying a visit.  the garden was actually bigger than I thought, and it took about an hour to see all the places. Spent a lovely few hours wandering through the caves. Definately worth a visit if you are in Jeju. Lots of signs written in English giving excellent detail of the lava formations that can be seen. Easy to return home - same process, but your return ticket on the bus.Remember to wear sensible shoes and bring a jacket. The floor is very wet and pretty uneven and it is cold down there!

one of the many trick art museums in Korea. The first bit has the usual pose-with-renaissance-paintings stuff but if you don't have that much time skip that stuff and make your way through to the end where there's a pretty cool arabian nights themed room where you pretend to run from giants climb into the sky or escape over burning bridges. the station where you pretend to skydive while strapped to a backpack on the floor is quite special. warning : wear pants when visiting this museum if you wish to avoid inadvertently flashing other tourists. the sculpture garden is nothing fantastic and   little provence   is a bunch of stuffed dogs dressed in french peasant outfits in a lackluster room.

One of the finest lava tunnels in the world and listed as Unesco World Heritage. Only 1km of the 13,422m Manjanggul Cave is open to the tourists. Temperature inside the cave is low (around 11 to 21'c) so bring a cardigan or jacket if you afraid of cold. Do wear a covered shoe (best is sport shoes) as the surface of the cave is wet and water are ponding in some area and your shoes is definitely going to get wet. Also, the floor / surface is rough and uneven, not easy to walk fast especially for elderly who have weak knees or children below 2. Along the route there are board with explanation about different kinds of lava rocks in the cave (in English, Chinese, Japanese and Korean). It's interesting. At the end of the route is the Lava Column behind a platform where everyone will take a picture before going back. Oh..this is not the end, you still need to walk another 1km to go back to where you begin (that's where you exit too). So total journey is actually 2km.

One of Jeju's three UNESCO world heritage sites, only a 1km section is open to tourists. It took about 40 minutes to walk to the huge lava column and back to the entrance. The tube is interesting and quite impressive as it is very large. There are also many interesting formations and explanations to look at along the way.It is cold inside about 11-15 degrees, so do bring a jacket. Wear good walking shoes as the floor is wet and very rocky. I saw people walking with wedges and shivering in their t-shirts, can't be nice. There are dim lights all along the cave. For people who are afraid of dark, wet caves, go look at the replica fountain of the lava column in the park.
Not a very big place, but there are lots of teddy bear in this museum. There are a couple of floors of teddy bears you can see, there is also a shop where you can buy teddy bears there

Nice place to visit. U walk into the tunnel until its very derp end almost 1km in..... Then finally at the end of the tunnel u will get to see the light and the only stalagmite in the entire cave.... Lights in the caves are sufficient but not bright enough. The thing is, we thought the wet floors would be slippery but surprisingly thruout our entire walk into and out of the cave, there was absolutely no spot thatvwas slippery, thanks to the natural grooves on the ground which may have been created by the lava flow hundreds of years ago. Nice to explore, but obviously not for those who are claustrophobic.

After the hike, we went to a bakery just by the entrance.  From the second floor, we had a nice view of the Ilchulbong and enjoyed cup of coffee with various breads. My family visited the Teddy Bear Museum in Jeju. My family and I visited this UNESCO World Heritage and South Korea National Monument cave on a late afternoon for 2 hours. There were not many visitors and we didn?t find any tour buses when we reached here.   Getting there & fees: Manjanggul Cave is located in the north western part of Jeju-do. To get (drive) to Manjanggul Cave, key in GPS coordinate 7834818. There is no parking fee at the huge car park. Entrance fee is 2,000 won for adults and 1,000 won for teenagers and children.Manjanggul Cave Museum: Upon climbing up the stairs from the car park, you will reach the Museum and a cafeteria/restaurant on its right. You could go in and have a look at the interesting exhibits, including how the Manjanggul Cave was formed from the volcanic activities.Manjanggul Cave: To get to the underground Cave, we followed the sign-posts ? it?s within 5 minutes? walk from the Manjanggul Cave Museum. Trek the entire 1 km stretch that?s opened to public and you will end with a colourful lit lava column - created from the dripping of lava from a hole in the ceiling ? which at about 8 meters high, is the tallest lava column on Earth. Nevertheless, there are a few things you have to take note while you are in the Cave:(1) The entrance to the Manjanggul Cave is also the exit ? there?s no exit at the end of the 1 km trail, which means you are walking 2 km return (2) Make sure you bring and wear a jacket or sweater with you because it?s freezing cold and chilly inside the cave. (3) Wear a cap or the jacket or sweater can be waterproof because you get water ocassioanlly dripping from the cave top onto you (4) The surface (floor) of the Cave is full of solidified lava flow terrain (i.e. extremely uneven surface) and water puddles, so you have to wear a pair of good walking shoes and walk carefully. Hold on to the railings of the stairs.(5) You probably don?t need a torchlight because the Cave is illuminated just enough by ground lightings. Some parts of the cave even have colourful lights shining at the dome shaped ceiling (cupola) (6) If you would like to take photographs inside the cave, you would need a tripod and switch to manual mode for long exposure (I used 4 seconds to 10 seconds exposure on my digital SLR).   There are displays at certain parts of the cave in English explaining the geology of the cave and the formation of the interesting structures (e.g. stalactites). In particular, there?s one structure ? ?Stone Turtle? ? in which the shape looks like Jeju-do Island, and which you could reach in about 30 minutes of one-way walking as it?s about 400m from the entrance. Along the Manjanggul Cave wall, we saw varied patterns of lava flow lines, some are straight while some are wavy. Really interesting! I have been to over 10 limestone caves around the world, but this is my first visit in a lava tunnel cave or lava tube cave (and Asia?s longest lava tube cave for that matter). You have to experience being transported to another world in this ?out of this world? cave for yourself ? don?t miss it!

Museum is set in quiet surrounding with viewing deck on 3rd floor overlooking the sea. Manjanggul is a must see when in Jeju. It is easy to get (near) there from the main bus terminal in Jeju City, just take bus 701. It drops at the highway at the crossroad (there is an audible announcement in English on the bus as well as written on the screen) in about an hour's time, or just under. From there you can walk (under two KM) or take a cab (about 1000 Won per person). There is also a large parking lot if you have your own car or take a taxi.The entrance fee is 2000 Won and once you have your entrance ticket you follow the crowds of people down the steep set of stairs (be careful - it can be a bit slippery) and into the cave itself. The floor of the lava tube can be difficult for some (elderly, disabled, children) as it is rather uneven and tends to be rather wet. With proper shoes one should be able to navigate the 1 kilometer tube with no issues. It isn't very lighted inside so take care and watch your step.It's a pretty cool (in every sense of the word) experience and definitely looks very different from a   normal cave   in that it is one long tube with high ceilings and lacking the traditional stalagmites/stalactites.if you have a tendency to get chilly, do take a sweater or light jacket as the temperature inside is cooler than the outside, regardless of the time of year.

Manjanggul Cave is one of the top ten lava tubes to visit that was formed about 200,000-300,000 years ago. It is one of 7 Geomunoreum lava tubes of Jeju Island and located in the North East area.The visit can be done using either bus (another 30 mins or 2.7km walk to the entrance) or car. I'd suggest to rent a car while in Jeju because it will make it super easy to get around the island. If you drive, the number you want to input into the GPS is 7107903 :-).It was really windy and cold on the day we went to the cave. We walked for about 5 minutes from the free car park to the ticket booth but the temperature inside of the cave was very comfortable.The first lava related item that we saw was the lava column cascade. It would be there on the way to entrance, to greet everyone who came to visit the Manjanggul Cave.?The entrance started with two flights of stone stairs that might get a bit slippery during the rainy or winter period. Even though you wear non-slip shoes with you, it's definitely worthwhile to hold on to the railing when going down and up the stairs.The cave was definitely not wheelchair friendly since the stony surface is always wet, rocky and covered with puddles. Water will occasionally drop from the ceiling of the cave but it didn't really bother us. We saw that some people carried an umbrella with them or wore the plastic rain poncho but since you'll be walking a lot, it would be too warm if you wear the poncho. Another suggestion is just to wear a hat/ baseball cap in summer and stick to your winter jacket in the winter time.I tried to take some photos inside but it was pretty hard because the cave was quite dark. It was a really enjoyable walk and we got to learn about how the lava stream formed the lines on the cave, stalactites and stalagmites.There were a lot of rocks around our path and we learnt later on that big and fragmented rocks fell from the ceiling during or after the formation of the lava tubes! There were a lot of lava columns as well that was formed when lava flowed from the ceiling to the floor of the lava tube.Manjanggul Cave closes on the first Wednesday of each month. Their opening hours is from 9 AM to 6 PM with last admission at 5:10 PM.

Lee Jung-Seob Art Gallery, like most government run museums in Korea, had a low display items to museum area ratio.? It is dedicated to Lee who spent the last few years of his life in Seogwipo after being raised in present-day North Korea and spending a significant part of his life in Japan.? In a three floor building it was just one room with about 20 pieces of artifacts.? Fortunately the few artifacts which consisted of postcards Lee sent his wife, his earlier sketches, letters to his children, and his palette donated by his wife were all interesting to check out.

LEE Joong Seop Street is lovely and there are some art shops where you can do window shopping. Then this small street lead you to the house where Lee's family lived for certain period, in a 4.6m2 room for 4 family member. You will be stunned to see how small it is!! But they loved this place where they could hug all the time, kids, and the couple. Behind those free zone, the art museum is located. Admission is 1,500 KRW(1.10 USD, 0.80 Euro). You can request docent on the spot. Korean is always ready, for English, better to call in advance when you will visit. At the end of the street, there is small traditional market where you can get some street food and fresh fruits. Strongly recommend to visit to feel the artist' spirits who lived miserable period. He made lots of work for 6 years before he died, age of 40's. It looks like Van Gogh did lots of works during short period. Good to visit 3rd floor to enjoy the view toward south part of Ocean.

Korean women divers are called haenyeo. They dive in the ocean without any special tools to gather abalone, clams or seaweed. Wearing a lead weighted  vested and goggles, they plunge into 20 meter depths and stay underwater holding their breaths for two to three minutes.  Once they come up to the surface, they make a whistling sound, which is their unique way of breathing out carbon dioxide and breathing in fresh oxygen. The museum is in a four story building and housed many exhibits.  Gallery 1 on the first floor depicts the haenyeo's way of life. On the second floor at Gallery 2, you can see haenyeo's working life.  On the third floor at the observation area you can get a view overlooking the sea.  Gallery 3 displays exhibits of the sea around Jeju.  Outside the museum there is a lawn with statues, including one honoring the haenyeo. You can also admire the architecture of the museum. Further down, we chanced upon the haenyeo who were starting their show by singing a song. We were indeed lucky on that Tuesday afternoon as we managed to watch the show which started at 1.30.

I liked the experience, there are a few steps to go down which are easy at the start of the walk but if you walk to the end and back, those steps are a killer at the end. All-in-all, I loved it, nice little solo adventure; loads of couples down there (but well behaved) and it is cheap as chips for the entrance fee of just over 짙1.GBP. It's for kids.  Good to take pictures at a distance, but when watching closely, I got the feeling that things are not that clean and new.  The cafe is particularly messy with no one clearing up the food leftover or liquid on the floor, table sticky.

In this cave, you're allowed to walk about one kilometer in the lava tube where you'll find a lot of variation in the formation and environment. In the tube, there has been several different lava levels and different factors, creating unique patterns on the walls, floor and ceiling. It's recommended to bring something warm down the cave, since it's a bit chilly.Along the way, there is several signs about detail information (both in Korean and English) about the different shapes and things in the cave.

In the summer heat, Manjanggul is the perfect place to escape the heat. It's quite cold inside, and water drips from the ceiling. I changed into jeans and a light sweater before going in, which was perfect. The texture of the cave is fascinating! There are good informational English placards that explain how the cave formed. The floor of the cave is quite bumpy, so take care not to trip.It's a popular destination but getting there and leaving can be time-consuming unless you are with a tour. I took a bus from the Bijarim Forest to get to the cave, which dropped us off right at the cave. The bus leaving right from Manjanggul only leaves once an hour, so I recommend checking the bus departure times before you go into the cave and plan your stay accordingly. Otherwise, there are taxis but the drivers are rudely persistent, charge a non-negotiable flat price, and refuse to go by the meter. They kept pestering us the entire hour we waited for the bus, even after we rejected many times and had begun ignoring them.

I'm glad I went, as I've never seen a lava tube before. Great multilingual explanatory signs. Four dots instead of 5 because even on the pristine day that we went, the wet, uneven floor made it mildly perilous and only a small portion of the tube is open to tourists.

If you've never been to a Korean public bath then there are some things you should know. First go in and pay - currently it's 6000 Won for the baths (segregated by gender) and 8000 Won for both the bathes and the   jimjilbang   (which is a unisex area filled with different hot rooms to enjoy a sweat lodge style experience). You can stay as long as you want and even sleep there. I would never suggest doing so however since even though this is a standard option for most Korean baths and they are arguably the cheapest place to sleep in Korea they are also loud sometimes crowded and generally pretty damned uncomfortable for sleeping. You will be given a set of shorts and a shirt. If you are large like me you can expect to have to cram yourself into them. Use the key provided to find a locker in your respective undressing area. Don't worry even though it doesn't seem like you should be naked in this area it's okay.From here you will go into the showering/bathing area. DO NOT get into any of the pools without first scrubbing yourself down. Soap is provided as well as some abrasive washcloths but you will need your own shampoo which you can buy in the changing area. Once you are clean you can enjoy a variety of different temperature pools and sauna options ranging from the almost freezing to the almost boiling. After you are finished soaking you can either shower again and leave or put on the shorts provided and go to the jimjilbang common area. Here you will find several different hot rooms including a traditional mud hut style outside that looks like a giant wasps nest. Some of these rooms are intense so work your way up to the higher temperatures don't stay in for too long and remember to drink lots of water. Food and beverages will be available in the common area so remember to stash some cash in your shorts before going to the jimjilbang. You can also relax on the floors in the common area watching some bad TV or just snooze. There are a few other nooks and crannies you can explore but this is a basic sketch of what you can expect. Once you're done at the jimjilbang you can go back for another shower and soak dry off enjoy some complimentary personal hygiene products (although I urge caution with their aftershave) get dressed and go home.  Yongduamhaesu Land is a decent example of a Korean bath. It's fairly clean and has some nice facilities. It's also pretty busy so expect high volumes of people especially tourists. Oh and for all you   foreigners   out there of non-Asian decent please expect an awkward amount of interest in your body especially those regions that you'd rather not have a room full of Koreans staring at.
