Self-Drive Holiday in Jeju:Everyone loves going on holidays and I believe a great percentage of these do so on guided tours. Guided tours are fine where convenience is concerned; hotels, meals, itineraries, transport, flights, places of interests to visit, entrance fees etc. etc. are all taken care of by the tour company. As I had discovered decades ago, despite all the conveniences of a guided tour, there are drawbacks that would put one off such tours completely; not being able to sleep-in and wake up as and when you want, having limited time to enjoy the various places of interests or enjoy your lunch while taking in the magnificent scenery from a mountain top restaurant , having to put up with other travellers who simply cannot or are not bothered to be on time, not being able to visit or enjoy other interesting places that are rarely included in tour itineraries, to list a few. Ever since my first guided tour holiday overseas, I have opted for a self-drive holiday and I am very sure there are many out there who would love to do so too,  but refrained from doing so because of a lack of information and perhaps, apprehensive about what it would entail to do a self-drive holiday in a foreign land. This guide is to help dispel those apprehensions and provide the necessary information for you to successfully make that first self-drive holiday in the Honeymoon Island of Jeju, and hopefully, many more thereafter in other destinations of your dreams.Preparation:Many experts would advise, and rightly so, that you should first read up all the necessary information on driving at the destination that you will be holidaying in. However, in my opinion, what is more important is having the self-confidence to drive in a foreign land. Sometimes, things can go wrong, road and weather conditions can change to the extent that no pre-reading or preparation can help, but, with that very important self-confidence, it will see you through. You must also have a flexible mind set and be ready to accommodate changes when necessary ? only then will you be able to thoroughly enjoy your self-drive holiday. Having said that, I must say that driving in Jeju is a walk-in-the-park, quite unlike, for example, driving through the mountain pass between Sun Moon Lake and Hualien County in Taiwan ? that is a drive I would never recommend to the feint hearted.International Driving Permit ? you will need to obtain an International Driving Permit to be able to rent a car in Jeju, and for that matter, in most other countries. It can be easily obtained at AAS and it costs only $20.00 and is valid for one year. You would also want to search for information on all the places of interests and decide on which of those to visit during your stay in Jeju. This is to help you plan and minimize travelling time. These can be had at the Korea Tourism Centre at Samsung CentreChoice of Hotel ? There are many hotels catering to different needs and budgets to choose from. The one most often asked question is the location ? to stay in Jeju-si or Seogwipo-si? My experience tells me that it makes no difference ? it is just a matter of choice. If you are arriving in Jeju late at night, then, perhaps, you may wish to stay in a hotel that is near the airport, to minimize your night driving had you decided on a hotel in Seogwipo-si. We landed in Jeju at 2000 hrs, collected our car at 2100 hrs and drove to Seogwipo-si where our hotel was situated. It was a pleasant forty-five minute drive with guidance from the GPS unit.Car Rental Company:There are many car rental companies in Jeju, but you will most likely come across only a handful if you search the internet ? Kumho, AJ Rentals (AVIS), SIXT, Donga and Jeju Rent-a-Car. Do note, though, that there are more than a dozen of competing rental companies at the airport to choose from if you prefer to shop around for the best rates and cars upon your arrival. I book mine through AJ Rentals, not only because of the brand name, but it also provided the best rates among the others on the net and it did not require me to pay in advance upon confirmation of my reservation. To rent the car, you will need to have an International Driving Permit (obtain it from AAS), your local driving license and passport. You can pay either in cash or credit card. Type of Car:The type of car you choose is totally dependent on your preference and budget ? luxury or basic. However, do consider the available boot space that will be needed to accommodate your luggage. As a guide, the boot of a KIA K3 can accommodate only three large suitcases with no space for a smaller, fourth piece. In a situation where there are four adults, the smaller, fourth suitcase will have to share estate space in the back seat with two other passengers. The cost of rental is dependent on the type of car, number of days and the period of travel. As a guide, a KIA K3 cost approximately S$60.00 per day for 5 days during the holiday season in November. The rate includes insurance, CDW and the use of a English language GPS, with collection and return at the airport. The rates of the other rental companies that I surveyed were cheaper, however, I cannot vouch for their quality nor service support. You decide at your own risk. The overall condition of the car was good. The only ?defect? was the slight steering alignment problem but it was not something that would put us in danger at any time. Maps:Do you need a map when it is very likely that you will be relying on the GPS? YES! A map is necessary for planning your routes and selecting the places of interests to visit.You can easily obtain a detailed map of Jeju Island, with all the major highways and feeder routes from your local Korean Tourism office. You can also obtain these from the car-rental companies when you collect your car in Jeju. You can use it to plan your route, estimate the travel time and locate other possible places of interests that you don?t find on the standard tourist trail. You can use this same map to write down the telephone numbers of the places of interests that you plan to visit. You will need these numbers for keying into the GPS system to guide you to your destination. I made it a point to re-confirm that the telephone numbers are current by asking the hotel staff to extract the numbers from their computer system. This proved to be very useful. Collecting Your Car At The Airport:After clearing immigration and customs, proceed to gate 5 of the arrival terminal. Opposite the gate, there is a green, covered walk-way with a sign that says ?Car Rentals?; it will lead you to a building where there are a lot of car-rental companies. If you had pre-booked your car, look for the car-rental company in the building. However, do take note that this building houses the local car rental companies. For the international brands such as Avis, Hertz and the other bigger local companies, they are housed in another location outside the airport. You will need to check with them when you are doing the booking or email them for the information. If the collection centre of the car rental company that you booked with is located outside the airport, wait for their shuttle bus at Gate 5. You will recognize their shuttle bus by their brand name boldly emblazoned on the sides of the bus. Since I booked my car through Avis, I took the ?AJ? shuttle bus to their rental office on the outskirts of the airport. The shuttle bus runs on a regular schedule. Arriving at the front of the office, you take a queue ticket. If you had made reservations, it takes just a few seconds to call up your reservation after presenting your passport, driver's licence and International Driving Permit. You will be shown the rental agreement with all the details pertaining to the type, class, number of days of rental, total costs and any other relevant information. With Avis, the GPS is included in the rental, whereas for other rental companies that I had enquired with, the GPS is charged separately. After you have signed the rental agreement, you will be shown your car. You then drive it off to the inspection building where they will go through the car with you to identify any minor damages, scratches, dents etc. They will also have you verify that the fuel tank is full and instruct you on the use of the GPS before getting you to sign off the acknowledgement form. Do ensure that the GPS is an English language version. Keep the documents safely in the glove-compartment and be sure to get the telephone number of the station that you will return the car to. You will need this number to key into the GPS system to guide you back. You then proceed on your way, presumably, to your hotel for a much needed rest after the long flight to Jeju.When returning the car, you just need to drive back to the same depot from where you had collected it. Just key the given number into the GPS. Upon arrival, follow the sign, ?Car Return? and head for an available lot. The attendant there will check the car with you and when all is in order, he hands you a form to sign after you have returned the key to him. You then take the shuttle bus that will take you to the departure hall at the airport.The use of the GPS:Different makes and models operate slightly differently from one another, however, the common function that generalizes all of them is the use of the telephone number of a particular hotel, attraction or establishment to program the location into the GPS. For example, the telephone number of our hotel, Ocean Palace Hotel, Jeju, is 064 - 7305800. To navigate to the hotel from the airport, I just had to key in the number 7305800 and simply touch the 'Navigate' button and voila, it calculates the shortest route and starts the voice navigation system in a jiffy - it's as simple as that. From then on, just follow the voice navigation to get you to your hotel. If you make a wrong turn or pass a junction where you were supposed to turn, do not panic. Just relax and drive on ? it will re-direct you back to the planned route or at times, provide you with a new course. In fact, we had a lot of fun and discovered many new places of interest by intentionally turning off to smaller but interesting-looking roads just to see what lies ahead and where it will eventually lead us to ? that is the beauty of a self-drive holiday. Driving in Jeju:Jeju has a coastal ring road of approximately 181 km, not counting the connecting highways linking the North-South-East ?West regions. The coastal scene is a sight to behold! It is left-hand driving in Jeju.To those who have never driven on the left side of the road, it takes a little getting used to, physically as well as in your mind. It gets a little more confusing when turning at traffic junctions, especially when driving through ? stopping gives you an opportunity to orientate yourself and prepare in your mind the lane to take when turning. To minimize this confusion, always try to follow a car in front of you which is turning in the same direction as you. It is also helpful to remember that when turning, the roadside kerb will always be on the right of the driver. The roads, save for the highways, are slightly narrower than the roads we are used to in Singapore.Generally, the speed limits are:30 Km / hr within 100 m of school zones50 Km / hr in town areas60 Km / hr in the outskirts of town70 Km / hr along highwaysThe speed limits change quite frequently, so it is advisable to keep a look-out for the change in speed limits. There are speed-cameras practically everywhere, usually positioned up on traffic lights, lamp-posts and in some places, hidden behind 'boxes' manned by a policeman. So, if you wish to spend your money supporting the policemen, speed on at your own risk.The local drivers can, at times, be quite reckless. Just like we have hell-drivers here, there are hell-drivers in Jeju too, but not too many. Just stay alert and always be on the look-out using your wing and rearview mirrors all the time. Except for the main areas of Jeju-si and Seogwipo-si, most of the roads around the island are quite free of traffic.  To estimate the time needed to travel any distances, take an average speed of 45 km/hr.Parking:Generally free parking along kerb-sides and paid parking in some buildings and are generally available easily. Most hotels have free parking for their guests ? do check with the hotel management that you have booked with. Petrol cost: As at Nov 2014: Krw 1750 / ltrPlanning Your Routes:Planning your routes is totally at your own whim and fancy, depending on the places of interest as well as the available time you have on the island. If you have a few days ( I would recommend a minimum of five days), perhaps you may wish to consider the following suggestion:1. Day 1 ? Arrival and check into hotel. This sample itinerary is on the assumption that your hotel is in Seogwipo. 2. Day 2 ? Explore the west scenic coastal drive (Route 1132) of Sagye, Gosan-Ilwa, Hagwi-Aewol and visit the places of interest along this route ( Mt Sangkaksan / Songkaksan / Yongmeori). There are many cafes (especially along the Coastal Cafe Road) and bbq restaurants for stops of aromatic coffee and grilled black pig meat. Explore Jeju-si city (underground shopping mall) and return via highway 1131 where the famous ?Forest Tunnel? is located. After dinner, take a drive to the Lotte World Resort for some very beautiful night scenery of the giant windmills.3. Day 3 ? Go East this time along the Pyeoson, Sehwa-Jongdal and Gimyeong ? Haengwon coastal routes. Stopover at Seongsan Ilchubong (Sunrise Peak). Have dinner in Jeju-si before doing a night drive back to Seogwipo. 4. Day 4 ? Alternative 1Drive to Seongsan Port in the north-east via the eastern coastal route and park your car there. Purchase your ferry tickets to Udo Island and spend a very interesting day there. You can tour the island by buying the hop-off-on bus tickets or for the adventurers, you can hire the quad-bikes or scooters. Alternative 2 ? visit the popular tourist spots such as the Trick-art museum, teddy bear museum, waterfalls, submarine tours, Green Tea museum, Geomun Oreum, Citrus fruit farms, mysterious road, etc etc....5. Day 5 ? Check out of hotel for catch your flight back home.Have a safe and enjoyable holiday!Telephone Numbers of Attractions For GPS:Citrus Fruit Museum - 732 2114Geomun Oreum - 7108981Joongang Underground Mall - 723 1510Jusenggeolli Cliffs - 7381521Lotte Hotel - 731 1000Alive Museum - 805 0888Trick Art Museum - 787 8774Seongeup Folk Village - 787 1179Traditional 5 day market (Jeju-si) - 7435985Seongsan Harbour (Ferry to Udo Island) - 782 5671Seongsan Ilchubong - 783 0959Cheongyejeong Waterfall - 760 6331Cheongjiyeong Waterfall - 733 1528Jeongbang Waterfall - 733 1530Teddy Bear Museum - 738 7600Jeju Folk Village - 787 4501Jeju Sea-World - 784 2333Aqua Planet Jeju - 780 0900Manjanggul Cave - 710 7903Oedolgae - 760 3033

Sanbangsan (?곕갑?? isn't a really big mountain but it has an interesting and distinguishable shape. It is about an hour west of Seogwipo by bus which stops conveniently right in front of the mountain.There is a nice temple at the base of the mountain called Sanbanggulsa (?곕갑援댁궗) with a huge golden Buddha a wonderful view of the town below and the ocean and an army of miniature mint-coloured Buddhas (I think). All make for great photos. Further up the mountain (you can climb up a long flight of stairs) is a small temple in a cave with an even better view of the town below. Worth visiting if you have made it this far. There is also an interesting story about a monk who hid in the cave during a violent time (can't exactly remember details). Down below south of the street in front of the mountain is a really really nice coastal walk with impressive cliffs that have been ocean and wind-swept into wonderful formations. This place is called   Yongmeori Coast   and also makes for great picture. (Worth knowing that the coast closes during heavy rain for safety reasons.)(Also of interest in the area to some is Hamel's Ship (a replica/museum of an old Dutch ship that landed on Jeju ages ago and the story of the Dutchman that was held captive in the island) and horseback riding (though it's only in a circle). Could be good for kids though these two are the least attractive for me personally.)

Other than Hallasan...the massive shield volcano that created Jeju Island and now sits at its center, Sunrise Peak is perhaps the greatest of the nearly 400 craters, cinder cones or shield volcanoes (  oreums   in Korean) found around the island.  It's a bit of a hike to get to the top, seemingly straight up at times.  But the incredible views from every angle will reward your diligence.  depending on the season, you can see fields of yellow canola (or   rape  ) flowers; also Udo (Cow Island to the east, Hallasan to the north/northwest and the incredible Pacific all around...vast and hypnotic on a clear day.  Nearby, you can check out the Aqua Planet Aquarium and the Women Divers Museum. Be sure to drive along the coast road and enjoy a coffee and dessert at one of the many unique cafes.  Although there are now several franchise coffeeshops near Sunrise Peak, the independents offer a more relaxing atmosphere.

O'Sulloc Tea Museum is a small building set in a tea farm. It's a well designed lovely space with a display area about the history of tea and an exhibit wall of teacups and pots a shop where you can try some tea (only one kind though) and a restaurant featuring green tea beverages and sweets. You can also walk around outside there is a garden area in and around the building and also small rows of tea bushes just outside. There's no admission fee and it's not so much of a museum as a commercial venue for selling O'Sulloc products although items can be pricey for the budget traveller. I visited O'Sulloc with a few other backpackers (5 foreigners 1 Korean) and we all had a terrible experience of their customer service. The staff were sour faced and gave us the impression that we were not welcomed glaring at us and tidying their display in a huff when we looked at the product samples (these are samples ok - they're meant to be touched and looked at!). The staff at the counter literally sneered in disdain at my Korean travel companion when he tried to make friendly small talk while we were purchasing our items. This was the worst experience I've had in my 3 weeks in Korea. All the other customer service staff I've encountered in Korea were either very polite and lovely or just neutral. I'm writing in formally to the management about this so hopefully by the time other TripAdvisor members visit they would have improved.In spite of that I did enjoy my visit (no point letting the staff spoil it) but I would recommend coming here only if you've done all your   must-do's   in Jeju or on a rainy day.

Not only was the view after climbing to the top of Trail no. 2 breathtaking, the track up the steps and steep trail will also leave most breathless! There are markers that state you are at 2-1, 2-2 etc., the 2 in front meaning trail no. 2, but none tells you how much higher you must climb! Incidentally the top is 2-5. Its quite a struggle to reach the top but if you take it easy and take regular breaks along the way to admire the fauna & flora, take some photos and generally get your breath back, you should reach the top in about half an hour. The journey down is much easier and faster. The view on top is magnificent and definitely worth the climb! The fresh cool mountain air was great too. Highly recommend you try. PS : There were two ladies in their seventies from San Francisco who completed the climb and decent at the same time as my group. Two thumbs up to them!!There is also a museum and sculptured garden at the base of the mountain where you can sit on park benches and enjoy the air and general view of the Hallasan mountain and its surroundings.
Not a very big place, but there are lots of teddy bear in this museum. There are a couple of floors of teddy bears you can see, there is also a shop where you can buy teddy bears there

My mother-in-law bought my husband and I entry to this   museum   and I went in expecting ultra-hokey and a waste of time. I was really pleasantly surprised!There are a few   galleries  . The highlights for me were the Teddy Bear History gallery - where they use teddy bears to display historical dioramas including a Teddy Moon Landing, teddy bears knocking down the Berlin Wall, Teddy Disney World and more. These are pretty creative and well made. Some even include music.There's also an   art   gallery, with some famous paintings or sculptures reenacted with teddy bears. This gallery extends into more dioramas such as the   runway   and a Korean wedding scene. Not always logical in where they put things, but fun anyway. There are a few honestly significant teddies in the museum - a Louis Voittan teddy that cost millions at auction, and a small side gallery of Teddies combined with historical memorabilia from Teddy Roosevelt, with some brief English descriptions of where the teddy bear came from.It's not a top attraction if you're here for a short visit, but if you're around a while and want something cute and fun, it's worth an hour or two!

review: My family and I visited this UNESCO World Heritage and South Korea National Monument cave on a late afternoon for 2 hours. There were not many visitors and we didn?t find any tour buses when we reached here.   Getting there & fees: Manjanggul Cave is located in the north western part of Jeju-do. To get (drive) to Manjanggul Cave, key in GPS coordinate 7834818. There is no parking fee at the huge car park. Entrance fee is 2,000 won for adults and 1,000 won for teenagers and children.Manjanggul Cave Museum: Upon climbing up the stairs from the car park, you will reach the Museum and a cafeteria/restaurant on its right. You could go in and have a look at the interesting exhibits, including how the Manjanggul Cave was formed from the volcanic activities.Manjanggul Cave: To get to the underground Cave, we followed the sign-posts ? it?s within 5 minutes? walk from the Manjanggul Cave Museum. Trek the entire 1 km stretch that?s opened to public and you will end with a colourful lit lava column - created from the dripping of lava from a hole in the ceiling ? which at about 8 meters high, is the tallest lava column on Earth. Nevertheless, there are a few things you have to take note while you are in the Cave:(1) The entrance to the Manjanggul Cave is also the exit ? there?s no exit at the end of the 1 km trail, which means you are walking 2 km return (2) Make sure you bring and wear a jacket or sweater with you because it?s freezing cold and chilly inside the cave. (3) Wear a cap or the jacket or sweater can be waterproof because you get water ocassioanlly dripping from the cave top onto you (4) The surface (floor) of the Cave is full of solidified lava flow terrain (i.e. extremely uneven surface) and water puddles, so you have to wear a pair of good walking shoes and walk carefully. Hold on to the railings of the stairs.(5) You probably don?t need a torchlight because the Cave is illuminated just enough by ground lightings. Some parts of the cave even have colourful lights shining at the dome shaped ceiling (cupola) (6) If you would like to take photographs inside the cave, you would need a tripod and switch to manual mode for long exposure (I used 4 seconds to 10 seconds exposure on my digital SLR).   There are displays at certain parts of the cave in English explaining the geology of the cave and the formation of the interesting structures (e.g. stalactites). In particular, there?s one structure ? ?Stone Turtle? ? in which the shape looks like Jeju-do Island, and which you could reach in about 30 minutes of one-way walking as it?s about 400m from the entrance. Along the Manjanggul Cave wall, we saw varied patterns of lava flow lines, some are straight while some are wavy. Really interesting! I have been to over 10 limestone caves around the world, but this is my first visit in a lava tunnel cave or lava tube cave (and Asia?s longest lava tube cave for that matter). You have to experience being transported to another world in this ?out of this world? cave for yourself ? don?t miss it!

My family (2 adults & a 10 year old) recently spent 3 days doing a combination of private and small group tours of UNESCO sites in Jeju Island with June of Core Travel. It was a great balance of energetic activities (hiking craters, exploring lava tubes), museums and cultural attractions, and relaxing activities such as a sampling session at a tea farm or DIY foot massage at a herb garden.

Most of the park is outdoors, and we went when it was raining, so that wasn't that good. But the place is beautiful, with trees and stones lined up. There's also a museum about volcanoes as well as statues of historical figures. Very nice place although it is only accessible by car and very difficult to get a cab.

Meet them, watch them and read about them here, at their own museum( which even has electric car charging points) Given there are so many museum to celebrate the dead and gone, this one for the living, is special with moving exhibits

Massive ground. A full walk about will take 2hrs easily. Even though all the stones look similar after an hr, it's a very effective way to understand the folklores of Jeju. Cheap entrance fee of only 2K won.Some places near the museum are still under renovation when we were there.

Marado Island is remote, largely barren, and is   nearly   empty. There is a small population of island residents. There is a small oddly shaped church, a Buddhist temple, and a lighthouse. As far as buildings go, there is little of interest. The primary feature of Marado is the rugged coastline, typical of Jeju-do. Doesn't sound that appealing? Yet, I did enjoy my visit here because it is nice to see a part of Jeju that is largely unaffected by tourism, small museums, resorts, golf, or honeymooners. The ferry does not depart too frequently. Once you arrive on Marado, you really can only do one thing, walk around the entire island, which only takes 2 hours. If the weather is nice (May-August), you should be able to get some pretty pictures of the rugged coast, bright green grass, and some of the lonely buildings on the island.Some of these small island communities are such a contrast to our (foreigners) perception of Korea, that a visit in itself helps creates a more broad image of the country. A worthy experience, that I would recommend if you have plenty of time on Jeju Island.

It was between $11-12 for entry but of the   museums   in korea  this one is my favorite (lived in korea for 4 years). Located next to   Loveland   this museum is small modern place with beautiful outdoor features such as a reflecting pool sculptures and a small surrounding forest. There was a little bit of everything from an exhibit about a famous national artist who lived for decades on Jeju to an interesting video and poetry collaboration of Korean rappers talking about social issues. The upstairs is currently showcasing drawings and sculptures made by Korean schoolchildren in a surprisingly cheeky cheerful exhibit. Much of the museum was in English but others were only in Korean. The price of admission was only 1000 won well worth it for the experience. There were several pieces that didn't wow me and some outdoor floorboards that need repairs but all in all this is a nice little museum. Make sure to drop by the cafe on the way out for a lovely view of the reflecting pool outside as you sip your coffee!

Located just a stone's throw from O'Sulloc Museum, this place is a must-visit! I strongly recommend making your own soap here - it is such a fun and unique experience! Do grab a bite to eat at the cafe as well as the food is not only healthy but delicious!

Located in the middle of Jungmun Resort right across from a Ripley's Believe it or Not museum, I would only recommend this kitsch and cheese-tastic museum to visitors on a bleak and rainy day. The idea is cute, at best - history and art through the ages represented by teddy bears (My Fair Lady, Princess Diana and Prince Charles get married, the falling of the Berlin War, the Beatles, Mona Lisa, the Creation of Adam, etc.), but I would expect a museum in an expensive resort complex to at least have descriptions in English and other tourist languages (Japanese, Mandarin, Cantonese). The entrance fee of 8000 won is a little steep for what you are able to see. Not surprisingly, there is an entire floor dedicated to a pricey gift shop. The most impressive parts of the museum are the architecture of the glass pyramidal shaped building and the views from the garden to the rear. Overall, it's an alright way to kill an hour or so, but definitely not a must-see for me.

Located beside O'sulloc tea museum. When I told the taxi driver he seem don't know the place but when I said O'sulloc he just get it. Outside you can see green tea plant. Lee Jung-Seob Art Gallery, like most government run museums in Korea, had a low display items to museum area ratio.? It is dedicated to Lee who spent the last few years of his life in Seogwipo after being raised in present-day North Korea and spending a significant part of his life in Japan.? In a three floor building it was just one room with about 20 pieces of artifacts.? Fortunately the few artifacts which consisted of postcards Lee sent his wife, his earlier sketches, letters to his children, and his palette donated by his wife were all interesting to check out.

LEE Joong Seop Street is lovely and there are some art shops where you can do window shopping. Then this small street lead you to the house where Lee's family lived for certain period, in a 4.6m2 room for 4 family member. You will be stunned to see how small it is!! But they loved this place where they could hug all the time, kids, and the couple. Behind those free zone, the art museum is located. Admission is 1,500 KRW(1.10 USD, 0.80 Euro). You can request docent on the spot. Korean is always ready, for English, better to call in advance when you will visit. At the end of the street, there is small traditional market where you can get some street food and fresh fruits. Strongly recommend to visit to feel the artist' spirits who lived miserable period. He made lots of work for 6 years before he died, age of 40's. It looks like Van Gogh did lots of works during short period. Good to visit 3rd floor to enjoy the view toward south part of Ocean.

Korean women divers are called haenyeo. They dive in the ocean without any special tools to gather abalone, clams or seaweed. Wearing a lead weighted  vested and goggles, they plunge into 20 meter depths and stay underwater holding their breaths for two to three minutes.  Once they come up to the surface, they make a whistling sound, which is their unique way of breathing out carbon dioxide and breathing in fresh oxygen. The museum is in a four story building and housed many exhibits.  Gallery 1 on the first floor depicts the haenyeo's way of life. On the second floor at Gallery 2, you can see haenyeo's working life.  On the third floor at the observation area you can get a view overlooking the sea.  Gallery 3 displays exhibits of the sea around Jeju.  Outside the museum there is a lawn with statues, including one honoring the haenyeo. You can also admire the architecture of the museum. Further down, we chanced upon the haenyeo who were starting their show by singing a song. We were indeed lucky on that Tuesday afternoon as we managed to watch the show which started at 1.30.

Kim Tschang-Yeul museum had a stylish exterior designed by Tadao Ando.? Featuring the namesake artist Kim’s sculptures and paintings, the museum is very chic for a government run museum. Kim’s trademark is the water drop, which is added to what would otherwise look like rather plain patterns painted on canvas.? The sculptures mostly contained large glass water drops.? Some of the outdoor sculptures complement Ando’s architecture very nicely.? This was an unexpectedly cool visit.

Kim Mandeok Memorial.I really liked this place personally. I came to know of this woman, Kim Mandeok from this memorial museum. She was the first CEO woman in Chosun Dynasty, which was quite unusual especially as a woman. And when a famine came to Jeju, she helped people in Jeju. Because of the benevolent act, she was still remembered even now. Even a Korean drama dealt with her life. Her life is very exemplary and inspiring. You can find a fraction of Korean history here.
Kids will love this museum but lesser for adults. There's around 3 levels of exhibition, but you can view them all pretty quick.

Just your run of the mill chocolate   factory   museum. They have all the info about the Cacao bean and how to make chocolate  a gift shop to buy chocolate  and that's it. It's mediocre and offers the same info about chocolate you could learn by googling it.

Jungmun-Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliff is beautiful place where, look at huge waves crashing against volcanic rocks, one can experience the power of nature. With so much to do and so much to see, the Jeju island is certainly one of the most prominent tourist places in the world. Just about an hour's flight from Seoul, it's a paradise for nature-lovers and surfers. There are countless world class museums offering education and entertainment based on themes like Glass, Ice Sculptures, Trick Art, Folk Lore, Health and Sex, War, Art - the list is endless. Best way to explore the Island is to take taxi tours with a driver who speaks and understands little English. They ask for W150,000 for 8 hours, however, you may beat them down to W115,000 or so. For sightseeing, 5-6 days should be enough.

Jeju's teddy bear museum is one of the most iconic destinations. I first heard about it from watching the show Goong years ago, and decided I had to visit it if I ever went to Jeju island. It was a small museum, but nonetheless i'm glad I paid a visit. The museum is a short walk from The Shilla Jeju  , which is where we stayed.

Jeju stone park was rated A by Korea Ministry of Culture and Tourism, in recognition that this park is excellent in term of its specialization in the theme of stone, differentiation from other facilities, and characteristics relating to mythology and the life of the people in the region.Get the map at the entrance and follow guided park course. Don't miss out the Jeju stone museum to know how the formation of Jeju Island. After a short nice walk from the entrance,the museum is just located in the basement of a building opposite the Sky Pond. Follow the map to look for Jeju traditional village with thatched roof houses. Before at the end of course, drop by the unique Gallery in the park which you may find artworks of domestic and foreign artists.It is indeed best travel Korea during Autum because even though it was sunny day, but the breeze was so cooling and the air was very refreshing. It is a museum as well as an ecological park. It is a very remarkable cultural park which sublimating nature in art ,really very fantastic.

Jeju Stone Park exceeded our expectations.  So much space and everything well laid out.  The museum was particularly interesting with some absolutely amazing pieces of lava, and microscopes set-up, which my 9-year old Daughter loved.  They also had an interesting photography exhibition (temporary).  If you are a geologist and/or simply interested in volcanoes and rocks, then you will probably spend all day here.  Appreciated the water machines everywhere but the restaurant was closed (just in case you are hungry).  We all enjoyed it immensely.  Children less than 12 are free and adults are KRW 5000 (very reasonable).

Jeju is well known by the haenyeo, or that we usually called it as woman divers. Since it was not a good time for diving like a haenyeo and it means that it was so difficult to find one of them when i visited Jeju, i decided to visit the museum. It's not so big, but shows completely how the haenyeo's life, their lives, and their historical stories. It shows not only the diving suit they wear since long time ago until nowadays but also their house, their foods, their tools, and everything. Your journey will be started by watching a video about history of haenyeo. Then you can walk through the dioramas to learn how haenyeo live and works.

Jeju has some very interesting museums, they seem to have them about everything from electricity ,to tea to, to robots! Quite quirky here and you'll see Teddy bears dressed up as Michael Jordan to famous re-enactments of history. Spent about 2 hours here just because it seemed interesting and a lot of effort has been put into the place.

Jeju has its rainy strong windy days and on a dsy like this, it was perfect for visiting the teddy bear museum.  I had to admit, my expectations were low so in turn, i quite enjoyed it!  There were sections about the history of teddy bears and even reenactment of historical scenes by the teddies!  There is also a free teddy bear Elvis performance on the other side of the museum that was quite amusing :)

Jeju has a park or a museum for just about everything. And so it is with Jeju Stone Park. It does have some interesting rocks.You know, some people think that Halla san is the volcano on Jeju. But, really the whole island is a volcano. If the volcano erupts again you will not have to worry too much about the lava flowing from Halla san because lava will be flowing from every little mountain on the island, which a lot of them are closer to where you live than Halla san. So, just about anywhere on Jeju you can find interesting rocks.especially along the coast. Even though it would be a nice walk around the park, you can just look out your window to see interesting rocks you don't necessarily have to go to the Stone Park. But, if you don't have anything to do and want to spend the day outside and see part of Jeju along the way, Jeju Stone Park might be a good way to spent the day.

Jeju hanyeo, women divers are the very best symbol of Jeju.You can watch them catch sea creatures mostly any place you go in the island.However, this museum is the only and best place you can get the whole idea of who they are, what they live up for, how they do it, etc.It's a lil dificult to get there, I know. But it's worth visiting.So I highly recommend you going this place.

Jeju Glass Castle is a must see museum. It has outdoor which can be seen with in 2 hours & indoor as well. There are a lot of glass shapes. This museum is good for people in all ages, Photographers and videographer. The entrance ticket is little bit expensive.

Jeju 4-3 Peace Park educates visitors thoroughly about the Jeju 4-3 Incident which was really almost a genocide when Korean government and US military killed over 30,000 Jeju residents and tortured many more.  With Korea on the brink of dividing into two, Jeju residents wrongly suspected of being Communists ended up being victims.  The government didn't even go public about the incident until the late 1990's and only officially apologized in the 2000's.  The museum describes the build up to the incident and depicts all the horrible details of what the Jeju residents went through.  Having gone through grade school in the 1980's when the incident was not public knowledge, this was a very educational experience for me.
I've visited the Teddy Bear Museum twice, once in 2008 and once in 2011. The collection of bears is amazing. Loved the new Elvis show, really cute! :)

I've been very interested in the haenyeo ever since I first visited Jeju-do. This museum has some interesting exhibitions about the life and work of the haenyeo. Admission is very cheap, a bit over 1000 won for an adult. It's recommended to watch the short documentary about the haenyeo before visiting the exhibitions, to get the most out of your visit. It plays near the lobby. There's a gift shop on site with haenyeo-related items.
Its really a museum.... i am not a fan, i wont say its bad place but just teddy bear aint for me. can have been better place for kids i believe.

It's my second visit to Jeju and since I am staying in Jungmun area, we decided to visit this nearby attraction. It's more of a shopping place. The green tea ice-cream is quite blandand there's not much green tea taste.But the   saving grace   is the tea plantation . There are giant cupslots of flowers and is overall a photo taking place. We did not have enough time and did not visit the museum . There are interesting sample tea blands that you can smell with names like   Moon Walk   and   Jeju Green Tea  . Overall could be better. Might come again.

It's just ordinary museum,not much to see,just a liitle teddy bear collection.in 30 min i can finish around it's.in the last floor there is souvenir shop.i think it's good museum for kid,and teddy bear  lover.

It's good for what it is.  Some people have been calling this place a glass museum - it's not.  It's a theme park for glass.  I say theme park, but if you're thinking rides then you're wrong.  What they do have is lots of things made out of glass to see.  It's pretty and often colourful.  My female partner enjoyed it more than I did, and there's nothing there that would make me want to go back.  I think children might get a little bored by the place, although girls would probably enjoy it more.  As far as adults are concerned, if you think it sounds like a place you'd enjoy, then you probably would.  But if you think it sounds kinda boring then you wouldn't enjoy it.

It's fascinating with everything they made or designed the teddy bears to be. There are a lot of museums that the teddy bear was part of - art, music, hollywood, pop culture. There's also an Elvis Presley teddy bear show. They have a small resaturant that serves juice and some snacks. There's also a garden with teddy and his friends as statues.

It's a Safari Theme Teddy Bear Museum. There are all kinds of bears, including giraffe, zebras, sheeps, monkeys, pandas, etc. On the second level, there is even Egyptian theme bears decorated with crystals. Don't miss that. There are also international bears on displayed on level 2. Enjoy your visit. Don't miss out on purchasing the bears at the gift shop for souvenirs, you will be spoilt for choices. All the bears are made in Korea and worth buying for keepsake.

It's a must do to spend some time at this museum. Located in a relatively new building right on the coast, it tells the story of these amazing women divers who work 52 weeks of the year diving for a abalone, conch and other sea products. How they managed in the winter time without wet suits astonishes me. These women also played a vital part of the resistance movement in World War II against the invading Japanese Army. Add this visit as part of your Jeju Island tour - best idea it to hire a taxi driver for a day (approx A$100). They turn out to be your tour guide, photographer and restaurant selector - fantastic value! Enjoy :)

it's a museum dedicated to teddy bear. use teddy bear to mimic some of the famous stars, drawings, icons and characters. there is a special Teddy Elvis Presley performance to watch the teddy sings. there is also a gigantic teddy in the park, which is a hotspot for picture taking. overall it's not really impressive as it is just a display for teddy bears.
Its a cafe/shop. Nice if you like tea but a bit out of thw way really...basically the title   museum   is a ploy to get people to thw cafe....
It?s a rather small place but filled with lots of cuteness. Safari themed, royal themed... etc. different from teddy bear museum but worth a visit at least once if you love teddy bears.

It worth a look just to see the beautiful coastline of the Island.Most of the rocks come in various heights and sizes shaped like hexagons and if you look at certain angles, they can take on various animals etc.The black lava colour offsets against the outstanding sea and coastline.These cliffs are very similar to the Giants Causeway in Ireland with a pancake rock system but on a much smaller scale.It was crowded the day were there and we assume it is the same most days in the summer months. So a lot of people were snaking along this narrow path around the cliffs and we needed to wait our turn to see over the barriers.There are a few stallholders near the carpark (fee charged) selling fruit, souvenirs and the local home made confectionary similar to nougat.On the way out you can go to a park with some gardens and perhaps a museum type building.The hours vary seasonally however it is the standard KRW 2,000 entry fee for most monuments around the Island.Place it on your ?must see? places to visit here just for the dramatic coastline and on a rough day you may get some blow hole situations with the force of the water.Enjoy your visit!

It was such a pain to get to but I loved the Stone Park. The main reason was to see the Dol hareubangs - the stone sculptures which represent Jeju. There was information about the mythology surrounding the formation of Jeju which was at times mind-boggling and contradictory. There are different routes around the park and there is an indoor exhibition which features the volcanic rocks and Jeju's origins as a volcanic island. I preferred the outdoor sections where the use of stone in Jeju was highlighted - used in things such as tombs/ shrines, walls, icons of spiritual beliefs etc. The largest sculptures are near the exit and the Dol hareubangs were awesome. They all had slightly different expressions and quirks which was cool. There are plans to expand the museum grounds and I would defo like to go back again in future. It was quite quiet when we were there and we only saw a few people except for a group on a guided tour at the end. Such a shame there are not more visitors but good for those who made the effort. Recommended visit in Jeju!

It was sooo much fun to visit this place. When I visited Jeju, my Korean friend brought me to Playkpop museum. I had so much fun to watch kpop stars' videos at the 3-D theater. I spent most time to take holographic pictures. It was a hidden jem in Jeju. If you love kpop music, you will love this place!!! I definitely wanna visit again, if I go to Jeju.

It smells so good as soon as you get off the car and pass the entrance. After a short walk, you get to the Forest.  It is also easily accessible for baby strollers as they put some straw mats alone the forest so the whole family can enjoy a wonderful walk in the forest.  Not sure if wheelchairs can roll easily on those mats though but I saw quite some baby strollers.We took a detour after Sangumburi crater (about 20 min away), and spent about an hour in the forest but didn't complete it. Then in another 20-30 min, we arrived at a Five Day Market, which is about 10 min from the Haeyeo (Women Divers) museum.So this was how we planned our route to and from the forest.

It rained almost nonstop on our trip to Jeju so we visited a lot of museums we probably would normally have not. The hologram concert is the major attraction in Play Kpop and it was good fun. The rest? Meh. The entry ticket is 15 000 won which is rather expensive since most museums on the island just cost a few thousand won. On top of that, a lot of the other attractions (like photo booths) cost extra. Kpop history was interesting enough, but most of the other stuff was quite boring.

It is worth the value to visit the Teddy Museum. There is a wide range of Teddy Bears on display. The History and Teddy Characters. Many photos opportunity. There is also an outdoor Teddy garden, a Elvis Teddy Stage performance. Of course, a Teddy Shop.

It is very interesting - the museum is right next to the house where he used to live. And there is a painting that paints the view from the museum looking down the port. it is called   The view of the port   I believe the city of Seogwipo has bought this painting a few years ago and placed it in this museum - this is my favorite. It is pretty expensive for the entrance fee, and we were disappointed as not so many bears to see. And the Elvis Presley cinema was closed too.Outside the museum there is a 9 meters bear. But yeah pretty much thats all.

It is one of many museums in Jeju, and it's dedicated to Teddy bears. It is full of its history with all the teddy bears from all over the world. All of the ancient teddy bears is well preserved but with relatively minimal background story. Some of the information are written only in Korean, so there isn't many interactive attraction here. There is also an open garden with a few sculptures on it, a Lotteria restaurant and of course the store. The merchandise there is quite expensive and we didn't buy anything. The entrance fee when we came there is 8000 won, a little bit expensive, but quite worth it.

It is located just beside O'Sulloc Tea Museum. To get there, just take bus no.755 from any bus stop bound for Pyonghwa-ro global education and alight at O'Sulloc Tea Museum station.They sell cosmetics, skin care products, stationaries, D.I.Y soap, etc..There are also cafe which sells bingsu, beverages and food. Tried the 珥덉퐫荑좏궎?먯씠?? (choco cookie shake), it costs 6000 won and tastes good but I think the portion is a little small (for me). Nice to visit if you are visiting O'Sulloc Tea Museum since it is just beside it. There is a big tea farm beside Innisfree Jejuhouse.. you can take some pics there, but it was raining when i visited the place so i didn't manage to take a lot of pictures.

It is definitely a park full of stones, but it is actually quite interesting.  There is also a museum in the park which is worth checking out.  It shows some of the history of the island and the different types of volcanic rocks that can be found on the island. If you aren't interested in parks or rocks this probably isn't a place you would enjoy, but my husband and I really enjoyed it.  Naturally shaped rock sculptures, carved rock sculptures, stacked rock sculptures, etc.

It is an interesting showcase of lifesize and all sizes of teddy bears being used to personify famous art pieces, fables, fairy tales and etc.  There are many interesting photo opportunities.  The Koreans are very creative in coming up with such a museum dedicated to teddy bear lovers, but I would not return a second time.

It is a teddy bear heaven. There are many cute teddy bears with different type and size. Every corner of the museum is a good spot for taking a picture :) The museum is quite large and the interior is good. At the end of your visit, you can buy some cute dolls on the merchandise shop, although mostly it is quite expensive. Overall it is a good place to visit, moreover for children.

It is a museum showing the history of Korea, the emotions and aesthetics of Koreans. Lee joong seop died at a young age and did not leave much work. However, the well-maintained birthplace, street and cafes and crowds around them show how this artist is popularly loved by Koreans.

It is a museum as well as an ecological park related to stone culture in the lives of Jeju people.  It is huge and you are required to walk a lot.  It is about 40-45 minutes drive either from Jeju Airport or Seogwipo area.  You need 1-2 hours to go around the complex and the museum.  Opening hours: 0900-1800 hrs.  Closed on first Monday of the month unless it is a holiday.  Entry fee: KRW 5,000.  It should be a MUST in your itinerary of Jeju Island.

It featured the women divers as the spirit of Jeju, displaying the culture and past of the people; clothes worn then, agricultural tools, even dishes and at one time, a wall with proverbs stemming from these women. It's a two floor museum only though, but holds alot of artifact

It costs 10.000 won to enter and without kids you are going to be done within half an hour but you'll have a big smile on your face. Teddybear Ghandi, Bear Elvis and more. Very funny. Is worth going if u have young kids and a husband/wife who enjoyed looking at vintage cars instead of young woman (:p). review: Interesting place... Love to see how they really appreciate haenyeos, as one of their mother culture... A unique and honourable profession for jeju women in the old days and even now... How women are very appreciated since born and high hopes for doing the profession as backbone of the jeju families..The museum really tells a lot about how the haenyeos lives and even their struggle in the war era... For those who loves visiting museums, its really recommended!
Interesting museum on teddy bears. Various sizes, in different clothings. If you are a fan of the korean drama   Gong  , then you should go. :)

Innisfree Jeju House is just next to O'Sulloc Tea Museum, so is great to visit both the places. Innisfree is just one floor in a glass house.Besides selling Innisfree products like facial care, there is also many other things to explore.There is a big space for soap making area, visitor can purchase a bag of soap making set at the counter, and do it at the available place. The staff will guide you on the soap making. A self making post card corner for visitor to bring back (free but with limited, per card per person).Nice cozy clean comfortable cafe. Don't forget to try the black pork hot dog. It is so delicious. I bought a soap making set for my son to enjoy the art work, while I enjoy my facial product shopping. My husband and mother where having a good time at the cafe.

Innisfree Jeju House can be got to by taking a bus to the O'Sulloc tea museum stop. The tea museum is a very short walk away from Innisfree Jeju House.The place is quiet and peaceful, save for the calming music they play and the chatter of tourists and other visitors, but that wasn't too bad when I was there. There's an area devoted to DIY lessons/sessions where one can try making their own soap. There's a few pretty exhibits where one can smell various scents or read a little about the Innisfree brand and its products. There's a store area, with a few products that are exclusive to Innisfree Jeju House. And there's a cafe with various light food, drink and dessert options.Outside, there are tables and benches that overlook a nice view of the tea plantation, which you can go and take pictures in. Rows upon rows of tea leaves and a few windmills. It's all very pretty and is probably the biggest selling point of the whole compound containing both Innisfree Jeju House and the nearby tea museum. It's really very pretty.I enjoyed my time there, but if Innisfree products are not for you, or if you're the thrill-seeking type, perhaps you should skip this place.

Innisfree is a well-known brand with numerous outlets throughout Korea and Asia. As it originated from Jeju, this is their main outlet in Korea. It was much smaller than expected, with only a single long building housing both the shop and cafe.The shop stocked quiet a good range of their toiletries and cosmetics, with an natural soap-making activity available. You can purchase a pack from the counter, choose the scent of soap you want, and there are stations with a screen to guide you through the soap-making process step-by-step. Shop staff are on hand for assistance as well. At the end of it, you can pack the soap into an eco-bag as a gift.The organic green cafe had ample seating and a good range of food, compared to the adjacent O Sulloc tea museum. Their drinks are served in funky bottles with interesting tastes, and make a pretty picture.If in the area, the soap-making is interesting and wouldn't take too long.

In short, I enjoyed the display of the teddy bear in this museum.  It comes with theme i.e. Snow White with 7 dwarfs, Titanic, Disney.   The museum also display famous people in Teddy i.e. Einstein, Michael Jackson.Worth visiting especially when traveling with kids.   If not mistaken, there are 2 teddy museums.   This one is the one located in front of Starbucks.*TK

I'm not a fan of teddy bears, so it just looks like teddy bears on display to me...not very museum-feel... thou some of the displays are really quite creative...

If your time in Jeju is limited, skip all those man made museums and put visiting Udo island as one of your priorities. If you have an international driving license, highly recommend to rent a scooter to tour the island, and don't forget to try the Hallasan Fried Rice.
If you watched Korean Drama   Dae Jang Geum   some scenes were taken here.  It speak volume of this museum.  The whole walk may take 2 hours or so if you read the description. Well recommended.

If you love Hello Kitty, I think you will really like it. That being said, though, I think it is better for adult fans than for kids. For the most part, it is a Hello Kitty museum with displays for looking at. There's not really much for kids to do, other than look. The cafe was good, and cute. The gift shop had some cool stuff I hadn't seen elsewhere, but it is pricey. All in all, I would say that I am really glad I saw it, because it was super cute, but it wouldn't warrant a return visit.

If you like Hello Kitty, this is an interesting place to go. a 2 storey building converted into wholesomeness of Kitty everywhere. The cafe is nice too - but you need to pay for entrance fee to the museum in order to get into it. The food is average, but presentation is what people are paying for. Definitely a nice place for tonnes of photo taking. It's suitable for any weather. I went when it was snowing outside - so it's nice and warm inside.

If you are women or man, either case you will be surprised and proud, to see the courage and dedication of Jeju women divers. This museum is dedicates to history of women divers and their success and spread worldwide.  Overall museum is average compared to other museum, but what it makes stand out is unique concept everything is build on. It is worth a trip to be fascinated by rare profession by women.

If you are planning to visit the Hello Kitty Island, beware: there is a specific audience that his place caters to; it is not recommended for everyone. Our tour group went here in lieu of the Trick Eye Museum.Little girls and Hello Kitty fans would love this place. Hello Kitty merchandise are displayed everywhere. There is also a room that narrates the history of how Sanrio characters came about.  There is a Hello Kitty Caf챕 at the 2nd floor. On the 3rd floor, there is an auditorium that plays a Hello Kitty-themed show. Outside is an open-air Hello Kitty-themed miniature garden maze. The view of the landscape from here is wonderful. For me, it was meh. I am not among those that this place was built for.On the plus side, there a postcards available at the souvenir shop, which you pass through as you exit the building. I also liked the stamping stations spread around the place, which are reminiscent of postmarks.

If you are not familiar with the Korean love of 'cute', you won't get what's going on at the Teddy Bear Museum. Don't expect a history of the teddy bear; expect teddy bears placed in historic events. It is cute. Kids love it. If you are searching for something serious, skip this one, but if you're looking for a bit of quirky fun that you will only find in Korea, check it out! *The gift shop is pricey.

If you are not a fan of BB, don't bother to go. Literally waste your entrance fee, if you want to get the gift, the gift shop is just rite at the entrance, no entrance fee requiredI think going to the GD Caf챕 is better than this KPop Museum. And the Teddy Bear museum next door worth 10 times more. I am not a huge fan of BB  but definitiely I know many KPOP stars.

If you are going with little kids, definitely go. But otherwise it's just OK though I would say worth a visit if you are bored. Pretty much all the information is in Korean, but then again doesn't take much to identify the teddy bear version of Steve Jobs or Albert Einstein ;) The place has two floors of teddy bears, and I must say after about 25 teddies they all start looking the same. This was close to our hotel and it was raining so we paid a visit. I would advise the museum to put more info in English as Jeju is becoming more internationlised in terms of tourists.

If you are an avid bear lover then this would interest you. This is a pretty informative museum where it shows how teddy bears in the past till where it is presently.However, adults wont probably enjoy it as much. The place is small and this attractive can be finished easily within 40 mins. Go only if you have time or when it rains

If you are a Hello Kitty lover and an adult, it will be nice to see all of the different Hello Kitty items, but it will also be pretty boring for you as well.  This museum is definitely geared towards kids, though I think that there could be more activities for them. The gift shop at the end of everything is quite nice but rather expensive.

I?m not a big fan of Kpop, but I do enjoy their music...and this Play Kpop Museum did impress me with their hologram concert by GDragon, photo session in holographic & can be downloaded into phone for free!!!!Definitely must go place in Jeju for Kpop fans!

i wouldnt have rate poor until i went to   Teseum  . things in teddy bear museum all mini sizes in a box well protected. they have 3 floors, and only the ground floor have some bears for picture. For me kind of bored compare to Teseum, Teseum you can touch and picture closely with those teddys. I would say that this waterfall is higher and have better view than cheonjaeyeon waterfall althought cheonjaeyeon waterfall is close by from teddy bear museum, we take taxi in the afternoon from teddy bear museum to jeongbang waterfall and it cost around 25-30 usd, and the street is almost empty. The road down to the waterfall is much nearer and easier than cheonjaeyeon waterfall. When you take pictures, off course you would like to get closer to the waterfall, but be carefull of the rocks, they were quite slippery, we spend an hour to take pictures and sitting in the rock. The admission fee on nov 2014 is still 2,000 won per adult about $2. On winter it opens from 08.00 to 18.00

I would recommend that you read the book ?The Island of Sea Women? by Lisa See before visiting the museum. I felt an emotional connection to the museum, the observatory and the grounds around the area, primarily because I had some background knowledge. The museum is well laid out and interesting. Do take the time to watch the video on the main floor before going through the exhibits. If you are there around 10:00 a.m. or 1:00 p.m. you may be able to see the women divers from the observatory on the 3rd floor.  Getting there: we were on a cruise ship and took a taxi from the ship terminal in Jeju City. It took about an hour and was a very scenic drive.  Our taxi driver gave us an hour to tour the museum and grounds and then dropped us off by the main market area in downtown Jeju City. It was under $100 for four people in a taxi.

I went to this museum just because a friend has suggested. Despite I am not a big fan of teddy bears this museum is really amazing! You will see the major events from the world history, famous singers and artists, as well as some scientists! I better don't tell everything not to ruin the surprise! There happens an Elvis Show at every hour or so. If you have time, definitely give it a go.

I went here on Friday 31.05.2019. The front desk staff were very helpful, the museum is really easy as there's arrows on the floor directing you where to go. There is loads of information in English, it's easy to follow and very informative. The island has some really sad history, for anyone interested in history, and the impact of splitting Korea, this is a must do. The information does not make easy reading, but you will never forget this story, and it's an important one to remember. The gardens have lots of memorials, and outside is a nice space.It's not a pop in memorial/museum, it's bigger than expected. I'd recommend 2.5 hours to do the museum and outside. Unfortunately I had to rush as I got there late in the day and wish I'd had more time, but I'm pleased I went, and got most stuff done. It's accessible by bus. Horses are a big part of the Jeju culture  and Jeju Horse Park is a pretty cool place. Its museum includes many photographs  artifacts and a video telling the story of the Jeju   ma    or pony  which is descended from the ponies brought to the island by Mongol invaders. The island was considered a good place to raise horses  and the Mongols used it as such. At the park  you can also ride the horses. There is a great giftshop with lots of local handmade items. Children or even adults can make related crafts in an activity room. The building itself is round like a ger  the traditional nomadic tents used by the Mongols. The top deck includes a fabulous 360-degree view of the   oreums   (small cinder-cones or parasitic volcanoes) that literally ring the area of the park. Inside the railing  an artist has painted the oreums  along with their names. So  you can know exactly which oreums you are viewing. There are also some actual Mongolian gers (also known as yurts in other nomadic cultures). I believe tourists can actually spend the night in one of the gers. One thing to consider: If you want to visit  you must either have your own transportation or go with someone who does. It's kind of far from anywhere  and bus service may not operate in that area. Likewise  taxis don't just happen by. But  it is a beautiful area and interesting for the entire family We visited in the spring  and there were also lots of colorful wildflowers. Plan to spend a few hours there  especially if you will ride the horses.

Having been to the sex museum in China near Shanghai I was somewhat disappointed by this one mostly because I found it more biased and sexist than I would expect a museum to be.  It started out good with a fairly progressive and balanced presentation albeit almost entirely in Korean talking about sexual freedom and equity.  But the vast majority of displays were very...vanilla and heteronormative.  There was very little depiction or discussion of anything besides sex between one man and one woman.  Furthermore the depictions of women and closeups of vaginas far outnumbered depictions of the male form with many showing women in very submissive poses such as on all fours and wearing a leash!  There were even a few instances where the English text accompanying a display used rather judgmental language describing certain sex acts as   abnormal   or   depraved   which I found very shocking.  I think it's great that Korea which is typically very conservative has a museum about sex at all.  But to a more sexually progressive westerner it will probably seem outdated and disappointing.  It's also hard to get to if you don't have a car.

Half science, half art. A museum dedicated to the formation of the igneous rocks in the area, tectonic plate movements, volcanic eruptions, formation of lava tubes, and various methods of making craters. Extremely interesting!Then rock art. Lots of interesting rocks from around the island, arranged in a way that makes them just so fascinating.Budget a couple of hours here for a leisurely walk through these sections. Haenyeo Museum which is dedicated to the female sea divers of Jeju was an excellent museum about the matriarchal culture of Jeju that used to exist.  Despite the large building that houses the museum, there isn?t that much on display.  However, visitors get an idea about the amount of responsibilities the typical haenyeos had, basically raising their children (some dived until the day before their children were born) and running the family finances while going out diving everyday.  The donated artifacts on displays were interesting but the information about the lives of haenyeos was fascinating.

Haenyeo literally means, 'Women of the Sea' and this museum pays tribute to the historical significance of this dying profession.  Solely carried on the backs of women on this island, these incredible ladies have carried their over 400 year old craft into the 21st century where instrumentally built the economic foundation for many of the Jeju natives.  Mothers who passed on their skills and knowledge of the sea to their daughters ensured that this lineage would endure the centuries of time.  However, as the world faces rapid changes and economies - the Haenyeo divers are slowly becoming a ghost of the past.  Recently recognized as an UNESCO intangible Cultural Heritage in 2016, tremendous efforts are in place to preserve this historical tradition.  A bonus of a visit to this museum is a trip to Sunrise Peak where there is a traditional Haenyeo performance.  (admission fee required)However - enroute to Sunrise Peak is the opportunity to meet a handful of Haenyeo divers!  What a thrill to visit with them in their modern 'bulteok' - warming huts.  Of all the sights of Jeju - this is perhaps the one that represents the very backbone of this amazing culture!This is definitely a 'must see'

review: From Segiowipo (Jangung rotary) the park can be reached in a little over an hour on the 231 bus which will drop you at the front of the park.   Fare 1200krw. Park admission is 5000krw. I spent 2.5 hrs here doing course 1 and 2. I think you might enjoy it more if you were an artist but I liked it all the same. The stone museum, which is the first stop on course 1 tells you all about how lava rocks are formed, their different types and would be a geologists dream. After that you'll walk around the park and see the different stone sculptures, most of which are natural,  some manmade. There are also a couple of replica traditional jeju houses and local pottery too. The Obaek gallery has some driftwood on display along with 1 hall of art but it is mostly empty. I thought there would be more info on the local traditions and how they lived but the park is still a work in progress. Its not due for completion until 2020. Rug up because it seems to be colder here than other areas of the island and you will be outside most of your visit. Recommend you go on a sunny day as this area gets very heavy fog too.

After that you follow the path around the exhibits until you get to the other end.In this mainly outdoor museum, there are glass plants, flowers, and an eclectic collection of glass made curiosities that make a very pleasant way to spend a couple of hours. There is a small cafe in the middle of the exhibition, and the gift shop just before you exit. The bathrooms are at the entrance exit, so go before you start!

review: Built on a reclaimed land-fill site, this vast area of pathways, statues, displays, museums and traditional villages is very worth a visit if on Jeju. From the impressive stone structures and flat basalt 'floor' at the entrance of the park, I was blown away by the vast array of statues that are displayed, explained and on show in this area. There is ample car parking that is only a short walk form the entry way. A small fee is required and then you are free to wander the area that included a massive and spectacular 2 store (below ground) museum that outlines the geographic development of Jeju along with many interactive displays, a short film with subtitles, examples and galleries of 'stone art'. A gift shop of course, provided a range of traditional and specific items and there are amenities spread throughout the part. Water features, a traditional village, an art gallery and a vast array of stone sculpture will give you hours of things to view and read as you wander through the park In my humble opinion, not to be missed!!!

The spacious surrounding area is a nice spot to chill after checking out the art if the weather is nice and despite the steep admission, it was still a worthwhile stop.

Back in the days of yore --  how far back, no one can be certain --  three demigods came forth from three holes in the ground located near the northern coast of an island to the south of Korea.  These three demigods lived as hunter-gatherers until a ship arrived bearing three princesses, domesticated farm animals and seeds for growing grain. The princesses married with the demigods, and the Tamna Kingdom was born. Today, we know Tamna, which ended in 1404 with the coming of the Joseon Kings -- Korea's last imperial dynasty -- as Jejudo or Jeju Island.  We know that beloved and mystical site as Samseonghyeol (  sam   means three in Korean). It is a special place and, particularly for history buffs, a   must-see   in Jeju.  The holes, which likely were once active thermal vents on this volcanic isle, are surrounded by a protective Stonehenge-like ring and a mini-forest/park of lush and majestic, mature trees and flowers.  It is quite pleasant, and on a warm summer's day, a cool respite from the city that has grown around it.  There's a small museum showing a film about the founding of Tamna.  The film is in Korean, but if you look at the exhibits there before watching the film, you will understand it much better.  It is not readily possible to actually photograph the holes unless you have a ladder, a drone, a long selfie stick or happen to be about 8 feet tall...this would be my one disappointment about the site.  But there is an official photo mounted nearby.  If you have the time, plan to spend 1-1.5 hours there, to take in the walking trails, museum, movie and various historic buildings.  You will also be greeted by some of the original 18th century dolhareubangs (protective   stone grandfathers  ) remaining on the island.  It's a good outing for singles, couples, friends and families.  Even young children can enjoy the birds, flowers, stones and many benches located throughout the park.  Admission is quite nominal...2,500 KRW adults, 1,700 teens; 1,000 children 7-12.

Is cute that we walked the 30 steps from Osulloc to Innisfree we see a sign that there are snakes... we would think with the amount of crowd and noise, the snakes would have been gone. At first  we thought this would just be a display of various seashells from around the world. But it was so much more than that! Just amazing and so artistic. This is more like a gallery of seashell and bronze art than a typical   museum  . The artist has a brilliant eye for unique creations with seashells  making some of the installations really come to life. The staff were friendly and there is something to see at every turn (even the bathrooms!). Adult entrance fee: 6 000 won (approx. $5) and well worth it. You will not be disappointed with this museum! A wonderful surprise on our rainy day of touring.

At ARARIO MUSEUM TAPDONG CINEMA unique art works of various artists (including Ugo Rondinone Kohei Nawa Andy Warhol and more) will be displayed all throughout the 1st to 5th floor. Super-sized arts which requires complicated installation such as   Hero No.2   by Zhang Huan and   What does the vessel contain that the river does not know   by Subodh Gupta will be premiered in Korea for the first time. In addition display of 4 large scale paintings by German Neo-expressionist Sigmar Polke will also contribute to create an overwhelming ambiance at the museum.

After hiking up some trails on Hallasan, we decided look at the Manjang Cave. Located on the north east of the island, one should know that it will take driving or riding a bus to get there.  We ended up there around dusk, and it was sort of a break from the winter wind.  We were lucky because during the week between Christmas and New Years, the Cave admission was free of charge.  Nothing is very difficult about managing the cave. If you can walk and handle a few stairs at the entrance you can handle this attraction.  Although it was dark outside and underground, the cave was lighted for foot traffic and more than manageable.  Lighting and some signs help highlight the different formations in the cave (i.e. stalagmites, lava lines, and rock formations).  The 'stone turtle' formation is supposed to be shaped like the island itself. I didn't see it, but some have a better imagination than I do.In any case, this attraction is one of the natural monuments of not only Jeju, but Korea and  one of the longest of its kind.  If you're into geology and cultural interest, you cannot miss the UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site and volcano museum that is Manjang. Geoparks, Geosightseeing, hiking recovery day

According to legend, Samseung Hyeol is where three demigods emerged from the ground to become the founding fathers of Tamna. This is the basis of the legend, and it is well-known to most Jeju residents. The Tamna kingdom ended in 1404 when it was absorbed by the newly founded Joseon Dynasty. While this rather small shrine is undobutably not THAT ancient, it is a unique site. There is a small museum which shows a video that tells the full legend of Tamna's founding.One plus of this site is the original Dol hareubangs (Grandfather statues) located at the entrance. These statues are unique to Jeju island, with a similar variation in Korea's southern coast. There are only 48 remaining Dol hareubangs left on Jeju-do. These   grandfather   statues were made between 1763-65.

A quiet valley in an evergreen forest, the place is almost free of foreign tourists and allows one to capture the most tranquil moments of nature. Where cliffs and reflective pools of crystal clear water meet, lined by stones, guarded by trees and filled with crisp air. The sunlight peeking through the trees permeates a serene and mesmerising ambience in the valley. Look out for the stone wells and Rock Shade Residence along the way. The Rock Shade Residence formed from volcanic lava were used by ancient inhabitants of Jeju Island as shelter. It is said that Andeok Valley has water flowing all seasons long.  With such charming beauty, its no wonder Chusa Kim Jeong-hee, a renowned Joseon-era scholar, used to visit here for contemplation and perhaps, inspiration. Spring and fall would be great for light trekking while the cool forest provides the ultimate summer shade. Nearby attractions: O'Sulloc Tea Museum, Camellia Hill and Jungmun Resorts.Trivia: Andeok Valley was also the filming location of historical K-drama   Slave Hunter   (Chuno in Korean)
